stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic. He has heterozygous polycystic kidney disease with a creatinine of 190 μmol/l and evidence of renal and hepatic cysts. He wants to start a family. What is the chance of his children having the disease?
explanation:
50%
Adult-onset polycystic kidney disease has an autosomal dominant inheritance, hence many clinicians also think of ADPKD as autosomal dominant or adult polycystic kidney disease. Given that the man in the present case will carry one gene for the disorder, he has a 50% chance of passing it to any offspring. Any children who inherit their father’s ‘faulty gene’ will develop the condition. Around 85–90% of patients with ADPKD carry a mutation on chromosome 16, the remainder carrying a mutation on chromosome 4. Significant kidney disease usually develops after the 4 th decade of life

100%
100% is incorrect. 100% only fits with the inheritance rate for an autosomal dominant condition where the affected individual is homozygous.

33%
33% is incorrect. This doesn’t fit with the inheritance pattern for an autosomal dominant or recessive condition.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the renal clinic for review. He has been taking risperidone for some months after an acute presentation with symptoms of schizophrenia. His GP is concerned that he may have urinary dysfunction. On examination his BP is 120/70 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. Which of the following is risperidone associated with?
explanation:
Pollakiuria
Risperidone is associated with increased daytime urinary frequency, a condition known as pollakiuria. It is also associated with enuresis, urinary retention, urinary incontinence and dysuria.

Alkaptonuria
Alkaptonuria is incorrect. Alkaptonuria is black urine associated with abnormal phenylalanine and tyrosine metabolism. This is a rare inherited genetic disease caused by a deficiency of homogentisate 1,2- dioxygenase.

Haematuria
Haematuria is incorrect and is associated with nephritis due to damage to the glomeruli and urinary tract infections. It is not associated with risperidone use.

stem: You are asked to review an 82-year-old man on the orthopaedic ward, 1 week after surgical repair of a neck of femur fracture. He has heart failure, for which he has been prescribed furosemide, but no other significant past medical history. Post-operative recovery has been complicated by an episode of urosepsis, treated with gentamicin. The surgeons notice that his serum creatinine is 350 μmol/l. On examination the patient is euvolaemic, has a BP of 134/77mmHg and is afebrile. Urinary sodium is 48 mmol/l and urinary osmolality is 320 mosmol/kg. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
Diagnosis of ATN, as opposed to prerenal acute kidney injury, is made on the basis of a urinary sodium concentration of > 40 mmol/l and a urinary osmolality of < 350 mosmol/kg. The patient has received IV gentamicin, of which his continued furosemide is likely to have increased the plasma concentration and led to ATN. Other agents that may result in ATN include amphotericin B and heavy metal poisoning. Oliguria during the initial stages of ATN is followed by polyuria, and even after a relatively minor insult, recovery may take up to 6 weeks.

Acute septicaemia
Acute septicaemia is incorrect. A history of urinary tract infection has been given, but this has been treated and no clinical indicators are described to suggest acute sepsis.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with renal colic. She has recently moved to the area and reports having recurrent urinary tract infections in the past, but nil else of note. She has haematuria on urine testing but no evidence of acute infection. Excretion urography demonstrates small calculi in the papillary zones with an increase in radiodensity after contrast medium is injected. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Medullary sponge kidney
Medullary sponge kidney has a prevalence of 1:1000 to 1:5000. The condition is characterised by dilatation of the collecting ducts in the papillae, with accompanying cystic changes. One or both, or part of one kidney, may be affected. In severe cases the medullary area has a sponge-like appearance. Cyst formation is commonly associated with the development of small calculi within the cyst. Diagnosis is made via excretion urography, showing small calculi in the papillary zones with surrounding increased density; this is because the dilated collecting ducts are filled with contrast medium. About 20% of patients have associated hypercalciuria or renal tubular acidosis. Skeletal hemihypertrophy may be associated. Kidney disease is highly unusual.

Adult polycystic kidney disease
Adult polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. This often presents in young adult life with hypertension. There would be multiple cysts in both kidneys rather than the excretion urography signs as mentioned in this case.

stem: The pathogenesis of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is unknown. Increased glomerular permeability and injury to podocytes have been postulated as possible aetiological factors. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of primary FSGS?
options: It commonly occurs following HIV infection
It is a known cause of nephrotic syndrome
Most patients gain full remission with corticosteroid therapy
Kidney disease commonly occurs within 2 years of the onset of proteinuria
Renal histology is typically normal and may be confused with minimal change nephropathy (MCN)
explanation:
It is a known cause of nephrotic syndrome
FSGS is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults after membranous glomerulonephritis (GN), and also accounts for 7–10% of paediatric nephrotic syndrome.

It commonly occurs following HIV infection
It commonly occurs following HIV infection is incorrect. AIDS-associated nephropathy can include a focal segmental glomerulosclerosis pattern, but this is not typical. This would be classified as secondary FSGS.

Most patients gain full remission with corticosteroid therapy
It responds well to corticosteroid therapy is incorrect. After treatment with corticosteroids, 20–50% of primary FSGS patients show complete remission. The mainstay of management in secondary FSGS is treatment of the underlying cause.

stem: A 25-year-old woman who is 10 weeks’ pregnant attends for a routine check-up. She has no symptoms of urinary tract infection. Routine urine dipstick reveals blood and protein, and urine culture is positive for Escherichia coli. Which one of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Do nothing and review at her next antenatal visit
Repeat urine sample and treat if positive
explanation:
Treat with nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin and cephalexin are both potential first-line options for treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. Nitrofurantoin should be avoided if the patient is at term and if the GFR is below 45 ml/min. Both should be given over a 7-day course.

Do nothing and review at her next antenatal visit
Do nothing and review at her next antenatal visit is incorrect. As mentioned above, studies have suggested that asymptomatic bacteriuria in the presence of previous renal disease may predispose to the pre-eclampsia anaemia of pregnancy and small or premature babies. It would be appropriate to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria

Treat with ciprofloxacin
Treat with ciprofloxacin is incorrect. It is important to submit a repeat urine sample. Most studies have found no adverse effects on mother or foetus when taking ciprofloxacin although it is contra-indicated because of increased risk of tendon rupture seen in juvenile animal studies.

stem: A 51-year-old patient attends for his regular haemodialysis session in hospital. By what mechanism does solute removal occur on haemodialysis?
explanation:
Diffusion
In haemodialysis, the patient’s blood is separated from the dialysate by a semi-permeable membrane. Solutes diffuse down their respective concentration gradients through the semi-permeable membrane from one compartment to another, and this helps achieve electrolyte correction and optimal acid–base balance for patients on haemodialysis.

Conduction
Conduction is incorrect. The process in haemodialysis is diffusion.

Convection
Convection is incorrect. This is the main process of solute removal during haemofiltration.

Osmosis
Osmosis is incorrect. The process in haemodialysis is diffusion.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with visible haematuria and acute-onset, severe right loin pain radiating to the groin. She is restless and unable to find a comfortable position that would ease the pain. On examination her abdomen is soft with tenderness over the right lumbar region; she is afebrile. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 67 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 12 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Urinary tract calculi
The patient presents with acute renal colic, which can be very severe. The pain that radiates from the loin to the groin represents the stone moving towards the vesicoureteric junction.

stem: A 26-year-old man attends for his regular hospital haemodialysis session, which he undergoes through a tunnelled dialysis catheter. While on dialysis, he becomes pyrexial and develops rigor. What is the most likely infective agent?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
A patient with a tunnelled haemodialysis catheter who develops a fever on dialysis should be considered to have line-related infection until proven otherwise. Blood cultures should be taken from the line and peripherally, and if the same organism is growing from them both, this strongly suggests the line is the source of the infection. The most common organisms for line-related sepsis are gram-positive bacteria, namely S. aureus.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is incorrect. E. coli would be a differential in this scenario, however gram-positive organisms are the most common cause of catheter-related infections, with both coagulase negative staphylococcus and S. aureus accounting for the majority of cases.

stem: A patient has been diagnosed with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Which of the following organs will most likely have additional cysts?
explanation:
Liver
Hepatic cysts occur in 40–90% (very rarely causing liver failure) of patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The gene responsible has been found to be localised to the short arm of chromosome 16 in the majority of cases, but approximately 10% have abnormalities in chromosome 4. The renal cysts form along the entire length of the renal tubule; however, in the less common recessive form, the cysts occur primarily in the collecting ducts. NB Cerebral aneurysms occur in 10–20% of patients.

Bone
Bone is incorrect. Bone cysts are rare.

Heart
Heart is incorrect. Cardiac cysts do not occur, but there is an association between ADPKD and both mitral valve prolapse and aortic incompetence.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Renal Clinic with a deterioration in her creatinine from 185 to 270 micromol/l over the past 2 weeks. She is 3 months post renal transplant from a CMV negative donor and is taking a Ciclosporin based immunosuppression regime. On further questioning she describes fevers over the past 3 weeks and a dull ache over the transplanted kidney. On examination her BP is 155/90 mmHg; pulse is 82 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft although she is tender to light palpation over the surface of the transplanted kidney. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 108 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 270 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 6.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Ciclosporin 285 ng/ml <300 ng/ml Which of the following is the most likely cause of her deterioration in renal function?
explanation:
T-cell mediated alloimmune reaction
This patient is suffering from acute rejection, which is thought to be primarily cell mediated (via a T-cell response). Anti-T-cell monoclonal antibodies and corticosteroids are both potential treatment interventions.

B-cell mediated alloimmune reaction
B-cell mediated alloimmune reaction is incorrect. B-cell mediated alloimmune reaction is caused by the recipient's B-lymphocytes producing alloantibodies against donor MHC class I and II molecules. These alloantibodies can activate complement leading to target cell lysis. Alternatively, donor cells are coated with alloantibodies that initiate phagocytosis through Fc receptors of mononuclear leukocytes. This type of humoral rejection produces hyperacute, accelerated and chronic rejection.

Ciclosporin toxicity
Ciclosporin toxicity is incorrect. Ciclosporin levels are within the treatment range; there is therefore neither toxicity, nor a need to increase the dose.

CMV infection
CMV infection is incorrect. CMV infection occurs earlier and is less likely given that the donor was CMV negative. Intrinsic immunity is responsible for hyperacute rejection.

Macrophage mediated alloimmune reaction
Macrophage mediated alloimmune reaction is incorrect. Macrophage mediated alloimmune reaction is important in both cellular and anti-body mediated acute allograft rejection. It has a part to play in rejection, but is not the key driving force in this case.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with an acute hot and painful right knee. He has a history of alcohol excess. On examination he is apyrexial and blood pressure was normal. Urine dipstick shows +2 blood; blood tests show a raised urea and creatinine level, with normal white blood cell count. Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely to explain the renal impairment in this clinical scenario?
explanation:
Urolithiasis
This man has gouty arthritis, as suggested by the alcohol history and inflammatory joint. A common cause of renal impairment in a patient with gouty arthritis is uric acid stones, which account for 3–5% of all stones in patients in the UK; but in Israel the proportion may be as high as 40%.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy may present with haematuria and renal impairment. This is the most common primary glomerulonephritis in the world. The condition may be associated with Henoch– Schönlein purpura, gut disorders (alcoholic cirrhosis, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease), and skin and joint disorders such as dermatitis and psoriasis. Gouty arthritis is not associated with this condition.

stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman presents to the Maternity Clinic for a routine 12-week appointment. She has been well so far, and has no past medical history of note. Her blood pressure (BP) is 105/70 mmHg and she is apyrexial. The mid-stream urine (MSU) reveals bacteriuria, although she has had no symptoms of urinary tract infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
7-day course of nitrofurantoin
7-day course of nitrofurantoin is the correct answer. Nitrofurantoin is the recommended first-line agent for confirmed urinary tract infection (UTI) and for asymptomatic bacteriuria according to NICE guidelines, Amoxicillin can be used where the bacteria are known to be sensitive to it.

7-day course of amoxicillin
7-day course of amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin is safe to be given in pregnancy; however, it is recommended that it only be used when sensitivities are available.

7-day course of levofloxacin
7-day course of levofloxacin is incorrect. Levofloxacin is not recommended, as fluoroquinolones are contra- indicated in pregnancy.

stem: A 23-year-old man is referred to renal physicians with non-visible haematuria. He has also had two episodes of frank haematuria in the past year that occurred after upper respiratory tract infections. On examination, his blood pressure is 144/92 mmHg, and cardiovascular and respiratory examination is unremarkable. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal value Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine Blood +, protein + Renal biopsy Suggestive of IgA nephropathy Which of the following is most closely associated with a poor prognosis?
options: Number of episodes of visual haematuria
explanation:
Hypertension
Hypertension is most strongly associated with deteriorating renal function in patients with immunoglobulin A nephropathy. Patients should be managed aggressively with respect to blood pressure control, with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors forming the backbone of therapy. Where creatinine is deteriorating, there is limited evidence for immunosuppression with a combination of corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. In the majority of patients, the disease follows a benign course, but some elements of chronic kidney disease may develop in up to around 30% of patients.

stem: A 62-year-old male smoker presents to the renal clinic for review. He has had increasingly severe peripheral oedema over the past 4 months. His GP has checked a 24-h urinary protein excretion and found it to be 5 g/24 h. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 145/82 mmHg, and his pulse is 80/min and regular. There are coarse crackles consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 124 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 133 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 23 g/l 35–55 g/l Chest radiograph Left upper lobe tumour He undergoes an upper lobectomy for treatment of the lung tumour and his proteinuria improves. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his nephrotic syndrome?
explanation:
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is recognised to occur in association with bronchial carcinoma. Case series also suggest that it can regress once the underlying carcinoma is removed. Apart from bronchial carcinoma, membranous nephritis is described in conjunction with a number of other tumours, including prostate, stomach and colon cancer. You may like to refer to an article by Lefaucheur et al. (2006) Membranous nephropathy and cancer: Epidemiologic evidence and determinants of high-risk cancer association. Kidney International. 70;8:1510–1517.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy is more likely to occur in smokers and is the most common cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide. However, it will present with haematuria and is not associated with malignancy.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is characterised by deposits in the glomerulus and basement membrane thickening. It accounts for approximately 4% of primary renal causes of nephritic syndrome in children and 7% in adults. It does not present with nephrotic range protenuria only, as in this case, as there would be haematuria as well.

Minimal change glomerulonephritis
Minimal change glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Minimal change glomerulonephritis is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It has a good prognosis in young children with response to steroids. It is not associated with malignancy.

Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis would present with blood and protein in the urine. There is no history suggestive of streptococcal infection in this case.

stem: An 18-year-old woman who has recently been referred to the ENT surgeons for deafness comes to the clinic complaining of pink stained urine, and she is concerned that she is losing blood into her urine. She has recently suffered a respiratory tract infection. Apparently her brother who is 21 has more serious hearing loss and has kidney trouble. On examination her BP is 135/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. General physical is unremarkable, but urine testing reveals 2+ of blood and 1+ of protein. Her creatinine is 113 micromol/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Alport’s syndrome
The big clue here is the familial nature of the symptoms of deafness and the fact that her brother is more severely affected. This suggests an x-linked dominant disorder, of which Alport syndrome is one of the few. It leads to sensorineural deafness and glomerulonephritis. Control of BP is important in minimising renal progression, with ACE inhibitors being the drugs of choice.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis in the world. It presents with haematuria in the second and third decades. Although idiopathic, IgA nephropathy is often found in association with Henoch–Schönlein purpura, gut disorders (alcoholic cirrhosis, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease) and skin and joint disorders. It is not inherited.

stem: A 45 year old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a large haemoptysis of 120ml. She has suffered from increasing nausea and lethargy over the past 2-3 weeks. On examination her BP is 155/90, pulse is 88 and regular. She has bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 98 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 271 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 359 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood ++ protein ++ Anti-GBM antibody Positive Chest X-Ray Patchy shadowing throughout both lung fields Which of the following HLA types is most commonly associated with her underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
HLA DRB1*15:01
Goodpasture’s syndrome is a disease of young males (6:1 male to female ratio). It is characterised by a triad of pulmonary haemorrhage, glomerulonephritis and production of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM) and there is a characteristic, continuous, linear pattern of IgG deposition along the capillary wall. An HLA-DRB1*15:01-restricted T cell epitope is recognised to play an important role in injury in anti-GBM associated glomerulonephritis.

HLA B8
HLA B8 is incorrect. HLA-B8 is found with increased frequency in European populations of northern Europe and Scandinavia, but is less associated with Goodpasture syndrome than B15, but is seen in some patients with severe disease.

HLA B27
HLA B27 is incorrect. HLA B27 is associated with increased risk of inflammatory bowel disease, reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.

HLA Cw6
HLA Cw6 is incorrect. HLA Cw6 positivity is associated with significantly increased risk of the development of psoriasis.

HLA B*57:01
HLA B*57:01 is incorrect. Positivity for B57:01 is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to the clinic with haemoptysis. Her GP has also noticed a significant rise in her creatinine from 110 μmol/l measured 3 months earlier, to 187 μmol/l measured in the last week. Past history of note includes a reconstruction for collapse of the nasal bridge. On examination her BP is 180/105 mmHg with pulse is 90/min and regular. Further blood testing carried out by the GP before her consultation reveals that she is cANCA positive. Which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
options: Necrotising glomerulonephritis without complement or immunoglobulin deposition
Thickened capillary walls with IgG deposition
explanation:
Necrotising glomerulonephritis without complement or immunoglobulin deposition
The clinical scenario fits best with a diagnosis of GPA, and this is the typical histological picture. Complement deposition is seen in SLE, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in diabetes mellitus, and thickened capillary walls with IgG deposition in membranous glomerulonephritis. Severe IgA nephropathy may be associated with necrotising renal disease, although this histological picture is of course not seen in the majority of patients.

Necrotising glomerulonephritis with IgA deposition
Necrotising glomerulonephritis with IgA deposition is incorrect. IgA nephropathy will produce this finding on renal biopsy. This condition will present with painless haematuria, and is the commonest cause worldwide of nephritic syndrome.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. A renal biopsy shows granulomas. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
GPA has hallmark features of necrotising granulomas and pauci-immune vasculitis in small- and medium-sized blood vessels. Typically, it presents with deteriorating renal function that progresses to kidney disease within 3 months (ie as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis), although a few patients have disease that is more indolent. Proteinuria (typically 2 to 3 g/24 h, but occasionally in the nephrotic range) and non-visible haematuria provide clinical evidence of glomerulonephritis, as does urine microscopy that reveals granular and red cell casts. There may be granulomas found in other organs, such as the lungs.

Hepatitis C infection
Hepatitis C infection is incorrect. Hepatitis C infection may be associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia, which is the principal cause of type 1 mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis. Renal biopsy will reveal cryoglobulins deposited in medium and small vessels in the glomeruli, fixing complement and causing inflammation.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the clinic after referral from his GP with haematuria which he first noticed 2-3 weeks ago. On reflection a screening urine specimen taken 3 months earlier at the orthopaedic clinic was positive for blood and negative for protein. He has a history of hypertension controlled with amlodipine but is on no other medications. On examination his BP is 145/80 mmHg, otherwise clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 342 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 149 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 59 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Urine blood +++, protein – Renal Ultrasound unremarkable Abdominal x-ray normal Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Cystoscopy and CTU
The isolated haematuria fits closely with a possible diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. For this reason we should aim to rule this out as early as possible. To do that the gold standard investigation plan is cystoscopy and CTU.

ANCA
ANCA is incorrect. The absence of proteinuria counts against vasculitis as the underlying cause of his symptoms.

Renal biopsy
Renal biopsy is incorrect. Renal biopsy carries with it a not insignificant risk of morbidity, and would only be considered if other investigations were negative.

Prostatic biopsy
Prostatic biopsy is incorrect. The absence of systems of prostatism counts more towards bladder rather than prostatic carcinoma.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred to the Renal Clinic with refractory hypertension on three oral agents. His BP is 155/95 mmHg, and he has haematuria (+++ on dipstick testing) and proteinuria (+ on dipstick testing). There is no significant past medical history apart from hypertension, and he is a life-long non-smoker. A recent creatinine is 155 micromol/l, up from 105 micromol/l some 12 months earlier. Where in the urinary system is the most likely underlying pathology?
explanation:
Glomeruli
This man has difficult to control hypertension, and the presence of a protein leak as well as haematuria raises the possibility of glomerulonephritis. Renal tract USS accompanied by autoimmune profiling, +/- progression to renal biopsy would be the next logical steps in evaluation of underlying pathology.

Bladder
Bladder is incorrect. Transitional carcinoma of the bladder is associated with micro or macroscopic haematuria, although proteinuria is usually absent.

Renal tubules
Renal tubules is incorrect. Tubular dysfunction / acute tubular necrosis is associated with the presence of casts within the urine. Frequently there is proteinuria or bland urine, there is typically no haematuria with tubular dysfunction.

stem: An 18-year-old student presents to her GP with a maculopapular rash which appeared initially on her forehead, spreading to her head and neck and then to the rest of her upper body. She was born abroad and had not been up to date with her childhood immunisations. Her GP thinks he can see Koplik’s spots on examination. Urine testing reveals proteinuria and haematuria, with no bacterial growth on culture. Which one of the following is a renal biopsy most likely to show?
explanation:
Type 2 mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis (MCGN)
Type 2 mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis (MCGN) 2 may be either idiopathic or occur after measles infection, as in this case. Remember that the terminology around membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is interchangeable. It is characterised by mesangial cell proliferation with electron-dense, linear intramembranous deposits that stain positive for C3. Partial lipodystrophy may be seen coexisting with this condition.

Crescentic glomerulonephritis
Crescentic glomerulonephritis is incorrect. This is glomerular disease that has extensive crescents (usually >50%) in the renal biopsy. There is rapid decline in renal function (usually a 50% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate within 3 months). Causes of crescentic glomerulonephritis include anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, immune complex-mediated disease, pauci-immune vasculitis and ANCA- negative pauci-immune renal vasculitis. It is not associated with measles.

stem: A 62-year-old man is noted to have a rising creatinine level 2 days after undergoing angiography. He feels increasingly nauseous and has developed hypertension with increasing shortness of breath. On examination his BP is 155/90 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular, and there are bilateral basal crackles consistent with pulmonary oedema. You suspect he may have cholesterol emboli. Which of the following features would be most commonly seen?
explanation:
Eosinophilia
Leucocytosis is usual with eosinophilia in 80% of patients with cholesterol emboli. Urine microscopy shows hyaline casts and eosinophils. The eosinophilia is thought to represent a foreign body-type response to cholesterol deposition. Inflammatory markers are raised, and complement may be low, but low complement does not occur as frequently as eosinophilia. No universally agreed management plan exists; patients are offered supportive therapy, but progression to chronic kidney disease is common and mortality is approximately 15%.

Low C3 and C4
Low C3 and C4 is incorrect. Low C3 and low C4 may be seen in septic emboli, i.e. from infective endocarditis, but not cholesterol emboli.

stem: A 72-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (CKD) (eGFR 32ml/min/1.73m 2) presents to radiology for elective peripheral CT angiography. He has had a mild episode of gastroenteritis but is keen to go ahead with the investigation. He is discharged immediately after but presents to the Emergency Department 2 days later feeling generally unwell. His serum creatinine level is 385 μmol/l; haemoglobin is 135 g/l and platelets are 198 × 10 9/l. He has no proteinuria and +1 haematuria on dipstick. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Contrast nephropathy
In patients with impaired renal function, the use of iodine-containing contrast media may be directly nephrotoxic. The mechanism is thought to be renal vasoconstriction and direct toxic effects on the renal tubules. The toxic effects appear to be dose-dependent; therefore, where large amounts of contrast are used, such as in angiography, there is an increased incidence of contrast nephropathy. The risks of contrast nephropathy increase where diabetic nephropathy is the cause of impaired renal function and there is coexistent hypovolaemia, as in this case, precipitated by his gastroenteritis. Pre-hydration with normal saline may reduce the incidence of contrast nephropathy, although care must be taken not to precipitate volume overload. Evidence for use of N- acetylcysteine is weak. It is worth noting that while this is the correct answer for the question, the incidence of contrast induced nephropathy in the general population is low, thought to be between 1-6 %.

stem: Which one of the following is the most important therapeutic step in a normotensive patient with Type 2 diabetes and without albuminuria, to prevent diabetic nephropathy?
explanation:
Optimal glycaemic control
Optimal glycaemic control, closely followed by blood pressure control, is the most important step.

Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor
Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor is incorrect. This patient is already normotensive.

Angiotensin II receptor antagonist
Angiotensin II receptor antagonist is incorrect. This patient is already normotensive.

Early switch to insulin
Early switch to insulin is incorrect. Switching to insulin is only indicated if glycaemic control is not achieved on oral agents.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of fever and haemoptysis. He is initially started on antibiotics for a chest infection, but he continues to have small-volume haemoptysis, and subsequent blood tests over the next 2 days show rapidly deteriorating renal function. On admission Day 2 Day 3 Na + (mmol/l) 135 137 136 K + (mmol/l) 4.2 5.0 5.9 Urea (mmol/l) 8 14 19 Creatinine (μmol/l) 143 175 240 Urinalysis shows +3 blood and +3 protein; an US scan shows two normal-sized, unobstructed kidneys. The latest chest X-ray reveals bilateral infiltrates in the lower zones. Which one of the following blood tests should be performed urgently to obtain a diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-GBM antibody
As this patient’s clinical presentation fits with Goodpasture’s disease, which presents as a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage. It is caused by circulating antibodies towards the non- collagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain on type IV collagen, which is highly expressed Chatinwith the glomerular basement membrane and alveoli.

stem: A 47-year-old man attends the outpatient clinic complaining of swelling in the ankles which has increased over the past 6 months, lethargy and tiredness. He has a chronic cough, he smokes 20 cigarettes per day and is an ex-intravenous-drug abuser. On examination, his blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg and he is found to have pitting oedema in both legs. Laboratory investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 115 g/l 135–175 g/l Urea 35 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 275 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Anti-nuclear antibodies Negative Urine Protein ++ What is the probable cause of his renal dysfunction?
explanation:
Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephropathy is secondary in 25–30% of cases and may be caused by hepatitis B virus. Most patients with membranous glomerulonephropathy present with proteinuria. This is the most correct answer.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic following a referral from his General Practitioner (GP). He has experienced several months of fever, general malaise, unintentional weight loss of 10 kg and myalgia. More recently, he has developed breathlessness and haemoptysis, prompting the referral. He appears to have saddle nose deformity. The GP requested several investigations at the time of referral. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are positive, although anti-serine proteinase 3 (PR3) and anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) antibody testing is awaited. A chest X-ray demonstrates several cavitating nodules of varying size. Based on the suspected diagnosis, which one of the following is the highest risk factor for poor prognosis?
options: Acute kidney injury suggestive of renal involvement
explanation:
Acute kidney injury suggestive of renal involvement
The diagnosis here is likely to be granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Patients typically have both upper airway and pulmonary involvement, although a minority may have just one or the other, and can have signs of cutaneous vasculitis and acute renal impairment. Constitutional symptoms, such as fever, lack of appetite, weight loss and fatigue, are often present. Chest X-rays are usually abnormal and can show nodules with cavitation, pulmonary haemorrhage and consolidation, and are usually followed up with computed tomography (CT) imaging. A tissue biopsy is usually required to confirm the diagnosis and typically shows evidence of necrotising granulomatous inflammation. The presence of acute kidney injury is an indicator of poor prognosis. Initial response to therapy (by two weeks) is also a useful indicator.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with facial and lower limb oedema. She believes she had a similar episode as a child that resolved with a course of steroids and has had no significant problems since then. Her BP is 122/82 mmHg and there is pitting oedema affecting both lower limbs. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 25 g/l 35–55 g/l Urine protein +++ Renal biopsy shows minimal change disease Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Prednisolone
Minimal change disease usually responds to high-dose steroids within 6 weeks of initiating therapy. In those where the response is inadequate, steroids can be considered for longer than 6 weeks and a steroid-sparing agent such as ciclosporin added. In those where proteinuria is marked, or who become hypertensive, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) should be considered in an attempt to reduce progression of renal disease. Chronic renal failure post-minimal change disease is extremely rare, although recurrent episodes may be seen, particularly in children.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Although an immunosuppressant, this would not be a first-line therapy because minimal change usually responds to high-dose steroids.

Lisinopril
Lisinopril is incorrect. Lisinopril will reduce proteinuria and will help blood pressure control; however, it does not treat the underlying condition of minimal change disease. As explained above, it should be considered in patients where proteinuria is marked.

Conservative management
Conservative management is incorrect. Conservative management would be inappropriate because minimal change will not resolve on its own.

Valsartan
Valsartan is incorrect. Similarly to lisinopril, will reduce proteinuria and would be a good anti-hypertensive choice; however, it will not treat the underlying condition.

stem: A 57-year-old man with a long history of gout presents with loin pain. Other history of note includes ileostomy after bowel surgery. There is no history of weight loss from malabsorption syndrome after his bowel surgery. Dipstick urine shows 3+ blood. Excretion urography reveals evidence of bilateral renal stones. Which one of the following is the most likely composition of his renal stones?
explanation:
Urate
A long history of gout is suggestive of urate stones. Although urate stones account for only 3–5% of presentations with renal stones in the UK (calcium oxalate stones are the commonest), his history of hyperuricaemia is a give-away. It is likely that his ileostomy has contributed due to acidification of urine and dehydration. Both of these conditions make urate stone formation more likely since uric acid is more soluble in an alkaline medium. Calcium stones may also occur in patients with hyperuricaemia and hyperuricosuria: it is believed that calcium crystals precipitate around an initial nidus of uric acid in these patients. Avoidance of large amounts of dietary purines, coupled with adequate hydration, should be advised.

Calcium oxalate
Calcium oxalate is incorrect. These occur more frequently in patients who have short gut syndrome due to significant small bowel resection, and there is no evidence of that in this case.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with an abnormal creatinine level. Past medical history includes type II diabetes which is currently treated with gliclazide, rheumatoid arthritis treated with daily naproxen and hypertension which is treated with indapamide. On examination, her blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg and her heart rate is 85 bpm and regular. Respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Her BMI is 29 kg/m 2. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Creatinine 180 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glycated haemoglobin 56 mmol/mol (8%), < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Urine dipstick Protein 2+, blood 1+ Ultrasound Bilateral shrunken kidneys Which one of the following is the most likely underlying renal pathology for this presentation?
explanation:
Chronic interstitial nephritis
Chronic interstitial nephritis leads to blood and proteinuria, as well as a gradual increase in creatinine level, and is associated with chronic use of NSAIDs, as here. Most cases of interstitial nephritis are seen in reactions to medication. Other medications that cause interstitial nephritis include penicillins, lithium, aciclovir, mesalazine,

stem: A 32-year-old African Caribbean man with a 5-year history of HIV infection presents with swollen ankles. He has been treated with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for 2 years, with partial response. His plasma creatinine concentration is 358 μmol/l, albumin is 12 g/l, CD4 count is 35/μl and 24-h urine protein excretion rate is 6.8 g. Renal ultrasound shows echogenic kidneys 13.5 cm in length. What would a renal biopsy show?
options: Microcystic tubular dilatation and collapsing FSGS
explanation:
Microcystic tubular dilatation and collapsing FSGS
HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN) is due to direct viral infection of the glomerular endothelial, mesangial and epithelial cells. While the mortality from HIV has declined since the introduction of HAART, the incidence of HIVAN has increased. It occurs predominantly in patients with long-standing HIV, and > 90% of affected patients is of African or Afro-Caribbean origin. In patients with HIVAN, the kidneys are typically large on ultrasonography. On biopsy, the pathological hallmark of HIVAN is focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with a collapsed glomerular tuft, with evidence of numerous tubuloreticular structures on electron microscopy. These are deposits of ribonucleoprotein and cell membrane that form under the influence of interferon alpha; the only other disease in which they are a feature is lupus nephritis.

Focal necrotising crescentic nephritis
Crescentic glomerulonephritis is typical of rapidly progressive GN found in immune-mediated processes such as glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who has had a renal transplantation previously is taking ciclosporin as part of her anti- rejection regimen. She sees the duty doctor service and is started on 100 mg fluconazole daily for 1 week for chronic vaginal candidiasis. Other medication of note includes pravastatin for hypercholesterolaemia. She returns to the clinic for review because her GP has checked her renal function and is concerned about a deterioration in her creatinine. On examination in the clinic her BP is 135/72 mmHg, her pulse 72/min. There are no significant abnormal findings. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 4.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 178 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l 222 μmol/l (baseline 140 μmol/l Creatinine 50–120 µmol/l 1 month earlier) Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the deterioration in her creatinine?
explanation:
Ciclosporin toxicity
Ciclosporin metabolism is particularly susceptible to co-administration with inhibitors of the CYP-P450 3A4 enzyme system. The azole class of antifungals, macrolide antibiotics, verapamil, diltiazem, amiodarone and protease inhibitors are all known to increase ciclosporin levels and may precipitate toxicity. For this reason, 3A4 inhibitors should only be prescribed if there is no alternative, and then only after consultation with the transplant physicians about reducing ciclosporin dose appropriately.

Fluconazole-induced nephritis
Fluconazole-induced nephritis is incorrect. Fluconazole exerts its effect on ciclosporin via CYP450 inhibition, rather than by a direct effect on the kidney.

Generalised candidiasis
Generalised candidiasis is incorrect. There are no symptoms to suggest generalised candida infection, and therefore sepsis as a cause of renal impairment here is very unlikely.

Graft rejection
Graft rejection is incorrect. Given the likely drug interaction between fluconazole and ciclosporin, this is much more likely than graft rejection itself.

Pravastatin accumulation
Pravastatin accumulation is incorrect. Pravastatin does not undergo significant metabolism via the P450 system.

stem: You are investigating a new therapeutic agent for the treatment of hypertension that is thought to have a partial thiazide-like action. You plan some basic scientific experiments to prove that the mode of action is similar. Which of the following correctly represents the site of action of bendroflumethiazide?
options: Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Descending limb of loop of Henlé
explanation:
Distal convoluted tubule
The thiazides, of which bendroflumethiazide and indapamide are typical examples, act by inhibiting reabsorption of sodium and chloride ions from the distal convoluted tubule, by blocking the thiazide-sensitive sodium and chloride symporter (also known as the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter). Other effects include hypokalaemia, increased cholesterol and triglycerides, and reduced calcium excretion.

Ascending limb of loop of Henle
Ascending limb of loop of Henle is incorrect. Loop diuretics primarily act on the ascending loop of Henlé, rather than thiazides.

Collecting duct
Collecting duct is incorrect. Anti-diuretic hormone has its primary action on the collecting duct.

stem: A 60-year-old woman recounts how she developed nephrotic syndrome many years ago when she was taking a treatment for her severe rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following is the likely culprit?
explanation:
Penicillamine
This is associated with causing nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy. It is rarely used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis due to the advent of TNF inhibitors (eg infliximab).

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is used in chemotherapeutic regimes as well as in the treatment of vasculitis. It causes myelosuppression, hair loss and subfertility. The risk of haemorrhagic cystitis is reduced by the co-administration of mesna, which limits the effect of the uro-toxic metabolites of cyclophosphamide.

Hydroxychloroquine
Hydroxychloroquine is incorrect. Hydroxychloroquine is used to treat malaria, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus erythematosus. The main side effect is retinopathy.

stem: A 52-year-old diabetic patient on metformin complains of feeling unwell. Apart from diabetes mellitus he has no other past medical history of note. Blood test results show a blood glucose of 4.2 mmol/l and an anion gap of 20 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause for his illness?
options: Type I distal renal tubular acidosis
explanation:
Lactic acidosis
Lactic acidosis can occur as a side-effect of metformin therapy. It is particularly likely to occur in diabetic patients with renal dysfunction, liver disease and heavy alcohol ingestion. Due to this complication, the NICE guideline (NG28) recommend that adults with type II diabetes should have metformin stopped if eGFR is < 30ml/minute/1.73m 2; there should be caution and metformin dose review if either eGFR is < 45ml/min/1.73m 2 or there is risk of sudden deterioration in eGFR.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a serious complication of Type I diabetes, consisting of very high blood glucose levels (> 11mmol/) and ketones in the blood. The presenting complaints may include nausea or vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, dehydration and reduced level of consciousness. In this scenario, however, the blood glucose level is not high. Further information on the recognition and management of diabetic ketoacidosis may be found in the NICE guideline (NG18).

stem: A 56-year-old man is listed for routine coronary angiography because of increasing chest pain over the past few months. Medication includes Simvastatin, Bisoprolol, Ivabradine, Metformin and Gliclazide. His BP is 125/80 mmHg, pulse is 65 bpm and regular, chest is clear and there is no ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 198 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 7.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* HbA1c 57 mmol/mol (7.4%) <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Low Density-Lipoprotein (LDL) 2.1 mmol/l <3.5 mmol/l Which of the following drugs should be discontinued before the angiography procedure?
explanation:
Metformin
Whilst debate exists as to the risks associated with Metformin and procedures involving IV contrast, most guidelines recommend discontinuation of Metformin some 48hrs prior to procedures such as angiography and contrast CT and not re-starting until 48hrs after the procedure. Metformin may both increase susceptability to renal damage associated with contrast media, and accumulate leading to increased risk of lactic acidosis in patients undergoing contrast procedures. Most guidelines also recommend discontinuing ACE inhibitors prior to angiography.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Gliclazide would not pre-dispose to contrast nephropathy. It selectively binds to sulfonylurea receptors (SUR-1) on the surface of the pancreatic beta-cells thereby reducing blood sugar. The hypoglycaemic action may be potentiated by phenylbutazone, alcohol, fluconazole and β-blockers.

Ivabradine
Ivabradine is incorrect. Ivabradine is used for heart rate control for symptomatic management of chest pain and heart failure which is not fully managed by β-blockers. It does not increase risk for contrast nephropathy.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is incorrect. Bisoprolol is a beta 1 selective inhibitor. Although it will reduce heart rate and does not increase incidence of contrast nephropathy.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. Simvastatin is a HMG-CoA inhibitor and competes for binding with HMGCR enzyme thereby reducing cholesterol levels. It does not predispose to contrast nephropathy.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has a history of type 2 diabetes and terminal kidney disease, treated with continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD), presents to the Emergency Department with a partially draining bag, which contains only small amounts of cloudy fluid. On examination, his blood pressure is 125/72 mmHg; pulse is 91 bpm and regular. There is erythema and pus around his peritoneal dialysis catheter site. His temperature is 38.4 °C, and his abdomen is generally tender to palpation. Peritoneal fluid reveals 300 white cells / microlitre. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his infection?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the most likely cause from the options given, especially when there are signs of a catheter exit site infection, as is seen here. Infections with coagulase negative Staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common causes of CAPD peritonitis worldwide. You may like to refer to the following review article for more information: Akoh et al. Peritoneal dialysis associated infections: An update on diagnosis and management. World J. Nephrol. 2012; 1(4): 106–122. Initial therapy of choice is vancomycin and gentamicin added to the dialysis fluid bag. The dose of vancomycin is calculated by weight, with 2 g being the recommended dose for an individual above 70 kg in weight.

Aspergillus fumigatus
Chatfor Aspergillus fumigatus is a rare fungal infection. If there is fungal peritonitis, this is an indication with peritoneal dialysis catheter removal.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents to the Renal Ward with developing vague abdominal pain. She has a history of polycystic kidney disease and underwent a second kidney transplantation about seven years after her first. She has full compliance with her immunosuppressive medication. A biopsy is arranged. Investigations: Investigation Result Result six weeks ago Normal value Sodium (Na +) 136 mmol/l 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.5 mmol/l 5.9 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 219 μmol/l 112 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Albumin 41 g/l 39 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following immunoglobulins is expected to account for this process?
explanation:
Immunoglobin G
Development of anti-human leukocyte antigen immunoglobin G antibodies after a first renal transplant can precipitate acute rejection of the second, the likely diagnosis here. Antigen–antibody complexes lead to complement activation and massive capillary thrombosis, resulting in failure of vascularisation of the graft. The

stem: A 23-year-old man has had recurrent attacks of hepatitis. He now presents with bone pain, muscle weakness, polyuria and polydipsia. His past medical history includes recurrent urinary tract infections; there is no family history of hepatitis. Slit-lamp examination shows a greenish-brown discoloration within the cornea. Which one of the following is the most common association with this condition?
explanation:
Hypophosphataemia
Wilson’s disease is a rare inborn error of copper metabolism (and is the diagnosis in the present case). This is evidenced by the clinical picture of the recurrent hepatitis and slit lamp showing Kayser–Fleischer rings around the cornea due to characteristic copper deposition in Descemet's membrane. It is an autosomal recessive disease; therefore, both parents need to be carriers of the disease and may not manifest symptoms themselves. This condition can cause type II proximal renal tubular acidosis (RTA). The cardinal features are acidosis, hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia. An inability to lower the urine pH below 5.5 despite systemic acidosis, and the appearance of bicarbonate in the urine despite subnormal plasma bicarbonate, help differentiate between RTA types 1 and 2. If the urine can be acidified, then this is more suggestive of type 2.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia may present with bone pain, and polyuria with polydipsia. However, the diagnosis in this case is Wilson's disease, which may be associated with hypoparathryoidism, leading to low calcium rather than hypercalcaemia. The bone pain is due to calcium loss from thewith Chat bones.

stem: A 50-year-old man with sickle cell disease feels generally unwell and lethargic, with no specific symptoms. Which of the following complications is he most likely to have a high risk of developing in the long term?
explanation:
Chronic kidney disease
Chronic kidney disease is an important contributor to illness and death among adults with sickle cell disease, especially those over 40 years of age. Chronic kidney disease in this condition is usually insidious in onset, manifested initially by a falling haemoglobin level attributable to lowered erythropoietin levels. Serum creatinine levels tend to be lower than normal in steady-state sickle cell disease, and creatinine levels within the accepted normal range should not be interpreted as indicating normal renal function – indeed in sickle cell disease it is likely that levels of 60–70 μmol/l reflect significant renal damage. The renal function of older patients with sickle cell disease should therefore be monitored regularly.

Hepatic fibrosis
Hepatic fibrosis is incorrect. Hepatic fibrosis is rare in patients with sickle cell disease despite chronic blood transfusions; therefore, they do not need to undergo routine liver biopsies for surveillance.

Lung cancer
Lung cancer is incorrect. Lung cancer is not associated with sickle cell disease.

stem: A 64-year-old man on peritoneal dialysis due to Type II diabetes is admitted with a fractured neck of femur. His serum calcium concentration is 2.91 mmol/l, phosphate is 2.21 mmol/l and PTH is 0.4 pmol/l (normal range 1.5–7.6). Medications include alfacalcidol 0.5 μg daily and calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. What would a bone biopsy show?
options: Aluminium deposition at the osteoid bone interface
explanation:
Adynamic bone disease
Adynamic bone disease is most prevalent in diabetic patients, and those on peritoneal dialysis, and is associated with an increased incidence of hip fracture. There is a tendency towards hypercalcaemia as the bone loses its capacity to buffer serum calcium. It can be caused by overtreatment with alfacalcidol. Histologically, it is characterised by a reduction in both bone formation and resorption, with thin osteoid seams, little active mineralisation and few osteoclasts.

Aluminium deposition at the osteoid bone interface
Aluminium deposition at the osteoid bone interface is incorrect. Aluminium bone disease may have a similar appearance, although it is now rare, as dialysis water treatment has improved and aluminium-based phosphate binders are largely out of favour.

stem: A 57-year-old man with advanced cirrhosis is brought to the hospital by his wife as he has become confused, drowsy and unwell. His blood pressure is 105/65 mmHg and his central venous pressure is 14 mm H 2O. Urinary catheterisation reveals a residual volume of 35 ml and he is anuric for the next 2 h. Urine sodium is low, at <10 mmol/l. An ultrasound scan reveals normal-sized kidneys with no evidence of obstruction and an empty bladder. Despite IV fluid replacement no improvement in urine output is seen. Blood tests reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 135–175 g/l Platelets 75 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Creatinine 385 μmol/l 60–110 μmol/l Urea 8.1 mmol/l 2.5–7.5 mmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute tubular necrosis secondary to sepsis
Pre-kidney disease due to volume depletion
explanation:
Hepato-renal syndrome
Hepato-renal syndrome is a feature of advanced cirrhosis. The likelihood of hepato-renal syndrome occurring in year 1 after a diagnosis of cirrhosis is put at 18%; by year 5 the chance of hepato-renal syndrome occurring during that year is put at 39%. There are many other causes of kidney disease associated with liver disease

stem: A 35-year-old patient who is usually physically fit, has no past medical history of note, and works as a fitness instructor presents to the clinic with polyuria and polydipsia, tiredness and lethargy. He is not on any regular prescription drugs but he does take ibuprofen and diclofenac on most days because of sports injuries. On examination he looks dehydrated and his blood pressure (BP) is 105/55 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 210 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 148 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 12 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Creatinine 156 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Random glucose 9.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Urine osmolality 450 mosmol/kg 350 – 1000 mosmol/kg Urinary protein and blood are negative Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Distal renal tubular acidosis
Distal renal tubular acidosis is associated with hypokalaemia, and possible causes include long-term use/abuse of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. It’s likely this patient has used pain killers over a number of years to cope with injuries associated with gym work. The random blood glucose is not indicative of diabetes mellitus, but should be followed up with a fasting blood glucose sample given his symptoms.

Diabetes insipidus
Diabetes insipidus is incorrect. Urine osmolality of 450 mosmol/kg argues against diabetes insipidus.

Psychogenic polydipsia
Psychogenic polydipsia is incorrect. This patient’s sodium is elevated as is his creatinine, hence psychogenic polydipsia is unlikely.

Hyperosmolar diabetic crisis
Hyperosmolar diabetic crisis is incorrect. Hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma is associated with markedly elevated glucose levels.

Interstitial nephritis
Interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Interstitial nephritis is associated with eosinophilia and mild to moderate proteinuria, neither of which is seen here.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who is known to have multiple sclerosis presents to the urology clinic with increasing urge incontinence and a sensation of incomplete emptying. On examination her BP is 120/80 mmHg. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, urinalysis is negative for protein and blood, and a post micturition bladder scan reveals 20ml of urine. Which of the following is the best option with respect to managing her symptoms?
explanation:
Oxybutinin
This woman has symptoms of urge incontinence, and the post-micturition bladder scan reveals no significant residual volume. In patients who fail to respond to oxybutinin, tolterodine and solifenacin are reasonable alternatives.

Intermittent self-catheterisation
Intermittent self-catheterisation is incorrect. It is usually considered as an option when there is significant residual urine in the bladder.

Intravesicular botulinum toxin
Intravesicular botulinum toxin is incorrect and is usually reserved for patients who fail medical therapy for over- active bladder.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He has been started on a number of medications by the team following an inferior myocardial infarction some 4 months earlier, including Aspirin, Amlodipine, Ramipril and Simvastatin. He has been taking Theophylline tablets and a Salbutamol inhaler for COPD for many years. He tells you that he has been nauseous and has frequently felt faint over the past 2-3 weeks. On examination his BP is 95/60 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He is not in cardiac failure. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 178 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 185 µmol/l (up from 135 µmol/l at discharge) 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Which of the following is the most likely cause of the increase in creatinine?
explanation:
Ramipril
The decrease in GFR associated with ACE inhibitor prescription is thought to be due to a reduction in intraglomerular pressure, the mechanism that may actually lead to renal protection. In this case there is likely to have been a degree of renal arterial insufficiency, and the initiation of Ramipril has led to an inability to maintain intraglomerular pressure above the level below which a fall in GFR ensues.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine has a common side effect of peripheral oedema, leg swelling. This is dose dependent.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin may have side effects of gastrointestinal upset, exacerbate gastrointestinal bleeds and also may cause angiooedema.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. Simvastatin may precipitate renal failure when associated with rhabdomyolysis, though we see no evidence of that here.

Theophylline
Theophylline is incorrect. Theophylline may cause nausea/vomiting, headache, insomnia, diarrhea, irritability, restlessness, nervousness and increased urination.

stem: Which one factor is most likely to trigger renin stimulation?
explanation:
Hypovolaemia
Renin secretion is stimulated by hyponatraemiaand low blood volume. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is converted in the lungs by angiotensin-converting enzyme to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce aldosterone and causes peripheral vasoconstriction. The remaining options are not involved in this pathway.

Adrenocorticotropic hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone is incorrect. Adrenocorticotropic hormone is not involved in the angiotensin pathway.

ANP
ANP is incorrect. ANP is not involved in the angiotensin pathway.

stem: A 59-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma has a haemoglobin of 190 g/l and a normal white cell count. He has a past medical history of chronic obstructive airways disease and was asymptomatic. Which investigation will conclusively prove that this patient has secondary polycythaemia?
explanation:
Erythropoeitin level
Low serum erythropoietin levels suggest polycythaemia vera. If the serum erythropoietin level is raised, it suggests either a hypoxic cause or an increase in the autonomous production of erythropoietin, as can happen with renal carcinoma.

Haematocrit
Haematocrit is incorrect. It is a measure of blood viscosity: because the red cells are filled with haemoglobin, the level of haematocrit correlates with the level of haemoglobin. Hence the haematocrit is raised in polycythaemia vera. This would be the case in both primary and secondary polycythaemia because regardless of the cause, there is an absolute overproduction of red blood cells.

Red cell count
Red cell count is incorrect. This would be raised in both primary and secondary polycythaemia because, as explained above, the absolute number of red blood cells is increased.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with haematuria and recurrent haemoptysis. He has a past medical history of asthma. His blood tests show a normal cholesterol level and low haemoglobin. Renal biopsy shows the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody. Which one of the following is the most significant feature with regard to the immune system in this disease?
options: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies occur in only 50% of patients
Autoantibodies are directed against type IV collagen
Positive c-ANCA always indicates pulmonary involvement
explanation:
Autoantibodies are directed against type IV collagen
In anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, autoantibodies are directed against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.

Antibody deposition causes mesangial proliferation
Antibody deposition causes mesangial proliferation is incorrect. Antibody deposition causes crescentic nephritis in > 50% of glomeruli rather, than mesangial proliferation. Mesangial proliferation may be found in focal segmental sclerosis.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies occur in only 50% of patients
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies occur in only 50% of patients is incorrect. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies occur in > 90% of patients.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with primary biliary cholangitis presents with osteomalacia and recurrent urinary tract infections; she has had renal calculi removed twice in the past year. There is hypokalaemia and hyperchloraemic acidosis. Which one of the following is the most likely finding on urinalysis?
explanation:
Decreased urinary citrate levels
This patient has type I distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA). In RTA, which may be caused by a number of autoimmune diseases, there is a failure of hydrogen (H) ion excretion in the distal tubule and it presents with hypokalaemia, acidosis and low urinary ammonium production; there is an inability to lower the urinary pH below 5.3 despite systemic acidosis. Other features include low urinary citrate and hypercalciuria, which predispose to renal stones, rickets or osteomalacia, and nephrocalcinosis.

Decreased urinary calcium levels
Decreased urinary calcium levels is incorrect. Decreased urinary calcium levels are a significant risk factor for predicting eclampsia in pregnancy. However, the most common causes of hypocalciuria are taking thiazide diuretics or reduced dietary intake of calcium. A rare cause is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy and learning difficulties presents with flank pain, hypotension and anaemia. A CT scan of her abdomen shows significant haemorrhage into a mass in her right kidney, with the mass being composed primarily of fat; there are two similar lesions (without haemorrhage) in her left kidney. Renal function is normal. Which one of the following is the underlying condition?
explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, often with incomplete penetrance. Two genetic defects have been identified, one on chromosome 9 (TSC1) and one on chromosome 16 (TSC2). Interestingly, the latter is adjacent to the PKD1 gene, which is deficient in adult polycystic kidney disease. The renal lesions are hamartomas, which tend to grow slowly over time and occasionally undergo malignant transformation. Astrocytomas can develop in 5% of patients with tuberous sclerosis and lead to presentation with epilepsy and hydrocephalus; pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis is seen in up to 40% of women with the condition. The CT scan appearance in the patient in this question is typical of angiomyolipoma, which when bilateral and associated with epilepsy, is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis. Bleeding into the angiomyolipoma is the most common means of presentation.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is incorrect. ADPKD is not associated with epilepsy or learning difficulties, and the cystic lesions are not fatty in nature.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness and lethargy. Her plasma sodium is 138 mmol/l, potassium 2.1 mmol/l, bicarbonate 12 mmol/l and chloride 113 mmol/l. Creatinine is 62 μmol/l. She is diagnosed as having type I renal tubular acidosis (RTA). Which one of the following is the most significant clinical presentation of distal RTA (type I) that differentiates it from proximal RTA (type II)?
options: Urinary pH in type I can be lowered below 5.3 after ammonium chloride administration
explanation:
Renal stone formation
Nephrocalcinosis and renal stone formation are features of type I RTA only.

Metabolic acidosis is common
Metabolic acidosis is common is incorrect. Normal anion gap, growth failure, hyperventilation and systemic acidosis are features of both types of renal tubular acidosis.

Potassium depletion occurs
Potassium depletion occurs is incorrect. Potassium depletion occurs in both types of renal tubular acidosis.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with two episodes of gross haematuria. Past history of note includes coeliac disease. On both occasions the haematuria appears to have been closely associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. Blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy specimen reveals diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion. IgA deposits are seen on immunofluorescence. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
Episodic haematuria associated with respiratory tract infection is the typical feature of IgA nephropathy, sometimes known as Berger’s disease. The light microscopy result is in keeping with the diagnosis. As well as presenting with episodic gross haematuria, other presentations include nephrotic syndrome with proteinuria and acute kidney disease. IgA nephropathy is seen in up to one-third of patients with gluten enteropathy. It is also associated with cirrhosis and HIV infection, and has a familial form. Chronic kidney disease occurs in up to 2% of patients per year who have IgA nephropathy. Medical treatment of IgA nephropathy includes angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) , which has been shown to delay progression to kidney disease; use of prednisolone in patients with severe disease may also be of benefit.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with a few months of progressive lethargy. He has also had increasing oedema of both lower limbs, for which his doctor has started furosemide, the dose of which has been increased to 120 mg/day. He has a long history of rheumatoid arthritis, currently controlled with weekly methotrexate therapy and hypertension for which he takes ramipril once a day. Upon examination he has gross peripheral pitting oedema to the mid-thigh bilaterally. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 108 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 187 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 22 g/l 35–55 g/l Urine protein +++, blood – Which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Subepithelial deposits
This man has nephrotic syndrome as characterised by hypoalbuminaemia, peripheral oedema and proteinuria. In adults, the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome is membranous nephropathy, in which case the mesangium is normal, with no hypercellularity. All glomeruli are involved. Capillary walls are thickened with patent capillary lumina. Subepithelial deposits are seen, and with trichrome stain they appear to have spikes. Immunosuppressive therapy may be considered for progressive membranous nephropathy. Regimens of chlorambucil and corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide and steroids have been trialled; response rates are reported to be relatively high, with only two out of 15 patients in one case series showing no response to therapy.

Endocapillary hypercellularity
Endocapillary hypercellularity is incorrect. This would present with haematuria and would not present with nephrotic syndrome. IgA nephropathy is the most common glomerulonephritis in the developed world.

Focal glomerulosclerosis
Focal glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Focal glomerulosclerosis may occur in focal segmental glomerulonephritis, which would present in nephrotic syndrome, but this condition is less common than membranous nephropathy.

Mesangial hypercellularity
Mesangial hypercellularity is incorrect. This is a feature of IgA nephropathy which presents with haematuria rather than nephrotic syndrome.

Normal light microscopy
Normal light microscopy is incorrect. Minimal change disease can also present with nephrotic syndrome; however, it is a far more common cause in children. This has good prognosis with steroid treatment in the young. Overall Explanation The mesangium in membranous nephropathy, (the diagnosis here), is normal, with no hypercellularity. The gross proteinuria coupled with the absence of blood in the urine, are both major pointers to membranous nephropathy as the underlying diagnosis. All glomeruli are involved. Capillary walls are thickened with patent capillary lumina. Subepithelial deposits are seen, and with trichrome stain, they appear to have spikes. Mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity are features of immunoglobulin A nephropathy. In minimal change disease, light microscopy of renal biopsy appears normal.
