stem: A 52-year-old man has developed acute kidney injury stage 3 secondary to sepsis and needs to have haemodialysis as he is oliguric and is in pulmonary oedema. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 17.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 366 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l What concentration should the potassium be in the dialysate fluid when he commences haemodialysis?
explanation:
2 mmol/l
In haemodialysis, solutes move down their respective concentration gradients between the dialysate and the patient’s blood. Therefore, in this case, to help correct the raised potassium, he will need to be dialysed against a low-potassium dialysate, as in this way the concentration gradient favours the shift of potassium from the patient’s blood into the dialysate.

stem: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes had a serum creatinine concentration of 250 μmol/l (60–110) before admission for a radiographic investigation that included intravenous contrast medium. He is admitted to the Emergency Department two days after discharge home. His creatinine concentration is now 470 μmol/l and he has only passed 20 ml of urine since being catheterised some 3 h ago. You suspect contrast nephropathy. Which of the following best describes the incidence of contrast nephropathy patients such as this?
explanation:
25%
In an unselected population, the incidence of contrast nephropathy is said to be between 2 and 7%. If renal function is impaired, then the incidence increases to around 25%. In those patients with pre-existing renal disease where the creatinine is above 400 micromol/l without diabetes, the incidence of contrast nephropathy is thought to be around 60%. If patients have a creatinine above 400 micromol/l and also have diabetes mellitus, then the incidence of acute kidney disease is said to be 100%. Diabetics are particularly at risk, possibly as a result of intra-renal microvascular disease. It is advisable to stop metformin for two days pre- and post-contrast procedure as there is a risk of lactic acidosis. Congestive cardiac failure carries a risk of contrast nephropathy of 7–8%. Other risk factors of note include multiple myeloma, pancreatitis, multiple contrast studies, dehydration and jaundice. Outcome figures from one study suggested that recovery of renal function occurs in 68% of patients, partial recovery in 14%, with death, dialysis or transplantation occurring in 18%. NICE guidelines (CG169) state that high-risk groups for contrast-induced nephropathy include the following: chronic renal disease diabetic patients with chronic kidney disease

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with flank pain and a 48-hour history of dysuria. Her past medical history includes polycystic ovarian syndrome. She is not in a steady relationship at present. There is haematuria, leukocytes, nitrites and proteinuria on urine dipstick testing. Examination reveals a pyrexia of 38.1°C and flank pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pyelonephritis
This woman presents with symptoms consistent with pyelonephritis. The two peaks of incidence for pyelonephritis in adults occur in young sexually active women and in men > 50 years of age. Gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli or Klebsiella species are responsible in more than 95% of cases. Unusual organisms may be responsible if there has been a history of urethral instrumentation. Staphylococcal urinary sepsis is usually indicative of haematological seeding of infection. Symptoms include fever, rigors, flank pain, dysuria, polyuria, haematuria, nausea and vomiting, headache and diarrhoea. In young women with a first infection, urine culture may be all that is required. Otherwise, work-up includes urea and electrolytes measurement, a full blood count and blood cultures, and renal ultrasound in compromised patients. Standard antibiotic treatment is with oral co-amoxiclav or ciprofloxacin. Surgical opinion may be required for recurrent infections or where there is evidence of vesicoureteric reflux on scanning.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who is 20 weeks’ pregnant presents with fevers. She has no past medical history of note and is not allergic to any medication. On examination she is pyrexial (37.8 oC), her blood pressure (BP) is 122/70 mm Hg and her pulse is 90/min and regular. She looks flushed and has suprapubic tenderness. Urine dipstick is suggestive of a urinary tract infection. Which one of the following antibiotics must be avoided in this patient?
explanation:
Ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin has been associated with tendon rupture in animal models of fetal development where studies were conducted at the time of licensing, and as such is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Amoxicillin
Amoxicillin is incorrect. Amoxicillin is commonly used in pregnancy with no associated adverse effects in the mother or fetus.

Cephalexin
Cephalexin is incorrect. There is considerable experience of the use of cephalexin in various stages of pregnancy without evidence of fetal adverse effects.

stem: A 62-year-old woman visits the diabetes centre for her annual review. She has had Type 2 diabetes for 9 years and is now on insulin therapy. She has diabetic nephropathy, noted by hypertension 165/88 mmHg and proteinuria (urinary PCR 155 g/mol). Her creatinine is 192 micromol/l, and her eGFR is 34 ml/min/1.73m 2. Which one of the following options best fits her prognosis or management?
options: Her systolic BP target should be 140 mmHg
Intensive glucose control will not affect prognosis
Non-dihydropyridine calcium antagonists have no effect on proteinuria
Tight blood pressure control is unlikely to affect prognosis
Treatment with angiotensin II receptor blocker (A2RB) or angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-I may
explanation:
Treatment with angiotensin II receptor blocker (A2RB) or angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-I may
slow further deterioration in renal function ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (A2RBs) are the treatment of choice for hypertension in diabetic nephropathy. The DD-ACE phenotype is thought to be associated with raised circulating levels of angiotensin II and a more rapid decline in renal function. Cross-sectional studies in Type 2 diabetes suggest a prevalence of microalbuminuria between 15% and 50% depending on ethnicity.

Her systolic BP target should be 140 mmHg
Her systolic blood pressure (BP) target should be 140 mmHg is incorrect. It is suggested that the target for systolic blood pressure should be 130 mmHg or lower. There is a strong association between nephropathy and markers of increased cardiovascular risk, such as insulin resistance, poor glycaemic control, dyslipidaemia, left ventricular hypertrophy, endothelial dysfunction and absence of nocturnal blood pressure dipping.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with bilateral loin pain and visible haematuria. He had a throat infection 3 days ago. He has no past medical history, but has a family history of renal stones. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 120 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urinalysis reveals blood ++++ only. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
This is a glomerulonephritis characterised by the diffuse deposition of IgA in the renal mesangium. It is the most common cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide. Peak incidence of presentation is in the second and third decades of life, and most commonly presents with visible haematuria in the setting of an intercurrent upper respiratory tract infection; loin pain may also be present due to renal capsular stretching. is Diagnosis confirmed from a renal biopsy.

stem: A 72-year-old bipolar patient is seen in the renal new-patient clinic complaining of thirst for 6 weeks. He is not previously known to have chronic kidney disease (CKD). Serum biochemistry reveals: Investigation Result Normal Value Urea 21.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 185 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Sodium (Na +) 146 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Urinary osmolality Low Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion
explanation:
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
It is likely to be a direct toxic effect of long-term lithium therapy. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may also be inherited as a X-linked recessive condition. Diagnosis is made on low urine osmolality (< 200 mosmol/kg) in the presence of raised serum osmolality, hypernatraemia and evidence of dehydration. Some improvement may be seen by switching his lithium to an alternative maintenance drug for bipolar disorder – such as lamotrigine and valproate – but this should only be considered after consultation with his psychiatrist. stem: A 56-year-old woman presents with aching joints, non-specific malaise and weight loss of 3 months’ duration. Her blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg, she has mild peripheral oedema, and dipstick urinalysis shows evidence of blood and protein. Her serum creatinine is 367 μmol/l, whereas 6 months earlier it had been a normal 86 μmol/l, and 3 months earlier it was 148 μmol/l. Her family doctor had 1 week previously prescribed diclofenac sodium for her joint pain. Complement tests reveal C3 of 1.2 (0.7–1.3) and C4 of 0.19 (0.12–0.27). Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the kidney disease?
explanation:
Microscopic polyangiitis
The history is most consistent with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, the pathological hallmark of which is crescentic glomerulonephritis, can be divided into three basic groups differentiated on the basis of the immunofluorescence pattern on the renal biopsy and the complement profile in serum. The most common cause, as in this question, is anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and renal-limited vasculitis), which is characterised by the presence of scanty or absent immune deposits in the glomerulus (‘pauci immune’). If a linear deposit of IgG is present, the diagnosis is generally anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture’s disease). The third group comprises those conditions with pronounced glomerular immune deposits, many of which are characterised by hypocomplementemia (systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE] nephropathy, cryoglobulinemia, mesangiocapillary GN). However, it would have been impossible to distinguish between the first two groups based on the information in the question, and both of these causes are associated with normal complement levels.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a known history of lung cancer presents with anorexia, malaise and drowsiness. A CT scan shows metastatic lesions in the liver. Laboratory test results are as follows: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 78 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Ferritin 87.5 µg/l 20–250 µg/l Urea 27 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 377 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 24-h urine protein 3.8 g A renal biopsy shows focal subepithelial deposition of IgG and C3. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Membranous glomerulonephropathy
Membranous glomerulonephropathy accounts for 50% of all adults with nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 37-year-old woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 37 kg/m 2 has been reviewed in the hypertension clinic. Abdominal ultrasound scanning reveals that her left kidney is much smaller than her right kidney. You suspect renal artery stenosis, as her GP noticed a deteriorating serum creatinine concentration within one month of starting ACE-inhibitor therapy. Most recent eGFR was 45 ml/min/1.72 m 2. Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Magnetic resonance angiography
In renal artery stenosis, radionuclide studies demonstrate reduced renal perfusion on the affected side. This is particularly marked after the administration of captopril. A completely normal result renders renal artery stenosis unlikely. Although a useful investigation, the issues of isotope handling and exposing patients (who may be normal) to isotopes mean that magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is the next investigation of choice. It has been shown to correlate closely to angiographic appearances and is non-invasive. In recent years, it has been found that exposure to gadolinium, which is used in the MRA, in patients with chronic kidney disease is associated with an irreversible condition known as nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. This condition involves dermal and organ fibrosis, with 5% of patients having a progressively debilitating course. Studies have shown, however, that patients with eGFR >30 ml/min are at a low risk.

Spiral CT scanning
Spiral CT scanning is incorrect. Because this involves a large dose of radiation, MRA is generally preferred.

stem: A 30-year-old man undergoes investigation for chronic upper urinary tract obstruction with intravenous urography. The patient should be informed about which one severe complication?
explanation:
Contrast nephrotoxicity
Intravenous urography will usually demonstrate the site, cause, and degree of obstruction. It is much less operator-dependent than ultrasound because the number of images checked by the clinician is equal to the number of images reported by the radiologist. Its major disadvantage is that the technique carries a mortality owing to contrast hypersensitivity reaction of perhaps 1 in 200 000. It also involves an IV injection, exposure to radiation (of particular concern in pregnant women and children), worsening of pain due to the diuretic effect of contrast medium when an upper tract (or tracts) is obstructed and the potential for contrast nephrotoxicity. Patients with impaired renal function, particularly those with diabetes and perhaps patients with myelomatosis, are at particular risk. Such risk is minimised by use of low osmolality contrast medium and the avoidance of prior dehydration.

Bleeding
Bleeding is incorrect. Apart from an intravenous cannula insertion for contrast, there is no risk of bleeding from an intravenous urography procedure.

stem: A 45-year-old inpatient is experiencing mild flank pain which woke him up from sleep three hours ago. He also reports a new generalised rash. Two weeks ago, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and was started on isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin and ethambutol. His temperature is 38.2 °C, his heart rate is 84 bpm, and his blood pressure is 124/68 mmHg. Examination of his skin shows diffuse erythema with confluent papules. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 60 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 12.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 156 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Eosinophils 4% 0.0–0.4% Neutrophils 59% 40–60% Red blood cell casts Absent WCC casts Numerous This patient is treated with aggressive fluid resuscitation. What is the next appropriate step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Discontinue rifampicin
This patient presents with flank pain, diffuse maculopapular rash and fever two weeks after the initiation of antituberculosis treatment. In combination with eosinophilia, haematuria, pyuria and eosinophilia on laboratory studies, these features suggest allergic interstitial nephritis. Allergic interstitial nephritis is an intrinsic renal cause of acute kidney injury. Initial treatment involves addressing the underlying cause (ie the offending drug) and providing intravenous (IV) fluids, as the condition will usually resolve spontaneously after discontinuation of the causal agent. Given that this patient recently began treatment for active tuberculosis, the most likely cause is rifampicin.

Administer ciprofloxacin
Ciprofloxacin is a first-line treatment for acute pyelonephritis, which commonly causes fever, flank pain and pyuria, as seen in this patient. However, patients with pyelonephritis are usually acutely ill and present with chills, nausea and costovertebral angle tenderness on examination. In the setting of an acute bacterial infection, moreover, leukocytosis with a left shift would also be expected. Furthermore, a maculopapular rash and eosinophilia are not features of pyelonephritis.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of cough and breathlessness. He has also noticed haemoptysis, which he says has gradually worsened. On examination, he has bilateral basal crepitations. His chest X-ray shows diffuse shadowing. His GP has measured his creatinine at 195 µmol/l and detected protein and blood in his urine. What is the best way to obtain the diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
This patient has Goodpasture syndrome, with diffuse pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis and linear deposition of antibody (90% of which is directed against the a-3 chain of type IV collagen) along the glomerular basement membrane. Serological testing for anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) is crucial to confirming the diagnosis, and a renal biopsy is almost always warranted. Some healthy individuals exposed to inhaled oils, hydrocarbons or solvents may have borderline raised anti- GBM antibody levels. Anti-GBM antibodies have also been detected in HIV-negative patients with pneumocystis pneumonia.

Bronchoscopy
Although bronchoscopy and biopsy may support a diagnosis of Goodpasture, renal biopsy will help better stratify risk of kidney disease.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents to her GP with symptoms of urinary tract infection. There is a history of multiple attendances for various aches and pains, and a previous neurology referral for headache. She admits to using large amounts of over the counter analgesics including paracetamol, ibuprofen and naproxen. BP is 165/95 mmHg. Urinalysis reveals haematuria and her GP commences her on a 2-week course of ciprofloxacin. She returns, still complaining of symptoms, at which point the presence of a normochromic normocytic anaemia is noted, along with a serum creatinine of 220 μmol/l. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to urosepsis
explanation:
Interstitial nephritis
NSAID use leads to chronic kidney disease (CKD) by a number of mechanisms including interstitial nephritis, tubular necrosis, nephrotic syndrome and afferent arteriolar constriction leading to reduced renal blood flow. Penicillins, including co-amoxiclav, may also cause an (acute) interstitial nephritis, but it appears in this case that her problem predated its use.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to urosepsis
Acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to urosepsis is incorrect. The presenting features do not fit with these diagnoses.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with a history of red urine. This has occurred intermittently over the previous 3 years, and on each occasion has occurred after developing a respiratory tract infection. His blood pressure is 140/85 mmHg and urinalysis shows +3 blood and +3 protein, with red cell casts evident on microscopy. His uPCR is 196 g/mol. What would a renal biopsy most probably show?
options: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with IgA deposition
Normal light microscopy with thin basement membranes on electron microscopy (EM)
Proliferative glomerulonephritis (GN) with deposition of C3, IgG and IgM
explanation:
Mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis with IgA deposition
The patient’s history is typical of IgA nephropathy, the most common form of glomerulonephritis in adults. Although clinical features may be very variable, the typical picture is of recurrent episodes of micro- or macrohaematuria. IgA nephropathy may also be familial. The pathogenesis is unknown, although various abnormalities in IgA homeostasis have been identified – these include elevated IgA levels in 50% of cases, circulating IgA-containing immune complexes and abnormal IgA glycosylation. In one study of 269 asymptomatic first-degree relatives of patients with IgA nephropathy, 46% had persistent non-visible haematuria. The renal lesions are indistinguishable from that seen in Henoch–Schönlein purpura, and it is generally agreed that they lie on a spectrum of the same disease process. IgA deposition may also occur in cirrhosis and gluten enteropathy, although this is usually clinically silent.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with IgA deposition
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) with IgA deposition is incorrect. Immune complex deposition Chat is not with a feature of FSGS.

stem: A 32-year-old woman complaining of painful hands is found to have hypertension, proteinuria and dipstick haematuria. Plasma creatinine is 147 μmol/l. Renal biopsy shows proliferative glomerulonephritis with occasional cellular crescents, and immunofluorescence shows diffuse granular staining for IgA, IgG, IgM, C3 and C4. Which one of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Lupus nephritis
This patient, with arthralgia, hypertension and the ‘full house’ on immunofluorescence, has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). LN Histology The pathological changes in lupus nephritis are very variable: from mild mesangial hypercellularity to a fulminant focal necrotising proliferative disease with crescent formation. It may also mimic membranous nephropathy. The changes described in this case are typical of type 4 (diffuse proliferative) disease. LN Immunology Importantly, the pathognomonic feature of lupus on renal biopsy is ‘full-house’ immunology on immunostaining, ie mesangial deposition of IgA, IgG, IgM, C3 and C4.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department 4 weeks after renal transplantation. She was initially well and discharged after a few days. She now complains of fevers, a sore throat and severe aches and pains. She has been fully compliant with her immunosuppressive therapy. On examination her blood pressure is 139/73 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and her temperature is 37.9 oC. There is evidence of mild pharyngitis but nil else of note. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 127 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 135 μmol/l (120 post-transplant) 50–120 µmol/l Urine culture Negative Donor cytomegalovirus Positive Epstein–Barr virus Negative Which one of the following treatments is most appropriate?
explanation:
Ganciclovir
More severe infection where there is deterioration in creatinine, such as that seen here, should be managed with IV ganciclovir. Following the acute episode patients are usually maintained on oral prophylaxis.

Co-trimoxazole
Co-trimoxazole is incorrect. Co-trimoxazole is an oral antibiotic which is routinely given post renal transplant as a prophylaxis and treatment against Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. There is no evidence of pneumonia in this case as there is only pharyngitis noted.

Methylprednisolone
Methylprednisolone is incorrect. Methylprednisolone is used in acute rejection of renal transplant. Although an acute rejection may explain the rise in creatinine post transplantation and certainly 93% of acute rejection occurs within the first month, the flu-like symptoms and fever would not be in keeping with acute rejection alone.

Pentamidine
Pentamidine is incorrect. Pentamidine is an antibiotic used to prevent and treat Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. Patients after renal transplantation, due to immunosuppressants, are at risk of opportunistic infections. However, in this scenario there are no respiratory signs of pneumonia.

Valaciclovir
Valaciclovir is incorrect. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation after transplantation of an organ from a previously infected donor occurs some 4–6 weeks after surgery. A fever with flu-like symptoms fits best with this underlying diagnosis. Minor infection may be managed with valaciclovir or valganciclovir.

stem: A 69-year-old man, who was known to have primary amyloidosis, is found dead in his apartment. Which one of the following is the most probable cause for his death?
explanation:
Cardiac involvement
Primary amyloidosis consists of deposits in the tissues of amyloid (a degradation-resistant fibrillary protein as a β-pleated sheet). In primary amyloid, monoclonal light chains, usually lambda, or light chain fragments from plasma cell dyscrasia form the amyloid sheets. The most common organs involved in primary amyloidosis are the kidney and the liver; involvement of the heart is the most frequent cause of death in primary amyloidosis.

Kidney disease
Amyloid deposits in the kidneys may present with significant proteinuria. Ultrasound of the kidneys may show an increased kidney size, while renal biopsy may show amyloid fibrils with characteristic appearance on electron microscopy, binding to Congo red staining with a characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Progressive amyloid build-up in the kidneys can lead to kidney disease; however, it is not the most common cause of death. Patients may also be eligible to undergo dialysis depending on prognosis at diagnosis. Renal amyloidosis frequently recurs following renal transplantation.

stem: A middle-aged woman is brought in to the Emergency Department after being found collapsed in the local park. No further history is available to you. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 12.4 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 180 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 13.0 mmol/l 3.0–6.0 mmol/l A blood gas is performed and shows the following on room air: pH 7.30 7.35–7.45 pCO 2 4.0 kPa 4.5–6.0 kPa pO 2 13.2 kPa 12–15 kPa Chloride 111mmol/l 95–108 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3-) 18 mmol/l 22–28 mmol/l BE -4.0 mmol/l -2–2 mmol/l Lactate 1.9 mmol/l 0.5–2.2 mmol/l The urine dip is pending. Which one of the following would this fit with?
explanation:
Diarrhoea
The anion gap is calculated as follows: ([Na] + [K]) – ([Cl] + [HCO 3]). This is typically in the range 10–18 mmol/l. If raised, then this suggests a disease process causing addition of anions resulting in a metabolic acidosis. If normal, the primary pathology is due to loss of bicarbonate with a compensatory increase in Cl − to achieve electroneutrality. In this case, the bicarbonate loss from diarrhoea leads to a normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Alcohol excess
Alcohol excess is incorrect. Ethanol is metabolised in the liver to acetic acid, which is converted to acetyl-CoA and can enter the ketotic pathway resulting in the formation of acetoacetic acid and β-hydroxybutyric acid.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. In DKA, a lack of insulin promotes lipolysis that results in the generation of acetoacetic acid, which is a ketone. This can be reduced to β-hydroxybutyric acid and both these acids are responsible for causing a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attended her GP for new-patient screening and was found to be hypertensive: BP 155/90 mmHg. Early retinal changes consistent with hypertension are seen on fundoscopy. A subsequent ultrasound scan reveals kidneys of normal bipolar length. Angiography reveals concentric narrowing of the left renal artery, with no evidence of atherosclerosis in the other areas of the vascular tree on imaging. Which of the following statements best fits the explanation, treatment and outcome for her condition?
options: Angioplasty resolves symptoms in over 90% of patients with this clinical presentation
Her hypertension is likely to be associated with reduced aldosterone secretion
Her renal artery narrowing is likely to be progressive
Her renal artery narrowing progression is variable
She is likely to have atherosclerotic disease elsewhere
explanation:
Her renal artery narrowing progression is variable
The patient in the question fits the picture of a woman with fibromuscular hyperplasia of the renal artery. Renovascular hypertension is the cause of hypertension in 0.2–5% of all hypertensive patients. Acute presentation due to renal artery occlusion may include fever and flank pain. Chronic presentation is associated with occult hypertension, retinal changes consistent with hypertension, episodes of pulmonary oedema in older patients, mild hypokalaemia, or kidney disease following the initiation of angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor therapy. Imaging may include a renal isotope scan, ultrasound to measure differential kidney size and angiography. Renal artery stenosis associated with fibromuscular hyperplasia has a variable course and often does not progress, although blood pressure control is clearly important to prevent associated complications. Angioplasty may result in resolution of hypertension for some patients with fibromuscular hyperplasia. Atherosclerotic renal disease is progressive: in patients with > 60% stenosis, 5% progress to total occlusion by 1 year, 11% by year 2.

stem: A 30-year-old male with kidney failure is about to start haemodialysis. He has a background of progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD), bilateral sensorineural deafness, hypertension and a family history of kidney failure and deafness. What eye abnormality would you expect to find in this patient?
explanation:
Anterior lenticonus
The patient has Alport syndrome. Anterior lenticonus is pathognomonic of the condition and is characterised by the protrusion of the anterior aspect of the lens.

Proptosis
Proptosis is incorrect. This may be an early sign of hyperthyroidism.

Cotton wool spots
Cotton wool spots is incorrect. This finding represents retinal ischaemia with oedema and is a common finding of diabetic retinopathy.

stem: You are called to the Emergency Department to attend to the cardiac arrest of a 60-year-old patient receiving maintenance renal dialysis. Her medication history included a statin, three antihypertensive agents, aspirin and erythropoietin injections. Unfortunately, resuscitation is unsuccessful. Which one of the following is the most common cause of death in renal dialysis patients?
explanation:
Cardiovascular disease
Patients undergoing haemodialysis have a number of risk factors associated with accelerated cardiovascular disease; this includes both traditional and non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Traditional cardiac risk factors include low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, raised triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels due to chronic kidney disease. Hypertension is common and patients require a number of antihypertensive medications to control blood pressure. They may have long-standing vascular disease, including renovascular disease, which precipitated the need for haemodialysis. Many patients have also had co- morbidities that put them at high risk of vascular disease, such as diabetes mellitus. Increasingly, it is recognised that non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors are important, such as a chronically elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and other inflammatory markers, left ventricular hypertrophy and mineral bone disease. Patients who have a high haemoglobin (> 130 g/l) and taking erythropoietin injections have been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular deaths. Taken together, these multiple risk factors lead to a process of accelerated atherosclerosis and high rate of cardiovascular death in renal dialysis patients.

stem: A 50-year-old man has been diagnosed with renal carcinoma; his brother was diagnosed with the same condition 3 years ago. Which one of the following inherited conditions is most likely associated with renal cell carcinoma?
explanation:
von Hippel–Lindau disease
Rarely, renal cancer appears to run in families, when a defect in the short arm of chromosome 3 is found in many cases (88% in one series). von Hippel–Lindau disease is an inherited syndrome in which cysts or tumours in the kidney, pancreas, adrenal gland, epididymis, cerebellum and spinal cord may form. Between one-third and one-half of patients with this condition develop renal cell tumours that are often bilateral and multifocal.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is incorrect. Alport syndrome classically presents with hereditary progressive nephropathy, sensorineural deafness and ocular abnormalities. It is an inherited defect in basement membrane formation in the glomerulus, cochlea and eye. The inheritance is varied, although X-linked inherited mutation in the gene encoding α5 type IV collagen accounts for 80% of cases. This leads to affected males, with female carriers having thin glomerular basement membranes and non-visible haematuria (but rarely renal impairment). Renal carcinomas are not a feature.

stem: You are asked by your orthopaedic colleagues to review a 28-year-old victim of blunt trauma after a motorcycle accident. He has extensive lower limb damage and requires large amounts of analgesia. The orthopaedic surgeons are concerned about his blood results: his K + some hours after the accident is 6.7 mmol/l, calcium is 2.05 mmol/l and urine is positive to dipstick testing for blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Direct renal trauma with perinephric haematoma
explanation:
Rhabdomyolysis
Rhabdomyolysis occurs after an extensive blunt trauma, such as that occurring after a motorcycle accident; it is also common after electrical injury, compartment syndrome, prolonged limb or tourniquet anaesthesia, extensive surgical dissection, and infectious or inflammatory myopathies. Diagnosis is made by the presence of myoglobin on urine dipstick (shows as haematuria), raised serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hyperuricaemia. The rise in CK levels is detectable a few hours after injury and peaks at the 48-hour stage. Aggressive IV fluid replacement is required to prevent acute kidney disease, which may occur in up to 30% of cases of rhabdomyolysis.

Acute sepsis
Acute sepsis is incorrect. Acute sepsis typically presents with fever, hypotension and tachycardia; it is not associated with haematuria alone.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a history of Sjogren syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) comes to the clinic for review. She has recently begun to suffer from increasing lethargy and bony pain. Her medication list includes hydroxychloroquine and low-dose steroids. On examination she has dry eyes and signs of active arthropathy, but there are no other abnormal findings. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 128 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.4 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 16 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Creatinine 138 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.1 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis Type 1
Renal tubular acidosis Type 1 is associated with metabolic acidosis and hypokalaemia. It is recognised as occurring in association with autoimmune pathologies such as Sjogren syndrome and SLE. In this condition there is disordered excretion of acid (H+) ions from the collecting ducts leading to systemic acidosis.

Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is incorrect. The association with autoimmune disease, acidosis and hypokalaemia suggests that the hypocalcaemia is secondary to renal tubular acidosis rather than being a primary diagnosis of osteomalacia.

Renal tubular acidosis Type 2
Renal tubular acidosis Type 2 is incorrect. Renal tubular acidosis Type 2 is usually associated with multiple tubular disorders/Fanconi syndrome. This condition involves an impaired retention of bicarbonate in the proximal tubules with resulting systemic acidosis. Hypokalaemia is present.

Renal tubular acidosis Type 4
Renal tubular acidosis Type 4 is incorrect. Renal tubular acidosis Type 4 is associated with a reduced response to aldosterone, leading to hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis often in patients with mild chronic renal insufficiency, usually caused by tubulointerstitial disease or diabetes. It is the most common of the renal tubular disorders. An identical syndrome may be caused by the chronic ingestion of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which impairs renin and aldosterone secretion.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is where there is a raised parathryoid hormone causing increased bone resorption and formation, haphazardly weakening the bone and leading to the classical condition known as osteitis fibrosa cystica. Biochemical findings include a raised parathyroid hormone (PTH), high alkaline phosphatase, raised phosphate, and the calcium may or may not be raised. Secondary hyperparathryoidism would not cause hypokalaemia and metabolic acidosis; therefore, it is an incorrect option in this case.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with malaise, ankle swelling and shortness of breath. Her BP is 215/140 mmHg, she has +2 peripheral oedema and the skin over her fingers appears very tight and shiny. Fundoscopy discloses bilateral papilloedema. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Plasma creatinine concentration 370 μmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Haemoglobin 89 g/l 115–155 g/l Platelet count 190 × 10 9/l 150-450 × 10 9/l Which one of the following is the pathological hallmark of this condition?
options: Aneurysm formation in the medium-sized arteries
Autoimmune destruction of red blood cells
Functioning adenoma of the adrenal cortex
Mucoid intimal thickening of vascular endothelium
Stenosis of one or both main renal arteries
explanation:
Mucoid intimal thickening of vascular endothelium
The history is suggestive of scleroderma renal crisis, a rare complication of scleroderma associated with the presence of ribonucleic acid (RNA) polymerase antibodies. Severe hyper-reninaemic hypertension may occur; this is frequently associated with a mild microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Underlying this process is a disease of the small vessels resulting in an obliterative vasculopathy and eventual ‘onion-skin’ lesions. Scleroderma does not cause glomerulonephritis. The treatment of choice is angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor control of blood pressure, which may result in improvement in renal function, and may even reverse dialysis-dependent kidney disease. Steroids are contraindicated.

stem: A 21-year-old woman is referred to the renal clinic due to hypertension. She has no significant past medical history but remembers taking antibiotics on a few occasions as a child for urinary tract infections. Only medication of note includes the oral contraceptive and ramipril 10 mg daily for her blood pressure. On examination, her BP is 155/92 mmHg. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 134 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 167 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine dipstick protein ++ Blood ++ Renal ultrasound scan right kidney 11 cm, left 9.5 cm (normal 11–12 cm) Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG)
The recurrent courses of antibiotics as a child suggest the possibility of recurrent urinary tract infection, and the blood and protein seen on dipstick also point towards more recent infection. A VCUG is the investigation of choice to demonstrate potential reflux disease. In addition, the anaemia, coupled with chronic renal impairment, would be in keeping with chronic reflux disease, for which management includes intermittent antibiotic therapy or surgical intervention where an anatomical abnormality has been identified.

Renal biopsy
Renal biopsy is incorrect. A renal biopsy is not required for diagnosis here. A renal biopsy in this case may detect scarring from chronic reflux.

CT abdomen and pelvis
CT abdomen and pelvis is incorrect. A VCUG is needed to confirm reflux. A cystoscopy may be indicated to visualize the bladder if an anatomical abnormality is suspected.

Renal isotope scan
Renal isotope scan is incorrect. With the wider availability of contrast CT and the potential for CT angiography, renal isotope scans are now rarely used.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is incorrect. A VCUG is needed to confirm reflux. A cystoscopy may be indicated to visualize the bladder if an anatomical abnormality is suspected.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line management in a 17-year-old girl presenting with recurrent lower urinary tract infection?
options: Attention to lifestyle measures (e.g. fluid intake, peri-coital hygiene)
explanation:
Attention to lifestyle measures (e.g. fluid intake, peri-coital hygiene)
Recurrent cystitis may often accompany the onset of sexual activity in young females, which is a possibility here. NICE guidelines state that behavioural and personal hygiene measures should be considered prior to specialist investigation or referral. The refore, the appropriate first-line management is to advise strict attention to personal hygiene, and an increase in fluid intake and subsequent urine flow around times of sexual activity, eg post-coital voiding.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is incorrect. Further investigations are only indicated if such simple measures as attention to lifestyle fail to alleviate the problem.

Long-term low-dose trimethoprim therapy
Long-term low-dose trimethoprim therapy is incorrect. Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not usually indicated in young females and may increase the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He had unprotected sex with several partners some 10 weeks earlier at a party. He says that he had a painless ulcer on his penis and some lymph nodes up in his groin, and the ulcer took a few weeks to heal. Over the past 2 weeks he has developed night-time sweats and a generalised, non-itchy erythematous rash affecting his face, palms and soles. His temperature is 37.4°C. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.8×10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 187×10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 82 mm/1 sthour 0–10 mm in the 1 sthour Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 232 µmol/l 50–120µmol/l Urine blood++, protein ++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis is associated with secondary syphilis, the most likely diagnosis here. Treponemal enzyme immunoassay is useful with respect to confirming the presence of syphilis infection. Treatment is with doxycycline orally. Oral azithromycin is the second-line option for patients who are penicillin- allergic. Patients with CNS involvement (not present in this case) are at increased risk of the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction; if this occurs, then prednisolone is the treatment of choice.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy commonly presents with marked haematuria, 48 h after upper respiratory tract infection. In the majority of patients, IgA nephropathy follows a benign course, although kidney failure occurs by 10 years in up to 20% of patients. The cause is unknown; it is not associated with secondary syphilis.

Membranous nephropathy
Membranous nephropathy is incorrect. The peak incidence is in the fourth to the sixth decade of life, with a male to female preponderance of 2:1. It is characterised by IgG-rich immune deposit accumulation in the outer aspects of the glomerular basement membrane due to antibodies directed against an as-yet-unknown antigen. It may be associated with hepatitis and malignancy; it is associated with syphilis, although the marked haematuria here makes it very unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s renal impairment.

Minimal change nephropathy
Minimal change nephropathy is incorrect. Minimal change nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. It presents with proteinuria. Glomeruli appear normal on light microscopy. Fusion of the foot processes of epithelial cells is seen on electron microscopy. The current scenario is not nephrotic syndrome.

Urinary tract infection
Urinary tract infection is incorrect. Urinary tract infection may present with blood and protein in the urine. However, there is an absence of symptoms to suggest this diagnosis, such as dysuria, frequency or suprapubic pain.

stem: A 74-year-old man is referred by his GP with deteriorating functional status. He has undergone an endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm repair 2 weeks earlier. He has a past history of a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) and a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), 3 years ago. On examination his BP is 155/80 mmHg; pulse is 90/min and regular. His feet look mottled and his toes look blue, with distal pulses being noted to be absent in both legs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.3 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 3.2 × 10 9/l 0-0.4 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 78 mm/1st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 19 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Creatinine 231 μmol/l (158 μmol/l on discharge) 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cholesterol emboli
The key point in the history here is instrumentation of his aorta, which raises the possibility of distal cholesterol emboli. The presence of acrocyanosis, absent distal pulses, rising creatinine and eosinophilia, further supports the diagnosis. Management of kidney disease in cholesterol embolism is supportive; unfortunately the majority of patients progress to some degree of chronic renal impairment.

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis would be seen in the initial period after instrumentation, related to a period of hypotension. There is no eosinophilia. Urine dipstick is generally bland with no blood or protein.

Interstitial nephritis
Interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Acute interstitial nephritis occurs in relation to drug exposure; it also occurs in patients with sarcoidosis and Sjogren syndrome. There is no history of the start of new medication in this case.

Renovascular disease
Renovascular disease is incorrect. Renovascular disease is not associated with a rise in eosinophils. Renovascular disease may present with progressive renal impairment, flash pulmonary oedema or resistant hypertension.

Ureteric obstruction
Ureteric obstruction is incorrect. Ureteric obstruction would not present with acrocyanosis and eosinophilia.

stem: A 40-year-old man with a background of hypertension presents with visible haematuria. On physical examination both his kidneys are enlarged and there is also 1 cm hepatomegaly. He remembers his father had kidney disease but does not know what the cause was; his father died of a brain haemorrhage 5 years ago. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
This is the most commonly inherited kidney disease and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Important complications include hypertension, which is often the primary presenting feature, cyst rupture, cyst infection, nephrolithiasis and progressive chronic kidney disease. In addition, a small percentage of patients may develop an intracranial aneurysm, which can result in a subarachnoid haemorrhage if the aneurysm ruptures. Extrarenal cysts are also common and can affect the liver, spleen or pancreas.

Renal amyloidosis
Renal amyloidosis is incorrect. Renal amyloidosis would be suspected in those with an underlying chronic inflammatory autoimmune condition or plasma cell dyscrasia, who develop nephrotic-range proteinuria. It can only be diagnosed on a renal biopsy.

Renal calculi
Renal calculi is incorrect. Renal calculi are not suggestive in the history due to a lack of loin pain.

stem: A woman with long-standing glaucoma and Type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted for an ophthalmological procedure. Her current medications include acetazolamide, metformin and atenolol. The operation is postponed because of an abnormal blood test, although she is asymptomatic. Plasma Na + concentration is 137 mmol/l, K + is 3.5 mmol/l, chloride is 115 mmol/l and bicarbonate is 15 mmol/l. Arterial pH is 7.26 and pCO 2 is 2.9 kPa. Which one of the following is the most probable pathophysiology responsible for the acid–base disturbance?
options: Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
explanation:
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Acetazolamide therapy frequently results in chronic asymptomatic metabolic acidosis, which is associated with a normal anion gap and partial respiratory compensation; this is usually discovered incidentally.

Ketoacidosis
Ketoacidosis is incorrect. An anion gap of approximately 10 mmol/l ( (137 + 3.5) – (115 + 15)) indicates non- gap (‘hyperchloraemic’) acidosis, which excludes ketoacidosis and lactic acidosis, as they are both prominent causes of raised anion gap acidosis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has undergone extensive small bowel surgery for Crohn’s disease presents to the Renal Ward for a follow-up after an acute admission with left renal colic. She is thought to have passed the stone. Further investigations indicate that she has increased urinary oxalate excretion. Which of the following is the optimal treatment to reduce the chance of further renal stone formation?
explanation:
Calcium supplementation
In enteric hyperoxaluria (the diagnosis here), supplemental calcium binds to any free intestinal oxalate, thereby reducing its absorption. Calcium supplementation may provide an additional benefit with respect to bone health, given that calcium absorption is often disordered in patients with small bowel pathology. Patients should also alter their diet, if possible, to reduce the amount of oxalate they consume (examples of very high- oxalate foods include rhubarb and beetroot) and increase their fluid intake. Potassium citrate may have a role in correcting metabolic acidosis, if present.

Colestyramine
Although colestyramine reduces intestinal absorption of oxalate, no trials have shown its efficacy in preventing recurrent stones. Indications for use of colestyramine include hyperlipidaemia that has not responded to diet and other appropriate measures, pruritus associated with partial biliary obstruction primary biliary cirrhosis and diarrhoea associated with Crohn’s disease, ileal resection, vagotomy or radiation.

stem: A 38-year-old man with chronic renal disease undergoing dialysis is anaemic with a Hb concentration of 85 g/l (NR 13.0–18.0); he has normal iron levels. You are considering him for erythropoietin therapy. Which one of the following best fits with the properties of erythropoietin when prescribed for renal anaemia in dialysis patients?
options: It has no effect on cognitive function
Up to 30% of patients may experience a rise in blood pressure
It has no effect on exercise tolerance
It has no effect on sexual function
Quality-of-life scores remain unchanged after erythropoietin therapy
explanation:
Up to 30% of patients may experience a rise in blood pressure
Erythropoietin is a safe and effective means of maintaining haemoglobin in patients who are iron-replete with chronic kidney disease. There are three major preparations: Epoietin-α, epoietin-β and darbepoietin. Erythropoietin is given subcutaneously or intravenously; epoietin-α and Epoietin-β are clinically indistinguishable and usually given subcutaneously 1–3 times per week; darbepoeitin has a longer half-life, so is administered weekly, fortnightly or monthly. The blood pressure, haemoglobin and reticulocyte count should be monitored regularly, every 2 weeks or monthly. Failure to respond may suggest underlying coexistent iron deficiency, bleeding, malignancy or infection. Disadvantages include the cost and a rise in blood pressure in up to 30% of patients, particularly during the first 6 months. There is a rise in peripheral vascular resistance due to a decrease in hypoxic vasodilatation and an increase in blood viscosity. Encephalopathy is a rare complication that results in fits and transient cortical blindness.

It has no effect on cognitive function
It has no effect on cognitive function is incorrect. Cognitive function is improved by erythropoietin.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents for follow up after three episodes of uncomplicated urinary tract infection and one of fever, with left loin and supra-pubic pain. These have been identified as Proteus infections. A left-sided stag horn calculus is identified. Which of the following is the most likely chemical composition of the calculus?
explanation:
Ammonium magnesium phosphate
Ammonium magnesium phosphate, also known as struvite, is formed in response to urinary infections with Proteus, Klebsiella or Serratia, capable of splitting urea to ammonium and hydroxyl ions (thus increasing urinary pH) and predisposing to struvite stone formation. The stones act as reservoirs for infection and often expand to fill much of the collecting system, typically being seen on ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters and urinary bladder (KUB). Treatment depends on size, but may involve nephrolithotomy then lithotripsy. Infection is treated vigorously.

Calcium phosphate
Calcium phosphate is incorrect. Calcium phosphate stones occur in association with a metabolic abnormality in most cases, but may be idiopathic. There is often a family history of renal stones. Risk factors include increased calcium loss in the urine and factors that promote solubility. These include: hyperparathryoidism, hyperuricosuria, hyperoxaluria and hypocitraturia with chronic acidosis.

stem: A patient presents with acute granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Which one of the following presentations has the poorest prognosis?
explanation:
Acute kidney disease requiring dialysis
The presence and severity of renal involvement are indicators of poor prognosis in GPA.

100% active crescents on renal biopsy
100% active crescents on renal biopsy is incorrect. A high proportion of active crescents is not a prognostic indicator.

Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA) positivity
Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA) positivity is incorrect. The presence of cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (c-ANCA), although a useful aid to diagnosis, is not a prognostic indicator.

Extrarenal vasculitis
Extrarenal vasculitis is incorrect. The presence of extrarenal vasculitis is not thought to be indicative of Tutor a poor prognosis – some studies suggest it may place patients into a good prognostic group.

stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes and CKD G4 is admitted with chest pain and acute coronary syndrome, and requires an angiogram. What is the best way to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy?
explanation:
Adequate hydration
Contrast has a direct toxic effect on renal tubular cells. The risk of contrast-induced nephropathy is increased in the elderly with a history of chronic kidney disease and diabetes. The key to prevention is adequate hydration with a regime of 1 ml/kg per h of normal saline 12 h pre- and 12 h post-contrast.

Antibiotics
Antibiotics is incorrect. There is no role for these in preventing contrast-induced nephropathy.

Corticosteroid
Corticosteroid is incorrect. There is no role for this in preventing contrast-induced nephropathy.

stem: A 27-year-old man, who has recently moved to the UK from Pakistan, presents with frequency, dysuria, haematuria and night sweats. He has lost weight over the past few months and his girlfriend noticed that he has a chronic cough. He is a smoker of 20 cigarettes per day. On microscopy of his midstream urine sample there are 30 neutrophils per high power field and urine culture was negative. Which investigation would be most helpful in reaching a diagnosis with respect to the cause of his urinary symptoms?
explanation:
CT urography
Tuberculosis of the urinary tract should be kept in mind in patients presenting with frequency, dysuria, haematuria and fever, particularly in the Asian-immigrant population of the UK. Sterile pyuria is characteristic. Three consecutive early morning urine samples with microscopy on centrifuged urine for acid-fast bacilli (Ziehl– Neelsen stain) and culture (takes 2–4 weeks) is useful for diagnosis. However, in terms of imaging technique, excretion urography may show cavitating lesions in the renal papillary areas, commonly with calcification. There may also be evidence of ureteral obstruction with hydronephrosis.

Non-contrast computed tomography (CT)
Computed tomography of the kidneys and renal tracts is incorrect. It may demonstrate calcification in renal tuberculosis. However, this would not be the primary modality of imaging in this condition, as calcification is non-specific.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with haematuria, haemoptysis, oedema and proteinuria. He is currently being investigated for respiratory symptoms, and has been recently diagnosed with hypertension. Dipstick of his urine shows +3 blood and +3 protein; his blood results show a normal albumin. Which one of the following investigations would be the most appropriate for arriving at a diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
Renal biopsy is the ‘gold standard’ for diagnosis of Goodpasture’s disease (which this patient most probably has) and would show the presence of crescentic nephritis. Immunofluorescence would show a linear ribbon-like deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane.

Anti-nuclear antibody estimation
Anti-nuclear antibody estimation is incorrect. Anti-nuclear antibody titres would not be raised. It is raised in autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, Sjögren's syndrome, polymyositis/dermatomyositis and mixed connective tissue disease; it is not positive in Goodpasture’s disease.

Antistreptolysin O titre (ASO)
Antistreptolysin O titre (ASO) is incorrect. The ASO titre would be raised in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is an immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis that usually occurs in childhood. Typical symptoms include gross haematuria, oliguria, oedema, hypertension and pulmonary oedema;

stem: A 35-year-old man, who has received a renal transplant, presents 6 weeks later with fevers and generalised lymphadenopathy. On examination he looks relatively well. His BP is controlled at 135/75 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular; his temperature is 37.9 oC. The scar over his transplanted kidney is healing well and chest/abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 126 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 10.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 179 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 135 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 62 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 185 U/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 35 g/l 35–55 g/l Alkaline Phosphatase 175 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Biopsy of cervical node Lymphoproliferation Ultrasound of transplant kidney No localised collections Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
CMV
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most likely cause of the lymphadenopathy and abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) seen here, particularly with first symptoms appearing at the 6 weeks’ post-transplant stage.

EBV
EBV is incorrect. Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is an important cause of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD), which is a polymorphic diffuse B-cell hyperplasia or polymorphic B-cell lymphoma. Although this may present with lymphadenopathy, it usually presents over 6 months after the renal transplant.

Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B is incorrect. Hepatitis B is associated with post transplant LFT abnormalities, but these are usually detectable within 1-2 weeks post transplant.

stem: A 30-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents with severe left-sided loin pain and haematuria. He has a past medical history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Blood tests reveal hypokalaemia and acidosis; the anion gap is 11 mmol/l; there is hypercalciuria. Abdominal radiographs show a left ureteric calculus. Which one of the following is the most likely cause for this condition?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis
Distal renal tubular acidosis (type I RTA) may occur in Marfan syndrome. This acidosis is associated with a normal anion gap (i.e. 3–11 mEq). In this condition there is disordered excretion of acid (H +) ions from the collecting ducts leading to systemic acidosis, and it presents with hyperchloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic acidosis.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a serious complication of Type I diabetes, consisting of very high blood glucose levels (> 11mmol/l) and ketones in the blood. The presenting complaint may include nausea or vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, dehydration and reduced level of consciousness. Further information on the recognition and management of diabetic ketoacidosis may be found in NICE guideline NG18 (

stem: A 74-year-old man is noted to have purplish-coloured right third and fourth toes 4 days after coronary angiography and a creatinine level of 240 µmol/l (the creatinine level was normal on admission). He has a history of adult-onset diabetes mellitus, hypertension and a 50 pack-year smoking history. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following statements about it is true?
options: Abnormal creatinine on admission does not increase the risk
Diuretics are the mainstay of treatment
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus is associated
Diabetes mellitus before an investigation increase the risk of developing the condition. Cholesterol crystal (atheromatous) embolisation is a common occurrence in patients with advanced atherosclerotic disease but is often either not recognised or misdiagnosed as 'vasculitis'. The exact incidence is currently unknown, but it is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. With a rise in the number of geriatric patients with arthrosclerosis, the recognition of this disorder is critical to prevent unnecessary diagnostic studies and treatment with high-dose corticosteroids/cytotoxic agents, which are of no benefit. The source of most cholesterol emboli is the abdominal aorta, iliofemoral or renal arteries, but cardiac and thoracic aorta sources have been described. The treatment is supportive.

Abnormal creatinine on admission does not increase the risk
Abnormal creatine on admission does not increase the risk is incorrect. The reverse is true.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents with brown, blood-stained urine after an upper respiratory tract infection. This is the third occurrence of post-respiratory tract infection haematuria in the past four years. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 145/88 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.6 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 245 x 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 54 mm in 1 st h 0–10 mm in 1 st h Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 149 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l IgA Elevated 1.0–4.0 g/l Urine blood Positive and protein Which one of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
options: Diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion
explanation:
Diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion
The history is classical for IgA nephropathy, and his clinical results also fit with this picture. Diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion is most likely to be found on renal biopsy. Immunofluorescence demonstrates deposits of C3, IgA and occasionally also IgG.

C2 staining on immunofluorescence
C2 staining on immunofluorescence is incorrect. Complement staining is associated with active systemic lupus erythematosus.

Glomerulosclerosis
Glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Glomerulosclerosis is associated with diabetes mellitus.

Glomerular microaneurysms
Glomerular microaneurysms is incorrect. Glomerular microaneurysms are not associated with IgA nephropathy and are seen in connective tissue disorders associated with renal impairment and in small vessel vasculitis.

Linear deposits of IgG
Linear deposits of IgG is incorrect. Linear deposits of IgG are most commonly seen in association with anti-GBM disease.

stem: A 42-year-old woman who has undergone a kidney transplant for diabetes-related end-stage renal failure comes to the clinic complaining of excessive hairiness. She takes a number of medications including anti- hypertensives, immunosuppressants and corticosteroids. Examination confirms significant growth of body and facial hair. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is a well-recognised, very common cause of hirsutism. Other pharmaceutical causes of hirsutism include anabolic steroids, danazol, minoxidil, metoclopramide, methyldopa, phenothiazines and progestogens. All other medications listed, apart from ciclosporin, do not significantly increase the risk of hirsutism.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is incorrect. The main risk of azathioprine is the potential for drug interaction with allopurinol, leading to inhibition of metabolism of 6-mercaptopurine and hence risk of bone marrow suppression.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Nifedipine may lead to gum hypertrophy.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with partial lipodystrophy presents with a three-month history of increasing swelling of her legs, which is now up to her knees. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria but no haematuria. A diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome is therefore made. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to help in the definition of the underlying renal pathology?
explanation:
Complement studies
Nephrotic syndrome in an individual with partial lipodystrophy is likely to be mesangiocapillary nephritis with C3 nephritic factor. The latter is an autoantibody, and interacts with the complement pathway to give a low C3 with a normal C4 level.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM)
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti-GBM) is incorrect. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are likely to be negative, as the patient is young and there is no haematuria or pulmonary involvement.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) is incorrect. She has no upper or lower airway involvement to suggest ANCA-positive vasculitis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with a history of recurrent urinary tract infection presents with a 3-week history of increasing left flank pain, fever, anorexia and weight loss. On examination a left-sided abdominal mass is palpable. Her white cell count is 17.5 × 10 9/l, Hb is 81 g/l and plasma creatinine is 190 μmol/l. There is a significant growth of Klebsiella spp. in her urine. Biopsy of the mass reveals a large number of lipid-laden macrophages. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP)
The case in question is the typical presentation of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP). Although rare, this is increasing in incidence. It develops as an abnormal macrophage response to infection, particularly in the presence of urinary tract obstruction, and is pathologically related to malacoplakia. A flank mass is usually palpable, thereby distinguishing it from simple acute pyelonephritis or renal abscess, and occasionally mimicking renal cancer. The disease is almost invariably unilateral and patients with XGP often appear chronically ill. Symptoms include anorexia, fevers, weight loss and flank pain. Computed tomography is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis, and it will show the replacement of renal parenchyma by rounded, low-density areas surrounded by a ring of enhancement; it will also establish the extent of the lesion (which may involve surrounding structures). The course may also be indolent and protracted, extending over months or years. In these cases, AA amyloidosis may develop, resulting in the onset of nephrotic syndrome

stem: A 78-year-old retired textile worker is noted to have painless haematuria on routine urinary dipstick by her GP. Her only past history of note is arthritis, for which she takes anti-inflammatories. Plain abdominal X-ray reveals no evidence of renal stones. Routine bloods reveal increased plasma viscosity and mild anaemia, with a Hb of 105 g/l and a ferritin just below the normal range. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bladder cancer
Bladder cancer has an increased association with cigarette smoking, occupational exposure to dyes or petroleum products, and chemical exposure to nitrosamines. Later-stage disease may also precipitate abdominal pain or kidney disease due to obstruction. In the Western world, around 93% of bladder cancers are of the transitional cell (TCC) type, squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) comprise around 6% of the total and adenocarcinomas less than 1%. At the time of diagnosis, around 70% of carcinomas are still localised to the bladder, 20% extend to involve regional lymph nodes and 3% present with distant metastases. Some 80% of superficial bladder tumours are said to recur. Bladder cancer characteristically presents with painless haematuria, which may be gross, or non-visible haematuria detected on dipstick in early-stage disease. Treatment of choice for localised tumours is transurethral tumour resection, with the use of intravesical chemotherapy where required.

stem: A 33-year-old man has hepatosplenomegaly. He has a urine output of 1.5 l/day with 2.2g proteinuria. His blood results reveal a serum calcium of 2.95 mmol/l, Cr 60 μmol/l and normal-sized, non-obstructed kidneys at ultrasound. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is the most likely diagnosis, the clues being the high calcium level and hepatosplenomegaly. Although this condition may be asymptomatic, it commonly presents with fatigue, weight loss, arthritis, dry eyes and breathlessness, and can lead to an acute or chronic interstitial nephritis. The classical feature is the presence of non-caseating granulomata (with giant cells). It may occasionally present with a glomerulonephritis, most often membranous, which would account for the proteinuria and impaired renal function in this case. The renal disease usually responds well to steroids.

Weil’s disease
Weil’s disease is incorrect. Weil’s disease (due to leptospirosis) results in oliguric acute kidney disease; it would not present with hypercalcaemia or proteinuria. Typical symptoms of Weil's disease include headaches, myalgia, fever and breathlessness due to pulmonary haemorrhage.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) on dialysis and diabetic nephropathy presents for a routine visit. She feels generally very weak and easily fatigable and has itchy skin. Her breathlessness has been progressively getting worse over the last six months. She denies any obvious bleeding from other sites of the body. She was diagnosed with type I diabetes at 24 years of age. She maintains a healthy and balanced diet. Her medications include insulin, aspirin, atorvastatin, ramipril and furosemide. On examination, her temperature is 37 °C, her heart rate is 80 bpm and her blood pressure is 145/86 mmHg. There is conjunctival pallor. Cardiac auscultation shows soft ejection systolic murmur best heard along the right upper sternal border. Sensation to pinprick is reduced over dorsum of both feet. Investigations show the following: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 80 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 84 fl 76–98 fl Creatinine (Cr) 274 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Ferritin 145 µg/l 10–120 µg/l Urea 17 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Reticulocyte count 0.6% 0.5–1.5% Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s fatigue and breathlessness?
explanation:
Decreased erythropoietin production
The heart murmur on auscultation is a flow murmur due to anaemia. Normocytic anaemia in a patient with CKD occurs because of decreased production of erythropoietin (EPO) by renal peritubular cells. Diabetes can also lead to microvascular damage in the bone marrow, which results in a reduced response to EPO. As a result, erythropoiesis is reduced and normocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte count develops.

Chronic occult blood loss
Chronic occult blood loss usually from gastrointestinal tract is most common cause of iron deficiency anaemia in adults. They will have microcytic anaemia and low ferritin level, which is not the case here.

Drug-induced bone marrow failure
Drug-induced bone marrow failure, which causes aplastic anaemia, can be caused by a variety of drugs, most commonly carbamazepine, methimazole, propylthiouracil and chemotherapeutic agents. Non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like the aspirin that this patient is taking, can occasionally induce aplastic anaemia. NSAID-induced aplastic anaemia, however, is extremely rare and would manifest with pancytopenia (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), which is not seen in this patient.

stem: Which one of the following conditions is most commonly associated with large kidneys despite advanced kidney disease?
explanation:
Amyloidosis
Besides amyloidosis, other causes of large kidneys include: Stage 1 diabetic nephropathy Hydronephrosis Acromegaly Renal vein thrombosis Adult polycystic kidney disease

Analgesic nephropathy
Analgesic nephropathy is incorrect. Sclerotic injury would result in scarring and kidney shrinkage.

Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis is incorrect. Longstanding hypertension would result in scarring and kidney shrinkage.

stem: An 82-year-old man is admitted with confusion. There is no evidence of acute infection. On examination there is a mass in the lower abdomen above his pubic symphysis. Blood testing reveals a urea of 42.1 mmol/l, creatinine 540 μmol/l and a potassium concentration of 6.7 mmol/l. He is given IV calcium, and insulin and dextrose. Which one of the following is the next most appropriate treatment intervention?
explanation:
Urinary catheterisation
This man has evidence of post-kidney disease with urinary obstruction and bladder distension, the most likely cause being benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). 80% of men have evidence of prostatic hypertrophy by the age of 80 years. Based on case series, prostatic carcinoma is found in 10–30% of patients with BPH; however, BPH is not considered to be a direct cause of prostate cancer. In this scenario, the initial treatment of choice is urinary catheterisation. It is vitally important to watch for the inevitable post-obstructive diuresis that occurs once the obstruction is relieved, and strict fluid–balance charting is essential so that losses can be adequately replaced. Medical or surgical intervention for problems associated with BPH is required in > 20% of men by 70 years of age. The medical treatment of choice involves alpha blockade for rapid symptom relief and 5α-reductase inhibitors to reduce prostate volume.

Furosemide therapy
Furosemide therapy is incorrect. Furosemide therapy is likely to result in further worsening of kidney Chat disease with by inducing intravascular depletion.

stem: A 56-year-old diabetic man came in for acute breathlessness in the middle of the night. There was no previous history of retinopathy or nephropathy. Chest X-ray revealed evidence of pulmonary oedema. His HbA1c is 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%), and his blood pressure (BP) was 180/112 mmHg. Investigations showed: Cr 251 μmol/l, urine dipstick protein +1 and blood +1. Which one of the following would best explain the above findings?
explanation:
Glomerulonephritis
Diabetic nephropathy does not normally present with non-visible haematuria as well as proteinuria; hence, the combination of haematuria and proteinuria suggests glomerulonephritis as a possible cause. In the absence of retinopathy, the presence of haematuria and proteinuria is strongly predictive of a non-diabetic cause (positive predictive value 94%). Further investigation of this patient involves urine microscopy for red cell casts, assessment of renal function by estimation of creatinine clearance and quantification of proteinuria. Renal biopsy may be useful to further elucidate the underlying cause. Presentation with cardiac failure in glomerluloneprhtis is secondary to pulmonary oedema related to hypertension.

Acute urinary tract infection
Acute urinary tract infection is incorrect. Acute urinary tract infection may present with blood and protein in the urine, but it would not account for the pulmonary oedema.

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted with acute kidney injury of undetermined aetiology. His creatinine is 1564 μmol/l and his urea is 76 mmol/l. His blood pressure is 200/110 mmHg, he is oliguric, and he has pulmonary oedema confirmed on chest radiography. A dual lumen dialysis line is inserted into his right subclavian vein, and the position is confirmed by chest radiograph. He is urgently commenced on haemodialysis, in a recumbent position, with a target weight loss of 1.5 kg. One hour into dialysis, he begins to complain of nausea, headache and blurred vision. Shortly afterwards, he becomes confused and disorientated. His blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Intravascular volume contraction resulting from rapid ultrafiltration
explanation:
Disequilibrium syndrome
These symptoms are typical of disequilibrium syndrome, which is caused by cerebral oedema, resulting from the rapid shifts of uraemic toxins associated with too-rapid haemodialysis in a severely uraemic patient.

Air embolism
Air embolism is incorrect. The symptoms of air embolism depend on the position of the patient. In a recumbent patient, air foam inside the heart impairs cardiac performance. air embolism is thus incorrect.

stem: An 18-year-old student presents to the clinic via his GP. He presented at first with facial oedema, but this rapidly progressed to involve significant peripheral pitting oedema. On examination in the clinic, he has an elevated blood pressure (BP) of 145/85 mmHg. There are no other abnormal findings.
