Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190×10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120µmol/l Albumin 22 g/l 35–55 g/l Urinary albumin excretion 31mg / 24hrs <30 mg/24hrs Renal biopsy Minimal change nephropathy Which of the following agents is likely to have the greatest impact in reducing proteinuria in this condition?
explanation:
Prednisolone
Corticosteroids are the treatment of choice for minimal change disease, which has been confirmed in this patient by proteinuria and renal biopsy. This treatment leads to the resolution of proteinuria over the course of 16 weeks in 80% or more of patients. Chronic kidney disease is extremely rare in patients who are steroid responsive, and survival rates are 90%+ in adults who develop minimal change disease after 10 years.

Ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is incorrect. Chlorambucil and cyclophosphamide, not ciclosporin, are typical preferred second-line agents for the treatment of minimal-change disease.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Steroids are the first-line treatment. If patients fail to respond to corticosteroids, then chlorambucil or cyclophosphamide are potential additional options.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is incorrect. Diltiazem is indicated to control blood pressure and reduce proteinuria in the event that ramipril is not tolerated.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Steroids are first line, but ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the blood pressure agents of choice, with the aim of both controlling blood pressure and further reducing proteinuria in the event that more marked hypertension is seen.

stem: A 45-year-old man on lithium for a bipolar disorder developed congestive heart failure 2 weeks ago. He now presents with drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, blurred vision and coarse tremors. Which one of the following concurrent medications, if taken in combination with lithium, would be most likely to cause these symptoms?
explanation:
Hydrochlorothiazide
Approximately 95% of a single dose of lithium is eliminated in the urine. The drug is handled by the kidneys in the same manner as sodium: most of the filtered lithium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Hence, loading with sodium will increase lithium excretion, while sodium depletion will promote the retention of lithium. All diuretics decrease renal lithium clearance; however, thiazide diuretics cause the greatest retention of lithium among all diuretics. Useful mnemonics/memory tools: You may want to remember the site of action of diuretics using a mnemonic: 'COLT Pee'. In the sequential site of action along the nephron: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (at the proximal convoluted tubule) Osmotic diuretics (at the loop of Henle) Loop diuretics (at the ascending loop of Henle) Thiazides (at the early distal convoluted tubule) Potassium-sparing diuretics (at the distal section of the distal convoluted tubule) Diuretics make patients pee like a horse, hence 'COLT Pee', because colt is a male horse.

stem: A 18-year-old boy is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and is started on treatment. A month later he presents with anorexia, malaise and fever. Laboratory investigations show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 128 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 2.8 × 10 9/l 0 - 0.4 × 10 9/l Urea 27 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 440 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urinalysis shows numerous pus cells but is negative for AAFBs on staining. Which one of the following conditions could be the most likely cause?
explanation:
Acute interstitial nephritis
The presence of pus cells in the urine during treatment with medications suggests interstitial nephritis. The eosinophilia points towards acute interstitial nephritis as opposed to renal tuberculosis or urinary tract infection. Chat A number of drugs (ß-lactams, sulfonamides, rifampicin, ethambutol, erythromycin) cause an with AI acute Tutor allergic reaction with infiltration of immune cells.

stem: You are asked to review a 56-year-old man with myocardial infarction who is on the third day of his admission. There is a history of arthritis for which he uses non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), but nil else of note. During his admission, he had a short period of atrial fibrillation that reverted spontaneously, and a period of left ventricular failure for which he was treated with high dose diuretics. It has been noted that his urine output is tailing off. His serum creatinine level has now risen from 156 μmol/l (60–110) on admission to 195 μmol/l, and his urea is 12 mmol/l (2.5–7.5). His urine osmolality has been measured at 1000 mosmol/kg (350–1000), with a low urine sodium at 15 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pre-renal uraemia
The urine results in the present patient suggest pre-renal uraemia, with raised urine osmolality and appropriately low urine sodium. It is likely that the patient in the present case received large amounts of diuretics at the time of admission and that this, coupled with any period of hypotension, is likely to have led to a drop in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and pre-renal uraemia. Drugs that impair renal autoregulation (e.g. angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)) may increase the tendency to develop the problem. All causes of pre-renal uraemia may lead to the development of established parenchymal kidney damage if not correctly managed.

stem: A 71-year-old patient with rheumatoid arthritis has been using above the normal recommended daily dose of NSAIDs to control her pain. Additional medication includes low-dose prednisolone and indapamide for hypertension. Over the past few weeks she has become increasingly lethargic and is now having nausea daily; she also has bilateral flank pain. On examination her BP is 148/93 mmHg. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 134 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 230 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine protein ++, blood + CT renal tract – bilateral small kidneys, ring shadows in the medullae, renal pelvis filling defects. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Papillary necrosis
A history of excessive use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), coupled with diuretic use, which may exacerbate any renal hypotension, leading to the clinical picture and computed tomography (CT) appearance is classic for papillary necrosis. Where there is demonstrable obstruction, review by a urologist is advised as ureteric stent placement may be required. If there is no obstruction then withdrawal of the offending agent, coupled with adequate hydration is the treatment of choice

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. This presents with a rapid deterioration in renal function and urine contains renal tubular epithelial cells.

Interstitial nephritis
Interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Interstitial nephritis is associated with blood and proteinuria, coupled with an elevation in eosinophils.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is incorrect. This is associated with marked proteinuria in the absence of the CT changes seen here.

Minimal-change disease
Minimal change disease is incorrect. CT changes are not present in minimal change disease, and it presents most often in children and young adults.

stem: A 26-year-old man registers with a new GP and is noticed to have non-visible haematuria, so is referred to the Renal Clinic. You note on further questioning that his mother had a history of deafness, but apparently his parents divorced and he has no further contact with his mother and could not comment on her current health status. On examination, his blood pressure is elevated at 150/85 mmHg. He also has evidence of deafness. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 197 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 190 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood + Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Alport syndrome
The combination of deafness, non-visible haematuria and developing kidney disease is classical for Alport syndrome. Skin biopsy is the least invasive way of confirming the diagnosis.

Goodpasture syndrome
Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. Goodpasture presents as a rapidly progressive vasculitis leading to pulmonary and renal haemorrhage.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. IgA nephropathy presents with episodes of haematuria, often after a respiratory tract infection.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. In polycystic kidney disease, renal masses are apparent on examination coupled with haematuria. There is also no link to deafness.

Renal carcinoma
Renal carcinoma is incorrect. At this age, and given the positive family history of deafness and kidney disease, an inherited renal condition such as Alport is much more likely to be the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with glycosuria at a new patient screening. Her fasting blood glucose concentration was 4.8 mmol/l (3.0–6.0). Body mass index (BMI) was 23 (18.5–24.9). Serum lipid screen, liver function testing and full blood count were normal. Glucose tolerance test showed a blood glucose of 5.0 mmol/l at 2 h after 75 g oral glucose. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Renal glycosuria
Glycosuria is unusual where no other urine abnormality is identified, the blood glucose concentration is normal and no other metabolic abnormalities are identified. Either there is a defect in the tubular threshold for glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule (a so-called ‘splayed’ reabsorption curve) or a defect in the maximum tubular reabsorption of glucose. The abnormality appears to run in families in some cases, and both autosomal- dominant and -recessive inheritance patterns have been described. In this case, renal glucose excretion appears to have no clinical significance. However, where glycosuria is present it is important to rule out diabetes mellitus or other tubular disorders such as Fanconi syndrome.

Impaired glucose tolerance
Impaired glucose tolerance is incorrect. This is a pre-diabetic state of hyperglycaemia, it may herald future onset of type 2 diabetes mellitus and is a risk factor for cardiovascular events. There will be a normal or mildly raised Chata with fasting blood glucose. The diagnosis lies in a 2 h glucose that is raised (7.8-11.0 mmol/l) after 75 gAIoral Tutor glucose tolerance test.

stem: A 68-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has multiple myeloma and has recently begun suffering from symptoms of right heart failure. You suspect that he may be suffering from cardiac amyloidosis. Which type of amyloidosis is most commonly associated with myeloma?
explanation:
AL amyloidosis
AL or light chain amyloidosis is seen in amyloidosis where immunoglobulin forms insoluble fibrillar deposits. These monoclonal light chains are usually lambda or light chain fragments. This more commonly occurs in males (2:1) compared with females, also in older adults (>50 years). Prognosis is poor.

AA amyloidosis
AA amyloidosis is incorrect and is seen in chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. It is described as a reactive amyloidosis resulting from the deposition of serum amyloid A proteins (acute phase reactant). Prognosis depends on the cause of the inflammation.

Beta-2 microglobulin amyloidosis
Beta-2 microglobulin is incorrect. It is a component of MHC class 1 molecules and accumulates to form amyloid plaques in patients undergoing long-term dialysis. It is also used to estimate overall myeloma load and hence prognosis.

stem: A 32-year-old man is referred to the clinic with refractory hypertension and a slow deterioration in his creatinine. On further questioning it transpires that his brother now requires renal replacement therapy. He has an ultrasound scan of the abdomen which is highly suggestive of polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Which one of the following proteins is associated with the development of the condition?
explanation:
Polycystin
Polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is thought to be related to an abnormal form of a protein known as polycystin. The precise mechanism by which abnormal polycystin leads to cyst formation is not known, although it may lead to changes in the pattern of epithelial cell maturation and tubular cell formation in the kidney

Anticystin
Anticystin is incorrect. Anti-cystin antibodies are used as a diagnostic tool in evaluation of biopsy specimens.

Elastin
Elastin is incorrect. Mutations in the elastin gene are associated with cutis laxa and supravalvular aortic stenosis.

stem: A 24-year-old man is found to have proteinuria on screening for medical insurance. On close questioning he complains of a burning sensation in his hands and feet. Blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg. He has several blanching red papules over his legs and buttocks and his urine protein:creatinine ratio is 164g/mol. An ECG reveals left ventricular hypertrophy and first-degree heart block. Audiometry is normal and a family history is negative for significant cardiovascular or renal disease. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the proteinuria?
explanation:
Fabry disease
This presentation is typical of Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder characterised by myelin deposits in tubular epithelium and vascular endothelium, resulting in ischaemic nephropathy. The molecular defect is a deficiency of α-galactosidase A. The most efficient means of diagnosis is by slit-lamp examination of the cornea, which reveals microscopic lipid deposits. Microscopy of the spun urine sediment may demonstrate ‘Maltese cross’ lipid globules. Further clues to the diagnosis include skin angiokeratomas, decreased sweating and leg lymphoedema. The condition may be complicated by peripheral neuropathy, which is usually burning in nature, and cardiac conduction defects are frequently present. Premature cerebrovascular disease is also a complication.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is incorrect. Deafness and haematuria would be expected in Alport Syndrome.

stem: You are asked to review in clinic a 26-year-old woman has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by her GP, which is proving difficult to manage. She has a history of three presentations with urinary tract infection as a child and two as a young adult. A urine screen by the GP has revealed asymptomatic bacteriuria, which he elected not to treat. Her current hypertension medication is amlodipine 10 mg po daily. Her blood pressure in the clinic is 145/85 mmHg. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next course of action?
options: Add enalapril to her antihypertensive medication
Repeat her urine sample and give antibiotics if necessary
explanation:
Arrange excretion urography testing
Chronic reflux nephropathy should be suspected in the presence of multiple urinary tract infections, including during childhood. This may explain the presentation in the present case at a young age with difficult-to-treat hypertension. The investigation of choice is excretion urography, which may show an irregular renal outline, calyceal clubbing and cortical scarring on the affected side. The best course of action is to recognise this condition in childhood and consider surgical management where demonstrable ureteric reflux exists, or early intervention with antibiotics where repeat infection exists. At this stage, scarring has developed and hypertension is already well established. Unfortunately, chronic reflux nephropathy is a relatively common cause of kidney failure in late childhood or early adult life if it goes unrecognised.

stem: A 74-year-old man has a history of a fusiform aortic aneurysm under surveillance. He is reviewed by the GP and found to be suffering from malaise, and back pain for the last few weeks. His blood results show a normochromic normocytic anaemia, raised ESR and a creatinine level of 285 μmol/l (60–110 μmol/l). CT scanning suggests that there may be a periaortic mass. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Retroperitoneal fibrosis
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is three times as common in men as it is in women. Retroperitoneal fibrosis has a recognised association with abdominal aortic aneurysm and prolonged exposure to methysergide, although it may also be idiopathic. The cause is thought to be an autoallergic response from the leak of ceroid material out of atherosclerotic plaques. The ureters become embedded in dense retroperitoneal fibrous tissue, causing unilateral or bilateral ureteric obstruction. This may extend from L2 as far as the pelvic brim. Excretion urography reveals ureteric obstruction at the level of the pelvic brim. Treatment is with corticosteroids medically, and with surgical stenting of the ureteric obstruction. Response to treatment with steroids may be assessed with serial measurements of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), supplemented by radiological examination. Relapse often occurs when steroids are withdrawn, so long-term follow-up is mandatory.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with left loin pain and is diagnosed with a left sided kidney stone which passes without intervention. She is previously well, on no regular medication, and attends the clinic for follow up. There is no family history of kidney stones, or any other medical conditions. Physical examination is entirely normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 102 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.90 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Phosphate (PO 4 3-) 0.7 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Magnesium (Mg 2+) 0.9 mmol/l 0.85 - 1.10 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism
This patient has symptomatic hypercalcaemia with normal creatinine and phosphate just below the lower limit of normal. This fits with primary hyperparathyroidism (option B) with hypercalciuria leading to renal stone formation. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels will be either inappropriately normal or elevated. Treatment is surgical, in the case of four-gland hyperplasia, a subtotal procedure to remove three of the glands is usually performed. In the case of tertiary hyperparathyroidism where the patient is unfit to undergo surgery, cinacalcet may be an option.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is an autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor gene (CASR). It is characterised by hypercalcaemia, hypocalciuria, hypermagnesemia and normal to low levels of parathyroid hormones. This condition is rare and less likely to be the correct diagnosis here - patients are often asymptomatic and the condition is usually picked up incidentally.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is characterised by an abnormal collection of inflammatory cells known as granulomas. This commonly affects the skin, lungs or lymph nodes. There may be hypercalciuria and hypercalcaemia in <10% of individuals from increased vitamin D production. The absence of other symptoms such as dyspnoea, fatigue, arthritis or dry eyes makes this diagnosis less likely. Sarcoidosis does not present with renal stones.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is defined by an excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone in response to hypocalcaemia. In this scenario the calcium is raised, which therefore excludes this diagnosis.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is described by an excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone after a long period of secondary hyperparathyroidism and resulting in a high blood calcium level and high phosphate levels. In this scenario the phosphate is only just below the normal limit, which makes this diagnosis less likely.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is reviewed eight months after a live renal transplant from her sister. Initial studies on the transplanted kidney showed it to be functioning well. You examine her and she has a well healed transplant scar, with nil else of note. Her post operation notes show a very slight rise in temperature to 37.4 oC the day after surgery, however she is currently apyrexial. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 114 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 160 µmol/l (125 taken 1 week earlier) 50–120 µmol/l Ciclosporin level 305 ng/ml <300 ng/ml Renal ultrasound normal sized kidney CT renal angiography blood flow appears normal within the transplant Which of the following is the most likely cause of the slight deterioration in her creatinine?
explanation:
Delayed graft rejection
Acute rejection, infection and ciclosporin toxicity can be excluded. Acute graft rejection would be expected during the first 4 weeks, ciclosporin is only just above the upper limit of normal, and the white blood cell count appears to be in the normal range. Therefore, of the options listed, delayed (chronic) graft reaction as the most likely diagnosis. There are several mechanisms of transplant rejection. Hyperacute rejection due to presence of recipient antibodies against the donor kidney occurs within minutes of revascularisation kidney swells and becomes discoloured there is clumping of red blood cells (RBCs) and platelets, fibrin is deposited and interstitial haemorrhage occurs rarely seen because of antibody cross-reactivity testing transplant nephrectomy is required. Acute rejection defined as an acute deterioration in allograft function that is associated with specific pathological changes in the graft. The two principal forms of rejection are acute cell-mediated rejection and acute antibody-mediated rejection acute rejection must be differentiated from other causes of graft dysfunction and/or similar biopsy findings, eg post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) or polyomavirus BK virus, because these may necessitate reduction rather than increase in immunosuppression cell-mediated rejection common in first two weeks but can occur up to six months after transplantation mononuclear cell infiltration occurs in the interstitium and subsequently in vessel walls treatment with high-dose steroids (often reversible) difficult to distinguish clinically from acute tubular necrosis (ATN) or drug nephrotoxicity. Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR). Diagnosis of AMR is provided by the presence of at least three of the following four criteria: graft dysfunction histological evidence of tissue injury positive staining for C4d presence of donor-specific antibody. Chronic renal transplant rejection:

stem: Which one of the following statements is true regarding retroperitoneal fibrosis?
options: Bilateral swelling of the legs is often due to inferior vena cava obstruction
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is a recognised association
Low back pain is the most common presenting symptom
Pizotifen (migraine treatment) is implicated in causing similar disease
Kidney disease is due to fibrous tissue infiltrating the kidneys
explanation:
Low back pain is the most common presenting symptom
Retroperitoneal fibrosis is one of the multifocal fibrosclerotic syndromes, which also includes mediastinal fibrosis, sclerosing cholangitis and Riedel’s thyroiditis. It is more common in males (2:1), with peak incidence in the fifth and sixth decades. The process usually begins over the promontory of the sacrum and extends laterally across the ureters and as high as the second or third lumbar vertebra. Hence low back is the most common presenting symptom. This may be accompanied by fever and weight loss. Diagnosis is suggested by the finding at intravenous pyelography of displacement of the ureters toward the midline. Thromboembolism and hypertension are recognised complications. Methysergide, a semi-synthetic ergot alkaloid used to treat migraine headache, can cause a similar syndrome. Other drugs such as beta blockers, methyldopa and hydralazine are also implicated.

Bilateral swelling of the legs is often due to inferior vena cava obstruction
Bilateral swelling of the legs is often due to inferior vena cava obstruction is incorrect. The fibrosing process may surround the inferior vena cava, but obstruction of that vessel is uncommon.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with vomiting, general malaise and weakness 5 weeks after delivering a healthy male infant. The pregnancy had been uncomplicated with no hypertension evident. Her blood pressure is now 210/110 mmHg, serum creatinine is 650 μmol/l and potassium is 6.9 mmol/l. Haemoglobin is 76 g/l, associated with a platelet count of 65 × 10 9/l, reticulocytes of 7%, normal clotting indices and lactate dehydrogenase levels of 800 IU/l. Which one of the following most accurately describes the underlying pathological process?
explanation:
Thrombotic microangiopathy
The differential diagnosis of acute kidney injury in the setting of pregnancy includes post-partum haemolytic– uraemic syndrome (HUS), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (which occurs invariably antepartum and usually before 24 weeks, and is associated with relatively mild kidney injury) and the HELLP syndrome (which is usually preceded by a history of pre-eclampsia and is characterised by evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation). All may be complicated by acute cortical necrosis, resulting in oligoanuria, haematuria and flank pain. The history is typical of post-partum haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS), which usually occurs 4–6 weeks post-partum and is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, severe irreversible kidney disease and hypertension. Schistocytes are evident on the blood film but the clotting indices are normal, the latter helping to distinguish it from the HELLP (haemolysis–elevated liver enzymes–low platelets) syndrome, which is far more common. In cases of post-partum HUS it is important to consider the possibility of retained products of conception.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for the fourth time this year with fever and signs of infection. One previous admission was for right lower lobe pneumonia, the others for urinary tract infection. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril and amlodipine, and he suffered an inferior myocardial infarction 3 years ago, since when he has been taking simvastatin 40 mg daily. On examination, his BP is 134/82 mmHg. He is pyrexial (37.9 °C) and has a heart rate of 90 bpm. His cardiovascular and respiratory examination is normal. There is suprapubic tenderness on abdominal palpation; PR reveals a smoothly enlarged prostate. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 247 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 149 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine Blood ++, protein ++ What next additional investigation would you recommend to elucidate the cause of his recurrent UTI?
explanation:
Post-void residual bladder volume measurement
If the suspicion is of prostatic hypertrophy, then post-void residual volume is the best way to estimate the degree of bladder obstruction. If there is significant evidence of chronic urinary retention, then combination alpha blocker 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy, intermittent catheterisation or transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) would be potential options.

CT pelvis
CT pelvis is incorrect. The smoothly enlarged prostate is the key feature here, driving BPH, and a post-void residual bladder volume measurement is the best way to assess the functional effect of it, rather than a CT.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is incorrect. Cystoscopy is most useful for visualising bladder lesions rather than a functional assessment of bladder emptying.

Intravenous Urogram (IVU)
IVU is incorrect. An IVU is best for imaging renal and ureteric abnormalities.

Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) measurement
PSA measurement is incorrect. Although PSA may be slightly elevated, measuring it would not contribute towards determining the cause of the recurrent UTI.

stem: A 62-year-old man attends the Nephrology Clinic. His background is CKD 4 presumed due to diabetic nephropathy, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and previous duodenal ulcer. He reports feeling generally tired. He feels he has a poor quality of life and is unable to really do anything because of absolute exhaustion, but there are no other systemic symptoms. You review his blood tests with him, which show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 91 g/l 135–175 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 84 fl 76–98 fl Ferritin 315 µg/l 20–250 µg/l Iron saturation 24% 15–45% Vitamin B12 345 pmol/l 160–900 pmol/l Folate 7.5 µg/l 2.0–11.0 µg/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 13.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 243 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l eGFR 22 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 What is the best course of action to manage his anaemia?
explanation:
Erythropoietin (EPO)
He has a normocytic anaemia with normal B12, folate and iron stores. His anaemia is likely due to chronic kidney disease as a result of decreased EPO production. EPO acts on EPO receptors on erythroid progenitor cells, preventing apoptosis, and thus helps to maintain red cell numbers and improve the Hb concentration. In the setting of chronic kidney disease, target Hb levels should be 110–120 g/l, as evidence shows that higher Hb levels result in increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. In correcting his anaemia, you should ensure that his haematinics are first all corrected prior to initiating EPO therapy. Follow-up blood tests will then be arranged to ensure a response to EPO is observed.

Blood transfusion
A blood transfusion is incorrect. This is a chronic picture and there is no urgency to correct his Hb, such as active bleeding. If his Hb was found to be less than 70 g/dl, then you may wish to consider a blood transfusion, while correcting any haematinic deficiency.

Oral iron
Oral iron is incorrect. His iron stores (represented by ferritin) are normal. The transit pool represented by the iron saturations [(serum iron/total iron binding capacity) × 100] is also normal. In chronic kidney disease, measurement of ferritin and iron saturations should be performed together and their results can be interpreted as shown below: Absolute deficiency Relative deficiency Ferritin Low Normal/high TSAT Low Low An absolute deficiency is reflected by low iron stores. The transferin saturation (TSAT) will be low as there is no iron to circulate around the body. In a relative deficiency, often reflective of an inflammatory state, the ferritin, which is an acute-phase reactant, will be elevated but iron stores are sequestered to limit ongoing inflammation and as a result iron does not get released to transferrin, which is why the TSAT will be low.

IV iron
IV iron is incorrect. There is no evidence of iron deficiency from his blood tests.

stem: A 53-year-old woman is sent as an emergency to you with an acute-onset headache and deteriorating conscious level. Her husband mentions that her brother has recently had a kidney transplant, although he is not sure why. What condition may be running in the family?
explanation:
Polycystic kidney disease
Intracranial aneurysms occur in approximately 10% of individuals with autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), and approximately 50% of patients with ADPKD have kidney failure by age 60 years. It is a relatively common genetic disorder and there are two known ADPKD genes – PKD1, accounting for about 85% of cases, and PKD2, accounting for about 15% of cases.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome causes kidney disease and deafness. The question does not mention deafness, which a question relating to Alport almost always will.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Cerebral atriovenous malformations can occur in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and these may result in intracerebral bleeding, but the kidneys are not typically involved.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a six-month history of fatigue. On examination, her BP is 110/72 mmHg. She has several patches of hyperpigmented skin on her trunk. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na +) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 64 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Persistent hyperkalaemia is associated with which of the following?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis type 4
Renal tubular acidosis type 4 results from an effective deficiency of mineralocorticoids, either through medications (e.g. NSAIDs reducing renin release, or ACE-inhibitors), Addison’s disease, or some congenital enzyme defects. The aldosterone deficiency means that there is less sodium resorption and consequently less potassium excretion, leading to a hyperkalaemia. Acidosis is uncommon in renal tubular acidosis type 4.

stem: You are asked to review a 25-year-old man whose urine output has fallen off some 48 hours after admission following a road traffic accident. On examination, his BP is 90/70 mmHg, pulse is 80 bpm and regular. JVP is just visible. The chest is clear and there is no ankle swelling. Creatinine has increased from 90 µmol/l on admission to 145 µmol/l now, and urinary sodium is markedly increased. His dipstick urine was negative for blood and protein. For a patient with this renal presentation, which of the following is the most common complication and cause of death?
explanation:
Infection
This man's renal presentation is acute tubular necrosis due to an ischaemic renal insult. Sepsis, particularly Gram-negative septicaemia, is the most frequent complication and cause of death in acute renal tubular necrosis while awaiting spontaneous recovery of renal function. Infections, when detected, should be treated promptly, bearing constantly in mind the need to avoid nephrotoxic medications and use drugs excreted by the kidneys with appropriate precautions, such as alteration of the dosage and monitoring of blood levels. Neither the use of prophylactic antibiotics nor barrier nursing has been shown to reduce infection risk in this situation.

Congestive heart failure
Congestive heart failure is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis could lead to fluid retention and congestive heart failure. However, since this man is brought into the Emergency Department, frequently dialysis Chattreatment with may be given to avoid this complication. Furthermore, in a young man with no previous cardiac history, congestive

stem: A characteristic of type I renal tubular acidosis is:
options: It may occur as a result of amphotericin toxicity
It is always due to a genetic disorder
It is caused by a failure of bicarbonate secretion
explanation:
It may occur as a result of amphotericin toxicity
Distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA, type I) may occur due to gene defects or specific effects of toxins or drugs such as amphotericin. A number of disorders predominantly affect the distal tubule, including hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, medullary sponge kidney, sickle cell disease and chronic urinary obstruction. In complete distal RTA there is persistent hyperchloraemic acidosis.

Hypovolaemia is a specific feature
Hypovolaemia is incorrect. Bicarbonate and potassium supplements should be given to maintain adequate plasma levels. Hypovolaemia is not a specific feature.

It is always due to a genetic disorder
It is always due to a genetic disorder is incorrect. A number of disorders predominantly affect the distal tubule, including hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, medullary sponge kidney, sickle cell disease and chronic urinary obstruction.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent sinusitis, cough productive of blood stained sputum and haematuria and proteinuria on routine urine testing. On examination, she looks unwell. Her BP is 159/92 mmHg. Further investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 490 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 245 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 65 mm in 1 st h 0–10 mm in 1 st h C-ANCA + Which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?
explanation:
Segmental crescenteric necrotising glomerulonephritis
The history and clinical findings here are entirely consistent with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Necrotising granuloma formation and small vessel vasculitis with the presence of giant cells is the cardinal feature of granulomatosis with polyangiitis as well an association with positivity for cANCA. In renal biopsy this is manifest as segmental crescenteric necrotising glomerulonephritis. High dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide are the mainstay of therapy for granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Microaneurysm formation
Microaneurysm formation is incorrect. This is more likely to be seen in patients with renal connective tissue diseases and small vessel vasculitis.

Focal glomerulosclerosis
Focal glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is not associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, it’s more likely to be associated with other forms of vasculitis.

Non-caseating granuloma formation
Non-caseating granuloma formation is incorrect. This is associated with sarcoidosis.

Large artery vasculitis
Large artery vasculitis is incorrect. Large artery vasculitis is more likely to be associated with cardiac chest pain, mesenteric angina, and aortic valve regurgitation.

stem: A 54-year-old man who is taking allopurinol for gout presents with a rash, fever of 38°C and mild haematuria. He has a urea of 15 mmol/l and creatinine 175 μmol/l. Full blood count shows the presence of eosinophilia. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following features is most likely to be present?
options: Effectiveness of steroid treatment in terminating the episode
Improvement in clinical features following withdrawal of the drug
explanation:
Improvement in clinical features following withdrawal of the drug
The majority of patients recover following withdrawal of the offending drug. Allopurinol causes acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). Eosinophils may be found in the urine in nearly 70% of patients. This finding, if present, however, is not specific for AIN as it may be present in other conditions such as urinary tract infection and cholesterol micro-emboli. Around half of patients will have eosinophilia on blood testing and eosinophils may be present in renal biopsy. Typically, eosinophilia is absent in AIN-induced by NSAIDs. Patients with non-oliguric acute kidney disease should always be investigated for AIN.

Effectiveness of steroid treatment in terminating the episode
Effectiveness of steroid treatment in terminating the episode is incorrect. There is no proof that corticosteroids are effective in drug-induced AIN.

stem: A 17-year-old man is being investigated for nephrotic syndrome. He has a past medical history of hypertension. His blood tests show a normal cholesterol level and there was +3 protein in the urine. Renal biopsy is suggestive of minimal change nephropathy. Which one of the following is most likely to be found in a blood test?
options: Presence of a monoclonal band on protein electrophoresis
explanation:
Normal high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels
Nephrotic syndrome is a syndrome comprising the triad of proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and peripheral oedema. Although serum cholesterol levels are usually raised in nephrotic syndrome, it is the low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations that are elevated; high-density lipoprotein cholesterol is usually normal.

Low C3 complement concentration
Low C3 complement concentration is incorrect. Serum C3 levels are decreased in immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis.

Presence of a monoclonal band on protein electrophoresis
Presence of a monoclonal band on protein electrophoresis is incorrect. A monoclonal paraprotein band is present in multiple myeloma. This disorder may also cause renal amyloidosis. Therefore, there is no monoclonal band in minimal change nephropathy.

stem: A 36-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use is found to have haematuria on dipstick. His blood pressure is 170/90 mmHg, he is systemically well and he has a small peripheral oedema. Plasma creatinine is 140 μmol/l, bilirubin is 65 μmol/l, ALT is 78 IU/l and his uPCR is 466 g/mol. Microscopy of the spun urine sediment reveals the presence of red cell casts. Complement C3 is 0.5g/l (NR 0.7–1.3) and C4 is 0.09g/l (NR 0.12–0.27). Which one of the following is the aetiology of the renal abnormalities?
explanation:
Infection with hepatitis C
Hepatitis C is now considered the principal cause of ‘idiopathic’ mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis (MCGN), an immune complex deposition disorder that presents with a mixed nephritic–nephrotic picture associated with pan-hypocomplementemia. It is also closely associated with the development of cryoglobulinemia. Other chronic sources of immune complexes, such as hepatitis B, schistosomiasis, chronic abscess, malaria and leprosy, may also be associated with MCGN.

Bacterial endocarditis
Bacterial endocarditis is incorrect. Infectious endocarditis is the principal differential diagnosis and may present with haematuria and hypocomplementemia. However, hypertension is unusual and other manifestations of infection, such as fever, would usually be present. Glomerulonephritis associated with endocarditis leads to hypercellularity and immune complex deposition on biopsy.

stem: A 24-year-old man was referred to clinic after routine blood tests at an occupational health check-up were abnormal. He had no existing diagnoses but had had lethargy and intermittent muscle spasms since childhood. Examination was normal; his blood pressure was 132/76 mmHg and his pulse rate was 68 bpm. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 2.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Chloride 91 mmol/l 98–106 mmol/l Magnesium (Mg 2+) 0.38 mmol/l 0.75 –1.00 mmol/l Urea 6.3 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 82 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 24-h urinary sodium 260 mmol 100–250 mmol 24-h urinary potassium 160 mmol 25–120 mmol What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Gitelman syndrome
This is an autosomal recessive condition usually caused by mutations in the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride symporter. This leads to hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesiaemia, with increased urinary sodium and potassium loss. Patients do not develop hypertension.

Conn syndrome
Conn syndrome is hyperaldosteronism caused by an adrenal adenoma. It leads to hypertension (not present in this patient) and sodium retention; you would expect serum sodium to be in the normal range or high, rather than low, and you certainly would not expect urinary sodium to be raised. This patient’s combination of normotension, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesemia, hypochloraemia and increased urinary sodium and potassium would be consistent with Gitelman syndrome.

Cushing syndrome
Cushing syndrome is excess glucocorticoids; these have a partial agonist effect at the mineralocorticoid receptors, leading to sodium retention (not seen here; this patient has increased urinary sodium and low serum sodium) and hypertension (this patient is normotensive). This patient’s combination of electrolyte deficiencies and urinary excretion of sodium and potassium in the context of a normal blood pressure would be typical for Gitelman syndrome.

Liddle syndrome
Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant type of pseudohyperaldosteronism; patients with Liddle’s are hypertensive, which is not the case here. It also causes excess urinary sodium resorption, but this patient has urinary sodium loss as evidenced by the increased urinary sodium and decreased plasma levels. This patient’s combination of a normal blood pressure with these electrolyte disturbances would be consistent with Gitelman syndrome.

Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is incorrect. Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension, which is not seen in this case. It would typically cause some renal disturbance but these blood results are normal in this patient. This patient’s combination of a normal blood pressure with these electrolyte disturbances would be consistent with Gitelman syndrome.

stem: You are reviewing a 79-year-old man who has had multiple myeloma for the past three years. He presents with lethargy, muscle aches and pain in his lower back. Arterial blood sampling reveals a metabolic acidosis. Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/l (3.5-4.9), and urine pH is 5.2. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis-type II
Proximal renal tubular acidosis (RTA type II) occurs due to decreased proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to hypokalaemia, hyperchloraemia and a metabolic acidosis. Causes of proximal RTA include Fanconi syndrome, primary hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma and medications such as acetazolamide.

Renal tubular acidosis-type IV
Type IV or hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronaemic RTA is related to diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease and Addison’s disease.

Renal tubular acidosis-type III
Type III RTA is historically described as a failure to generate NH 3 in the setting of a decreased glomerular filtration rate, resulting in normokalaemic hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and shares features of proximal and distal RTA. However, this is now not considered by many to be a condition in its own right.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with renal stones. He admits on further questioning to having intermittent polydipsia and polyuria and feeling quite washed out. You find out that his father also had a problem with kidney stones and, because of this, was always told to drink a lot of fluid. The man has a history of indigestion and has been taking some over-the-counter antacid regimens. On examination his blood pressure (BP) is 125/82 mmHg, with pulse is 75/min and regular. Other clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.5 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 204 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 119 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.86 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l PTH Just above the normal range 24 h urinary calcium excretion 180 mg (low) Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) is the most likely diagnosis, given the family history (FHH usually follows an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern) and the history of renal stones. Many patients with FHH are misdiagnosed with hyperparathyroidism, but the difference is that in FHH, urinary calcium excretion is low. The most common presentation is with renal stone disease. Patients rarely have episodes of acute pancreatitis, but the incidence of pancreatitis in association with FHH appears to be greater for males than females.

Milk alkali syndrome
Milk alkali syndrome is incorrect. Although this patient is taking antacids, which could cause milk alkali syndrome, this condition is not hereditary and does not cause renal stones.

Myeloma
Myeloma is incorrect. This is the wrong age group for myeloma, and it is not hereditary.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is seen in patients with chronic renal impairment.

Vitamin D intoxication
Vitamin D intoxication is incorrect. Vitamin D is not contained in commonly used antacid preparations.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with nausea and lethargy. The general practitioner (GP) has been treating her for essential hypertension with ramipril and her latest on-treatment blood pressure (BP) has been recorded at 149/89 mmHg. Other past history of note includes a symmetrical polyarthropathy, which may be rheumatoid arthritis, and a history of recurrent urinary tract infections as a child. On examination, she looks pale and thin, her BP is 165/90 mmHg. There are bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count 6.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l (WCC) Platelets 179 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 387 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l no evidence of obstruction,small kidneys with thinned USS renal tract cortices Urine protein +, blood - Which one of the following is most appropriate for confirming the likely underlying aetiology of her kidney disease?
explanation:
Micturating cystourethrogram
A micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) is a specialised X-ray test that visualises the urinary bladder and urethra while the bladder fills and empties. This test is particularly useful for diagnosing vesicoureteric reflux, a condition where urine flows backwards from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys, leading to recurrent urinary tract infections and potential kidney damage. The patient's history of recurrent UTIs in childhood and the finding of small kidneys with thinned cortices strongly suggest chronic reflux nephropathy. Therefore, an MCUG is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the presence of vesicoureteric reflux, which is likely the underlying cause of her kidney disease.

Renal biopsy
A renal biopsy is a procedure used to obtain a small piece of kidney tissue for examination under a microscope. While this can be useful for diagnosing various types of glomerular diseases or systemic conditions affecting the kidneys, it is invasive and carries some risk. In this scenario, the history of recurrent urinary tract infections in childhood strongly suggests a structural issue, such as vesicoureteric reflux, rather than a primary glomerular disease. Therefore, a renal biopsy would not be the most appropriate first-line investigation to confirm the underlying aetiology in this context.

MR angiography
MR angiography is a non-invasive imaging technique used to visualise blood vessels and assess for vascular abnormalities such as renal artery stenosis. However, the patient's clinical presentation, including a history of recurrent UTIs and small kidneys with thinned cortices, does not suggest a vascular cause for her kidney disease. Furthermore, MR angiography often requires the use of contrast agents, which can be problematic in patients with impaired renal function. Given these considerations, MR angiography is not the most suitable investigation for this case.

CT abdomen
A CT scan of the abdomen can provide detailed images of the abdominal organs and is useful for assessing structural abnormalities and masses. However, in this case, the specific concern is vesicoureteric reflux, which a CT abdomen is not well-suited to diagnose. Additionally, CT scans often require the use of iodinated contrast, which can be harmful to patients with significantly impaired renal function. Thus, a CT abdomen is not the most appropriate investigation to confirm the aetiology of kidney disease in this patient.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with mild jaundice, ankle swelling, nausea and anorexia. Serology reveals the presence of hepatitis B sAg and eAg. Blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg, urinalysis discloses +3 protein without haematuria, and he has gross bilateral pitting lower limb, sacral and abdominal wall oedema. His plasma creatinine concentration is 110 μmol/l, albumin is 11 g/dl and his urine protein:creatinine ratio is 754 g/mol. Which one of the following is the cause of the proteinuria?
explanation:
Membranous nephropathy
It has been proposed, although not proven, that subepithelial deposition of HBeAg and anti-HBe antibody results in membranous nephropathy in the setting of hepatitis B infection. The subepithelial space (between glomerular basement membrane and parietal epithelial space) is relatively immunologically privileged, compared to the subendothelial space (between vascular endothelium and glomerular basement membrane). Immune deposits in this region of the glomerulus tend to result in proteinuria without much in the way of active inflammation, whereas those in the subendothelial space (as may be seen in postinfectious glomerulonephritis and mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis) tend to result in ‘nephritic syndrome’, with haematuria and urinary casts.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome may be caused by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, but the concurrent presence of hepatitis B makes membranous nephropathy much more likely.

stem: A 78-year-old woman has been admitted in a dehydrated and confused state to the Emergency Department. She has a history of cervical carcinoma. Her bloods are markedly abnormal: K + of 7.2 mmol/l (NR 3.5–4.9), Cr 450 μmol/l (NR 60–110) and urea 31.2 mmol/l (NR 2.5–7.5). You repeat the serum potassium and it is still markedly raised. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management in this case?
options: Arrange continuous ECG monitoring and consider giving 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate iv
Arrange an urgent renal ultrasound scan
Give 250 mg furosemide iv to reduce the potassium concentration
Consider a third blood sample to confirm hyperkalaemia
explanation:
Arrange continuous ECG monitoring and consider giving 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate iv
Once true hyperkalaemia is confirmed via a repeat blood sample, the management pathway is clear: continuous ECG monitoring is a prerequisite. Intravenous administration of 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate should be considered for cardioprotection. As insulin drives potassium ions from the extracellular to the intracellular compartment, 50 ml of 50% dextrose containing 10 U of insulin should be considered as the next intervention.

Arrange an urgent renal ultrasound scan
Other management for this particular patient is likely to include central venous pressure monitoring, catheterisation for close monitoring of fluid balance and an urgent ultrasound scan to determine the underlying cause of her renal dysfunction. Although this would not be the initial management to treat hyperkalaemia, it should be done after the patient is stabilised.

stem: You are asked by your surgical colleagues to review a 70-year-old man with acute pancreatitis. He is clearly very unwell, and the surgeons have noticed deteriorating renal function. His current urine output is around 5 ml/h, with a raised urine sodium concentration of 55 mmol/l. The surgeons have been keeping him well filled, and a recent central venous pressure was measured at 16 mm H 2O. The latest serum creatinine that you have is 320 μmol/l (60–110 μmol/l). Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
ATN is associated with pancreatitis and a number of other conditions associated with hypotension and shock, such as haemorrhage, burns, diarrhoea and vomiting and myocardial infarction. Aminoglycosides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors and platinum-based chemotherapeutic agents may also be associated. In this case ATN is likely to have developed from a period of renal ischaemia, associated with hypotension and shock during the early period of his admission for pancreatitis. Helpful pointers towards a diagnosis of ATN include a urine osmolality <350 mosmol/kg, urine sodium >40 mmol/l and a fractional sodium excretion of >1%. Urinary sodium measurement is useful in differentiating between pre-renal and intrinsic renal dysfunction. The prognosis of ATN varies according to the severity and duration of the renal insult, but recovery of renal function typically occurs after 7–21 days, but may take up to 6 weeks in total. The mortality rate associated with ATN may be up to 50%, but this is largely dependent on the precipitating illness.

stem: A 74-year-old man with a background of heart failure has a fall at home and remains on the floor for up to 8 hours before a neighbour finds him and calls 999. He is on furosemide 80 mg and ramipril 5 mg. He has been previously well, with creatinine chronically in the 110-140 µmol/l range. He has extensive bruising over his left hip and thigh. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 22 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 340 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely cause for the nephrotoxic insult?
explanation:
Myoglobin
This patient has rhabdomylosis, whereby the long lie would have resulted in a pressure ischaemic injury to muscles and myonecrosis. Myoglobin is the main nephrotoxic agent in rhabdomyolysis; it is released into the circulation as a result of cell death and is freely filtered at the glomerulus, resulting in tubular cast Chat formation with

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with bilateral flank pain. Her GP had diagnosed a urinary tract infection (UTI) 2 weeks earlier on the basis of her symptoms and the presence of proteinuria, but she returned with further pain, tiredness and general malaise. The GP then noted a raised serum creatinine of 285 μmol/l at this time. Repeat urinalysis revealed dipstick blood and protein, but no bacterial growth. Her only past medical history is that she discontinued the oral contraceptive pill after a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 3 years ago. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Inadequately treated UTI with associated kidney disease
explanation:
Renal vein thrombosis
The clue in the question is that the patient appears to have a hypercoagulable state and has discontinued the pill due to DVT. Patients with a coagulation disorder are at increased risk of renal vein thrombosis. Abdominal ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or renal arteriography (delayed films during the venous phase) may be useful in making the diagnosis; selective renal venography may also be considered. Acute anticoagulation is useful in preventing worsening of renal function and proteinuria. The value of long-term anticoagulation is unclear, except in those patients with membranous renal disease or multiple incidences of thrombosis. Studies of the long-term prognosis in this condition are rare, but some long-term renal damage is to be expected.

stem: A 30-year-old male patient attends the hospital with worsening leg swelling. Investigations reveal him to have nephrotic syndrome. Which of the following blood tests is most likely to be raised?
explanation:
Cholesterol
The pathogenesis of this remains unclear, but is associated with increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis containing cholesterol.

Albumin
Albumin is incorrect. In nephrotic syndrome, by definition, the albumin is low.

Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is incorrect. This would likely be normal.

Potassium
Potassium is incorrect. This would likely be normal.

stem: A 54-year-old man with type II diabetes presents for review. His annual review bloods reveal a raised creatinine of 165 μmol/l, potassium of 5.9 mmol/l and bicarbonate of 19 mmol/l. Urinary protein excretion is normal. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis (RTA)-type IV
Type IV RTA, also known as hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, is commonly associated with diabetes mellitus. This condition is characterised by hyperkalaemia and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. The underlying issue is a defect in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to decreased aldosterone production, which in turn impairs potassium excretion and hydrogen ion secretion by the distal tubules. This explains the patient's elevated potassium level and metabolic acidosis despite a relatively preserved glomerular filtration rate (GFR). The lack of significant proteinuria further supports the diagnosis, as type IV RTA typically does not cause significant protein excretion.

Renal artery stenosis (RAS)
Renal artery stenosis (RAS) would typically present with hypertension due to reduced renal perfusion and subsequent activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Although it can cause chronic kidney disease, it is less likely to result in the degree of metabolic acidosis observed in this patient. RAS usually does not lead to significant hyperkalaemia unless there is concurrent use of medications affecting the renin- angiotensin system. Furthermore, RAS-associated acidosis would more likely correlate withChat the degree of renal with impairment, which seems disproportionate in this case.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents for a second opinion with severe, unrelenting, left flank pain with episodes of red urine. This has been present intermittently for 2 years. In addition, she complains of headache and a sensation of her own heartbeat. Urinalysis reveals +3 blood with no protein; urine microscopy discloses numerous dysmorphic red cells with some red-cell casts. The urine is sterile on culture. Renal ultrasound shows normal kidneys and no calculi are visible on plain X-ray. Her plasma creatinine concentration is 65 μmol/l and her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Loin pain–haematuria syndrome
Loin pain–haematuria syndrome is a poorly defined disorder characterised by loin or flank pain that is often severe and unrelenting and haematuria with dysmorphic features, suggesting a glomerular origin. Some have suggested that these patients have a subtle disorder affecting the renal vasculature, although this has not been a consistent finding. A recent report suggested an important psychological component, with patients often demonstrating medically unexplained symptoms. One possible explanation for the haematuria in some patients is coexistent thin basement membrane disease. One study found thin basement membranes in 7 of 15 patients in whom renal biopsy was performed for evaluation of possible loin pain–haematuria syndrome. It was proposed that bleeding into and obstruction of the renal tubules was responsible for the loin pain. The disorder is extremely difficult to treat; dependency on narcotic analgesia is common. Some patients undergo autotransplantation of the affected kidney in an attempt to relieve the pain; however, this is not generally advised as the disorder appears to settle, albeit often after > 10 years.

stem: A 32-year-old man with previous chronic kidney disease has undergone a successful renal transplantation. He has developed some symptoms related to his immunosuppressants. Which of the following symptoms is a recognised association of immunosuppression therapy?
options: Reduced incidence of new diabetes mellitus
Increased incidence of new diabetes mellitus
explanation:
Increased incidence of new diabetes mellitus
Both corticosteroids and cyclosporine are a common cause of new-onset diabetes. The incidence of new-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT) is greatest during the first 6 months post-transplantation, when the doses of immunosuppressants are at its highest. Renal transplant recipients with NODAT have similar complications as Type 2 diabetes in the general population, such as more cardiovascular events. As a result, it is suggested that there should be a risk assessment of patients before transplant, and least diabetogenic agents are chosen for those at highest risk.

Reduced incidence of new diabetes mellitus
Reduced incidence of new diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Other complications of corticosteroids include ‘mooning of the face’, skin striae, increased skin fragility, bruising and new Type 2 diabetes.

stem: A 45-year-old man had recurrent nephrolithiasis. Renal function tests and serum calcium measurements were normal. A 24-h urine collection revealed (normal range in brackets): Investigation Result Normal Value Volume 3 litres Calcium 15 mmol/24 h 2.5–7.5 mmol/24 h Oxalate 200 mmol/24 h 90–450 mmol/24 h Uric acid 3 mmol/24 h 1.48–4.45 mmol/24 h Citrate 2 mmol/24 h 0.3–3.4 mmol/24 h Which one of the following is the most useful therapy to reduce stone formation?
explanation:
Thiazide diuretic
Thiazide diuretics are the drug treatment of choice as they act directly on the renal tubule to reduce urinary calcium excretion. Potassium citrate supplementation also reduces calcium stone formation.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents to the general practitioner (GP). Most recently, he has suffered a respiratory tract infection and he is very distressed that on going to the bathroom he is urinating frank blood. The only history of note is non-visible haematuria diagnosed in childhood. Renal biopsy with histological staining is consistent with a diagnosis of Alport’s syndrome. Which of the following other features is likely to be present?
explanation:
Sensorineural deafness
Alport’s is the combination of nephritis and sensorineural deafness. It follows either an autosomal recessive or an x-linked pattern of inheritance. The condition is caused by abnormalities in Type IV collagen. Non-visible haematuria always presents within the first decade of life, and patients may present with acute visible haematuria post upper respiratory tract infection. Angiotensin inhibitors may have a role to play in reducing proteinuria and slowing progression of renal disease.

Red-green colour blindness
Red-green colour blindness is incorrect. Alport’s is associated with progressive retinopathy rather than red- green colour blindness.

stem: A 17-year-old boy with a history of Bartter syndrome comes to the clinic for review. He has failed to thrive in childhood, and is now of relatively short stature, at only 160 cm in height. His blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg and his BMI is 19. Which of the following findings would you definitely expect to find?
explanation:
Hypokalaemia
Bartter syndrome is characterised by hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis in the presence of normal blood pressure. There is also increased urinary loss of calcium and magnesium; this is in contrast to Gitelman syndrome, which is associated with reduced calcium excretion.

Hypercalcaemia
Urinary loss of calcium means that calcium is usually normal or at the lower end of the normal range.

Hyperkalaemia
Metabolic alkalosis is associated with hypokalaemia.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with renal colic. Dipstick urine shows blood and protein. She is diagnosed with renal calculi. What would be an absolute contraindication to lithotripsy in her case?
explanation:
Uncorrected coagulation disorder
Lithotripsy is a treatment that involves the use of ultrasound waves to pass through the abdomen to break up renal calculi. To ensure that the procedure is safe, any uncorrected bleeding disorder is an absolute contraindication to lithotripsy. It is important to stop any oral anticoagulants, such as clopidogrel or warfarin, and allow normalisation of clotting before the procedure. Other absolute contraindications to lithotripsy include: acute urosepsis, pregnancy and uncorrected obstruction distal to the stone.

Cardiac pacemaker
Cardiac pacemaker is incorrect. This is a relative contraindication, although seeking advice from a cardiologist for any possible changes to the pacemaker settings during the procedure would be prudent.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has had burning pain and peripheral neuropathy in her hands and feet for the past 18 months. She is known to have a problem with alcohol and drinks 4–6 bottles of wine per week. She also has rheumatoid arthritis. On examination her BP is 125/72 mmHg. Her JVP is raised 6 cm and she has ankle oedema and hepatomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 105 g/l 115–155 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 102 fl 76–98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 142 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 17 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 150 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) 166 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Alkaline Phosphatase 156 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 10 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Urine protein +++ Chest X-Ray no evidence of cardiomegaly Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis for her symptoms?
explanation:
Amyloid neuropathy
The history and clinical and laboratory findings in the present case clearly suggest severe neuropathy and raise the question of both right heart failure and nephrotic syndrome. Against the background of rheumatoid arthritis and a probable chronic inflammatory state, inflammatory amyloidosis is the most likely underlying aetiology. Rectal or renal biopsy is likely to yield the diagnosis. The aim of therapy is to maximise treatment of the underlying inflammatory condition, reducing the pro-inflammatory state that promotes amyloid accumulation.

Alcoholic neuropathy
Alcoholic neuropathy is incorrect. The marked proteinuria seen here is more consistent with amyloidosis as the cause of microvascular dysfunction, including neuropathy here.

B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency is incorrect. B12 deficiency isn’t associated with hepatomegaly or marked proteinuria seen here, both pointers to amyloidosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the Renal Clinic with long-standing chronic kidney disease. He is suffering from associated metabolic bone disease, and his GP has asked for an explanation of the causes and features of metabolic bone disease. Which one of the following best describes the biochemical changes involved?
options: Levels of 1,25-OH vitamin D are increased
Phosphate excretion is decreased, parathyroid hormone levels are increased and 1,25-OH vitamin D
Phosphate excretion is increased, parathyroid hormone levels are increased and 1,25-OH vitamin D
explanation:
Phosphate excretion is decreased, parathyroid hormone levels are increased and 1,25-OH vitamin D
levels are decreased Phosphate excretion is decreased, parathyroid hormone levels are increased and 1,25-OH vitamin D levels are decreased.

Levels of 1,25-OH vitamin D are increased
Levels of 1,25-OH vitamin D are increased is incorrect. Levels of 1,25-OH vitamin D are decreased, not increased.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred for aldosterone studies for the investigation of resistant hypertension. He is currently taking amlodipine, bendroflumethiazide, doxazosin, ramipril and spironolactone. His General Practitioner advises him that most of these medications need to be stopped before the test date. Which medication can be continued?
explanation:
Doxazosin
Alpha blockers such as doxazosin have very little effect on the renin-angiotensin system; they function by inducing vasodilation at post-ganglionic receptors. Alpha blockers can be continued.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Calcium channel blockers function by impairing intracellular calcium signalling, leading to smooth muscle dilation. They have variable effects on renin and aldosterone; they may inhibit the secretion of aldosterone. Consequently they should be stopped at least two weeks before any aldosterone studies.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Thiazide diuretics inhibit resorption of sodium from the distal convoluted tubules; salt depletion stimulates the release of renin and therefore can affect an aldosterone assay. Thiazides should be stopped at least two weeks before any aldosterone studies.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with symptoms of prostatism. He has a smoothly enlarged prostate on rectal examination, and prostatic biopsy is consistent with benign disease. Which one of the following classes of drug is the most appropriate to relieve symptoms?
explanation:
Alpha-adrenergic antagonist
Alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists such as tamsulosin, doxazosin and prazosin have action on α-1a adrenergic receptors found on the prostate, leading to improvement in symptoms of bladder outflow obstruction within a few days of starting therapy. Although not first line for the treatment of hypertension, they are effective blood pressure lowering agents. Tamsulosin is specific for alpha-1a receptors and thus causes less hypotension than other agents, making it preferable for isolated prostatic symptoms.

Alpha-adrenergic agonist
Alpha-adrenergic agonist is incorrect. Alpha-adrenergic agonist has different effects depending on the receptors of action. Alpha-1 agonists stimulate phospholipase C and are used as vasopressors, nasal decongestants and as mydriatic agents for opthalmic examinations. Alpha-2 agonists inhibit adenylyl cyclase activity and may be used as anti-hypertensives, sedatives and treatment of opiate overdose. Alpha-adrenergic agonists do not have a role in prostatism.

stem: A 65-year-old man with congestive heart failure who has received an excess amount of furosemide is now found to have hypochloraemic alkalosis. He has a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease. Which of the following investigative results would be most characteristic of this disorder?
explanation:
Hypokalaemia
The alkalosis is maintained by persistent contraction of the extracellular fluid volume and secondary hyperaldosteronism. Hypochloraemic alkalosis is associated with severe hypokalaemia.

Expanded extracellular fluid volume
Expanded extracellular fluid volume is incorrect. Diuretics such as furosemide acutely diminish the extracellular fluid volume.

Fall in pa (CO2)
Fall in p a (CO 2) is incorrect. There is an increase in p a (CO 2) to maintain homeostasis.

stem: A 73-year-old man is admitted hypothermic and unconscious, having been found collapsed on his kitchen floor. He is known to have diabetes, with previous alcohol excess. Biochemistry reveals a significant metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 8 mmol/l), Na + 139 mmol/l, K + 4.5 mmol/l, chloride 97 mmol/l and glucose 5.6 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the likely biochemical diagnosis?
explanation:
Lactic acidosis
The anion gap is calculated by subtracting the bicarbonate plus chloride concentration from the sodium and potassium concentration; the normal range is 10–16 mmol/l. The patient in the present case therefore has an elevated anion gap. In patients with elevated anion gap, it is important to identify the ‘exogenous’ anion; the most common are salicylate, ketoacids (in diabetic ketoacidosis) and lactic acid. You may find the mnemonic 'CAT MUDPILES' helps you remember some cause of high anion gap metabolic acidosis: cyanide poisoning, aminoglycosides, toluene, methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paracetamol, isoniazid, lactic acid, ethanol, salicylates.

Alcohol ketoacidosis
Alcoholic ketoacidosis is incorrect. A metabolic acidosis that typically occurs in people who chronically abuse alcohol and have a recent history of binge drinking, little or no food intake and persistent vomiting. This could potentially be the cause in the current case, but the normal potassium and sodium make this less likely, as these would more likely be low if excessive vomiting had occurred.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with a background of diet-controlled diabetes is in her 7 th year of haemodialysis. She visits her GP with symptoms of numbness and tingling in her left hand for the last 3 weeks, and also reports pain affecting both her shoulders over this time period. On examination there was no obvious joint deformity, but clinical evidence of carpal tunnel syndrome was present in the left hand. Which one of the following diagnoses best fits with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Dialysis-related amyloidosis
This is characterised by the accumulation of β2 microglobulin. This is a component of class 1 human leukocyte antigens (HLA), and is usually freely filtered at the glomerulus, reabsorbed and metabolised in the proximal tubule. The accumulation and deposition of β2 microglobulin in those with chronic kidney disease tends to occur in patients on haemodialysis for at least 5 years. Carpal tunnel syndrome and a chronic arthropathy, initially affecting the shoulders bilaterally, are most commonly seen. Other joints affected include knees, wrists and the small joints of the hand; periarticular soft-tissue swelling may occur.

Diabetic neuropathy
Diabetic neuropathy is incorrect. Diabetic neuropathy is unlikely given the patient likely has good diabetic control (she is not requiring oral hypoglycaemics or insulin), and it would not explain her arthralgia.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with known SLE presents with ankle swelling. Her blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg and she has marked lower limb oedema. Urine dipstick discloses +3 protein with no haematuria. Plasma creatinine concentration is 101 μmol/l, albumin is 12 g/dl and urine protein:creatinine ratio is 699 g/mol. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Class V lupus nephritis
Nephrotic syndrome without haematuria in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) suggests membranous nephropathy (class V). The lesion is differentiated from idiopathic (non-lupus) membranous nephropathy by the presence of tubuloreticular structures on electron microscopy, immune deposits along the tubular basement membrane (in addition to the glomerular basement membrane) and the presence of concurrent subendothelial and mesangial immune deposits (in addition to the subepithelial deposits typical of membranous). Class V lupus nephritis is the only form of renal disease in SLE where serological and clinical manifestations of the underlying disease may be absent. Complement levels may be normal and dsDNA antibodies may be absent. Lupus nephritis is staged according to the classification revised by the International Society of Nephrology: Class I: Minimal mesangial lupus nephritis, mildest form of glomerular involvement Class II: Mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis Class III: Focal lupus nephritis Class IV: Diffuse lupus nephritis Class V: Membranous lupus nephritis

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department for review. She is convalescing with her daughter 6 weeks after receiving a renal transplant in a private hospital in India. She does not know the cytomegalovirus (CMV) status of the donor where the kidney came from and was not given anti-viral prophylaxis after the transplant.
