Over the past few days she has begun suffering from night sweats, cramping abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Her BP is 132/72 mmHg; pulse is 74/min and regular. Her abdomen is soft but there is left-sided tenderness. Investigations: Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 3.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 189 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 281 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 22 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
explanation:
CMV polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
The suspicion is that this woman has post-transplant CMV infection, in the absence of information on the serology of the donor and the lack of anti-viral prophylaxis. This is usually seen up to 50 days after transplant, so the 6-week time frame is consistent with this. In immunocompetent individuals an IgM response is seen to primary CMV infection, but in patients treated with immunosuppressants, this may not be apparent. As such CMV PCR is the best approach. Treatment is with IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir for at least 14 days. Where CMV seronegative patients receive a renal transplant from a seropositive donor, the preferred strategy is oral valganciclovir for up to 200 days. You may like to refer to up-to-date guidelines on management of CMV infections from the British Transplant Society (BTS).

CMV serology
CMV serology is incorrect. The CMV serology test determines the presence of antibodies (IgM) to cytomegalovirus. However CMV serology does not cover the diagnosis of CMV infection in immunocompromised individuals (including HIV-infected, graft recipient, immunosuppressive treatment).

Colonoscopy with biopsy
Colonosocopy with biopsy is incorrect. Colonoscopy with biopsy may show CMV infection in the colonic cells. This is the most specific diagnostic investigation for CMV colitis. However, it would be invasive and therefore it would not be the first investigation of choice.

EBV PCR
EBV PCR is incorrect. EBV can present with diarrhoea and gastrointestinal upset; however, it is not as common post transplant as CMV disease.

Ultrasound kidney
Ultrasound kidney is incorrect. Renal ultrasound would not be helpful in this case because CMV infection would not be apparent from an ultrasound. This investigation would be useful post transplant to identify any abscess, collections and hydronephrosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with increased frequency of micturition, dysuria and suprapubic pain 5 days after completing antibacterial treatment for an E. coli urinary tract infection. She is also using a barrier contraceptive. Her past medical history includes recurrent urinary tract infection. Urine microscopy shows the presence of E. coli. What is the most likely cause for her problem?
explanation:
Renal stones
This patient has had a relapse, which is diagnosed by the recurrence of bacteriuria with the same organism within 7 days of completing antibacterial treatment, and implies failure to eradicate infection. It usually occurs in conditions in which it is difficult to eradicate the bacteria, such as stones, scarred kidneys, polycystic disease or bacterial prostatitis. Reinfection occurs when bacteriuria is absent after treatment for at least 14 days, usually longer, followed by recurrence of infection with the same or a different organism.

Atrophic vaginitis
Atrophic vaginitis is incorrect. Atrophic vaginitis is an inflammation of the vagina often due to reduced lubrication and lack of oestrogen during menopause. It presents with pain during sexual intercourse, vaginal discomfort, vaginal discharge and itch. The lack of these symptoms, and she is 45 years old, makes this less likely as a diagnosis.

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with nephrotic syndrome. A renal biopsy is undertaken to ascertain the cause and shows the following: Light microscopy: normal Electron microscopy: fused podocyte foot processes What is the underlying disease process?
explanation:
Minimal change disease
This is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, but can be seen in adults. It is called minimal change as light microscopy findings appear entirely normal. However, on electron microscopy, podocyte foot processes are fused.

IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is incorrect. This condition is characterised by deposition of IgA in the mesangium.

stem: A 68-year-old man visits his GP with symptoms of difficulty initiating urine flow. He also has to awaken on a number of occasions each night to visit the toilet to pass urine. His PSA is normal and a prostatic biopsy does not indicate carcinoma. Which one of the following treatment options is likely to bring most rapid symptom relief?
explanation:
Alpha blockade
This gentleman has symptoms of prostatic hypertrophy with no evidence of prostatic carcinoma (based on case series, up to 10–30% of men with benign prostatic hypertrophy [BPH] are said to have prostatic carcinoma). Alpha blockade relaxes the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and can improve urinary flow rates. These improvements in symptoms may be seen over the course of a few days’ therapy, and with appropriate therapy around 70% of patients with prostatic hypertrophy gain improvement in or stabilisation of symptoms. Urology referral should be considered for those with severe symptoms, or those who fail to respond to medical therapy or where carcinoma is suspected.

Beta blockade
Beta blockade is incorrect. Beta blockade does not affect prostatic symptoms.

stem: A 75-year-old man visits his GP for a new-patient screen. He has Type 2 diabetes and mild long-standing back pain but no prior history of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Screening tests reveal dipstick proteinuria, an elevated serum creatinine of 215 μmol/l and anaemia with Hb of 101 g/l. A plain radiograph of his thoracolumbar spine shows collapse of the lumbar spine and there is a monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his deteriorated renal function?
explanation:
Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis usually presents between the ages of 60 and 70 years. The cause in this patient is likely to be light chain deposition from a myeloma, exemplified by the monoclonal banding on electrophoresis and lumbar spine collapse. Causes of amyloid, apart from myeloma, are hereditary forms of amyloidosis, including familial Mediterranean fever and those related to chronic disease (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis). Symptoms of generalised amyloidosis include fatigue and dyspnoea, diarrhoea, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and weight loss. Cardiac involvement with amyloid may lead to a restrictive picture, with right-sided heart failure and jugular venous distension. The renal amyloidosis can precipitate development of nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis associated with myeloma carries a very poor prognosis (often less than 1 year); familial forms are associated with much better outcomes, with a prognosis up to 10–15 years.

stem: A 56-year-old woman with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis has been regularly taking diclofenac for pain relief. She presents with mild chronic kidney disease, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Blood tests show decreased plasma renin and aldosterone. Urine dipstick has trace protein. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Type IV renal tubular acidosis
Type IV renal tubular acidosis, which occurs because of deficient aldosterone action, is the most common of the renal tubular disorders. The cardinal features are hyperkalaemia and acidosis occurring in a patient with mild chronic renal insufficiency, usually caused by tubulointerstitial disease or diabetes. An identical syndrome may be caused by the chronic ingestion of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which impair renin and aldosterone secretion

Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis
Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis is incorrect. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis is inflammation affecting the tubules and/or interstitium of the kidneys, and may be caused by medications such as NSAIDs and antibiotics. However, it does not lead to hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, and therefore would be an incorrect answer.

stem: A 27-year-old African man is admitted with fever, severe joint pain and diarrhoea. Investigations reveal decreased urine osmolality. Which one of the following conditions is most likely to give rise to this clinical feature?
explanation:
Sickle cell nephropathy
Sickle cell disease causes a loss in renal concentrating ability due to medullary damage from sickling.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Chronic hyperglycaemia leads to diabetic nephropathy. Polyuria occurs but there is no decrease in urinary osmolality.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. Hypertension, renal mass and haematuria are the presenting features of polycystic kidney disease (PKD). From 29% to 73% of patients with the autosomal dominant form of the disorder have associated hepatic cysts; 9% have associated pancreatic cysts; and 5% have associated splenic cysts. Pulmonary cysts occur but are uncommon.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with acute-onset shortness of breath. His past medical history includes hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension, for which his General Practitioner recently initiated atorvastatin and ramipril. On examination, he is breathless, with a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 85% on air. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation. His heart rate is 120 bpm and regular and his blood pressure is 180/100 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal and his jugular venous pressure is distended and elevated to 6 cm. Investigations: Investigation Today's result Previous result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 135 g/l 139 g/l 135–170 g/l White cell count 6.5 × 10 9/l 5.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 148 mmol/l 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.6 mmol/l 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5 mmol/l Creatinine 244 µmol/l 125 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l C-reactive protein 10 mg/l 8 mg/l < 5 mg/l Which of the following is the investigation of choice to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureter and bladder
explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging renal angiography
This patient has acute pulmonary oedema, given the acute onset of shortness of breath, hypertension and elevated jugular venous pressure. Patients with renal artery stenosis are at significant risk of developing acute pulmonary oedema. Furthermore, the significant renal impairment following the addition of ramipril (an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) is even more suggestive of renal artery stenosis. The gold standard diagnostic investigation of choice is magnetic resonance imaging renal angiography of the renal arteries.

Brain natriuretic peptide levels
Brain natriuretic peptide is used in the diagnosis of cardiac failure. Although this patient is in acute pulmonary oedema, it does not play a role in the diagnosis of renal artery stenosis.

Echocardiography
Echocardiography is a reasonable investigation to assess cardiac function, given the acute onset of fluid overload. It is, however, likely that the presentation is secondary to renal artery stenosis, given the significant worsening of renal function following the introduction of an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureter and bladder
An ultrasound of the kidneys, ureter and bladder is a reasonable investigation to request, given the renal impairment. It is not, however, a diagnostic investigation for renal artery stenosis.

Urine protein : creatinine ratio
A urine protein : creatinine ratio is used in the investigation of renal disease and nephrotic causes of renal impairment. It would not be used to diagnose renal artery stenosis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a past history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents with severe right flank pain. The plasma biochemistry is as follows: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na +) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 2.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 3.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Chloride 115 mmol/l 95–106 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 12 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Urinary pH 6.5 4.5–8.0 Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Type I renal tubular acidosis
The presence of acidosis, hypokalaemia, low serum bicarbonate levels and relatively high urinary pH are characteristic of distal renal tubular acidosis (type I renal tubular acidosis). The problem hereChat is an inability with to maximally acidify the urine. Typically, urine pH remains > 5.5 despite severe acidaemia ([HCO 3] < 15 mmol/l).

stem: You are asked by a GP to review a 71-year-old man who has complained of chronic back pain for some time. Routine blood tests reveal a urea of 19.1 mmol/l, a creatinine of 285 μmol/l and normochromic normocytic anaemia. MRI reveals bilateral ureteric obstruction at the level of the pelvic brim. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ureteric compression from an expanding aneurysm
explanation:
Retroperitoneal fibrosis
Retroperitoneal fibrosis often presents with malaise, back pain, normochromic normocytic anaemia, uraemia and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). There is bilateral ureteric obstruction beginning at the level of the pelvic brim, and a periaortic mass may be identified on CT or MRI scanning. Surgery with ureteric stenting is the treatment of choice, although long-term corticosteroid therapy, azathioprine and mycophenolate may be of benefit. Methysergide and practolol are two drugs that were previously implicated in retroperitoneal fibrosis. Surgery should be used as an opportunity for taking local biopsies of the inflammatory mass to rule out an underlying lymphoma or carcinoma.

Abdominal lymphoma
Abdominal lymphoma is incorrect. Abdominal lymphoma may present with a painless lymph-node swelling elsewhere in the body, chills, recurrent fever, unintentional weight loss, appetite loss, lethargy, breathlessness, generalised itching or headache. Absence of these symptoms makes lymphoma in this scenario unlikely. Lymphomas may be classified as a Hodgkin lymphoma or non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL): the difference Chat is with determined by microscopy. NHL is far more common than Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with haematuria and recurrent haemoptysis. He has a past medical history of hypertension. His blood tests show low haemoglobin; renal biopsy shows the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody. Which one of the following is the most characteristic radiological finding on chest X-ray in this case?
options: Bilateral diffuse infiltrates in the lower zones
explanation:
Bilateral diffuse infiltrates in the lower zones
This man has Goodpasture’s disease (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease). In this condition, autoantibodies are directed against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. A characteristic chest X-ray finding would be bilateral diffuse infiltrates that represent areas of pulmonary haemorrhage, often in the lower zones.

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is incorrect. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is a characteristic feature of sarcoidosis, which is an inflammatory disease in which granulomas form in various organs, causing inflammation.

Lobar consolidation
Lobar consolidation is incorrect. Lobar consolidation is seen in pneumonias; there would be typical creptitations on auscultation of the chest.

stem: A 46-year-old woman complains of dysuria and flank pain. She also describes night sweats and gradual weight loss over the past few months. Her blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg despite taking three antihypertensives. Urine microscopy shows leukocytes and red cells, but there is no significant bacterial growth. Renal ultrasound shows both kidneys to be 9 cm in bipolar length, with medullary calcification and mild hydronephrosis on the left. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Renal tract tuberculosis
The combination of sterile pyuria, haematuria, dysuria and renal tract calcification is highly suggestive of renal tuberculosis. Many patients have refractory hypertension, which is renin-mediated and presumably due to segmental renal ischaemia. Glomerular granulomas develop at the time of primary infection due to haematogenous seeding. These usually heal without consequence, but may remain for many years, eventually caseating and rupturing into the tubular lumen. Granulomas then form in the renal medulla, the ureters (resulting in ureteric stricture), bladder (bladder contraction) and vas deferens. The histological appearance and clinical course are very similar to Balkan endemic nephropathy.

Acute pyelonephritis
Acute pyelonephritis is incorrect. The patient presents with a subacute, progressive illness not typical of acute pyelonephritis.

stem: A 35-year-old man was admitted to the Emergency Department having collapsed after suffering from an occipital headache. CT scan revealed a massive subarachnoid haemorrhage. Further investigations revealed multiple bilateral renal cysts. A defect on which chromosome is likely to be responsible for this clinical presentation?
explanation:
Chromosome 16
The patient has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney, and chromosome 16 is most probably affected. Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most commonly inherited kidney disease, and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Mutations in PKD1, located on chromosome 16, and PKD2, located on chromosome 4, cause defective production of the proteins polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, respectively. PKD-1 mutations are responsible for 85% of cases of polycystic kidney disease. Polycystin proteins are membrane proteins found within the cilia of renal-collecting duct epithelial cells that are involved in the regulation of cell proliferation, and defective synthesis results in dysregulated cell proliferation, which gives rise to cyst formation. Important complications of polycystic kidney disease include hypertension, which is often the primary presenting feature, cyst rupture, cyst infection, nephrolithiasis and progressive chronic kidney disease. In addition, a small percentage of patients may develop an intracranial aneurysm, which can result in a subarachnoid haemorrhage if the aneurysm ruptures. Extrarenal cysts are also common and can affect the liver, spleen or pancreas.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with Turner’s syndrome is referred by a GP as he is concerned about her blood pressure. A recent 24hr blood pressure monitor has shown an average blood pressure of 148/88 mmHg. She is managed with ramipril 10mg daily. A recent creatinine was 105 micromol/l and potassium 4.9 mmol/l. You examine her and elicit a murmur and evidence of radio-femoral delay. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
explanation:
Coarctation of the aorta
The heart murmur andradiofemoral delay would confirm a diagnosis of coarctation of the aorta. Performing the blood pressure on each arm would be important.

Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is incorrect. The normal creatinine on ACE inhibitor counts against a diagnosis of renal artery stenosis.

Single horse-shoe kidney
Approximately one-third of patients with Turner’s syndrome have associated renal abnormalities. Examples of associated disorders include renal artery stenosis, increased renal cyst formation and a single horse-shoe kidney.

stem: A 68-year-old man has undergone surgery for repair of a ruptured aortic aneurysm. Before surgery he was well, with a Cr of 119 μmol/l at baseline. Although the operative procedure went well, the period of acute hypotension has resulted in an episode of acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and he has undergone renal dialysis on a number of occasions in the past week. Which one of the following most accurately represents the chance of recovery of renal function to the level where dialysis is not required?
explanation:
95%
Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) usually occurs after an acute ischaemic or toxic event. In the present case, a period of severe hypotension resulting from the ruptured aneurysm was the underlying cause. Approximately 95% of patients go on to recover renal function to the level where dialysis is not required.

0%
Most patients with ATN recover to the extent that they do not need dialysis (95%). However prognosis of ATN is poorer in patients with severe sepsis or trauma, where mortality rates can approach 50-60%. Infections are the leading cause of death in acute kidney injury.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with haematuria and recurrent haemoptysis. He has a past medical history of hypertension. Blood results show low haemoglobin; renal biopsy shows the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody. What finding in a lung biopsy would be most suggestive of this diagnosis?
options: Linear staining of IgG along the bronchiolar epithelium
explanation:
Haemosiderin-laden macrophages
This young man has Goodpasture’s disease (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease). A lung biopsy may show disruption of alveolar septa and haemosiderin-laden macrophages because there may be pulmonary haemorrhage associated with the condition.

Increased neutrophils and macrophages
Increased neutrophils and macrophages is incorrect. Increased neutrophils and macrophages may be found in lung biopsies in infections or inflammations. It is relatively non-specific.

Linear staining of IgG along the bronchiolar epithelium
Linear staining of IgG along the bronchiolar epithelium is incorrect. Lung biopsy will show linear staining of IgG along the alveolar capillary basement membranes, not the bronchiolar epithelium.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted following a road traffic collision in which he sustained multiple injuries. He has no relevant past medical history. Upon examination he was hypotensive. Some 48 hours after admission, his urine flow is 0.4 ml/min. You suspect he has acute tubular necrosis (ATN). Which of the following investigative findings, if present on urine examination, would be most helpful in confirming acute tubular necrosis?
explanation:
Urine osmolality 300 mosmol/kg
ATN usually arises following an acute ischaemic or nephrotoxic event, and is characterised by 3 phases: 1. Initiation phase, with acute decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and sudden rise in serum creatinine (Cr) ± oliguria 2. Maintenance phase, with a sustained marked reduction in GFR and rising Cr (1–2 weeks) 3. Recovery phase, in which tubular function is gradually restored and urine volume gradually rises, with concomitant decrease in Cr to preinjury levels Urine osmolality decreases in ATN, reflecting reduced tubal function and filtration rate; this is in contrast to pre- kidney disease where osmolality is typically high in the context of poor urine output and high creatinine. Urine osmolality is therefore a useful means of helping distinguish between pre-kidney disease and ATN, and urine osmolality 300 mosmol/kg is the correct answer.

Visible haematuria
Visible haematuria is incorrect. Urine dipstick of acute tubular necrosis is typically bland.

stem: A 46-year-old man with end-stage renal disease complains of retrosternal pain. ECG shows concave ST segment elevation in all leads. His creatinine is 520 μmol/l. Which one of the following is most likely to resolve his symptoms?
explanation:
Haemodialysis
Concave ST segment elevation in all ECG leads is typical of pericarditis. As this patient has chronic kidney disease, the diagnosis is uraemic pericarditis. This condition requires urgent dialysis.

Aspirin, clopidogrel and glyceryl trinitrate
Aspirin, clopidogrel and glyceryl trinitrate is incorrect. In myocardial infarction, ST elevation would be convex in shape. This would not be a treatment for pericarditis.

Coronary angiography and angioplasty
Coronary angiography and angioplasty is incorrect. In myocardial infarction, ST elevation would be convex in shape. This would not be a treatment for pericarditis.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents to hospital with fatigue over the last 3 weeks. His blood pressure is 170/90 mmHg. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 12.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 560 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Phosphate (PO 4 3-) 2.31 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Haemoglobin 98 g/l 135–175 g/l Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 310 mg/mmol. Ultrasound of the kidneys shows two unobstructed kidneys measuring approximately 7.5 cm each. Which one of the following helps you differentiate this as chronic kidney disease as opposed to acute kidney injury?
options: Small kidney size on ultrasound scan
explanation:
Small kidney size on ultrasound scan
Kidney size typically is 10–12 cm in bipolar length. Small kidneys point towards chronic kidney disease due to progressive fibrosis and loss of nephron mass. However, one would expect to see large kidneys with chronic kidney disease in polycystic kidney disease.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. This can be a feature in acute (eg in nephritic syndrome or in the setting of volume overload) or chronic kidney disease (a cause of and consequence of hypertension).

Raised phosphate
Raised phosphate is incorrect. This can be a feature in acute or chronic kidney disease due to reduced excretion of phosphate.

Raised urine protein:creatinine ratio
Raised urine protein:creatinine ratio is incorrect. This can be a feature in acute or chronic kidney disease, due to underlying glomerular disease, for instance.

Anaemia
Anaemia is incorrect. This can be a feature in acute (eg in haemolytic uraemic syndrome) or chronic kidney disease, where it is almost a universal finding due to lack of erythropoietin.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of multiple myeloma presents with heavy proteinuria and deteriorating renal function. You suspect that he has amyloidosis as a result of the myeloma. Which one of the following types of amyloid deposit do you think is most likely to be found in this case?
explanation:
Light-chain amyloidosis
Light-chain amyloidosis is associated with multiple myeloma.

AA amyloidosis
AA amyloidosis is incorrect. AA amyloidosis is characteristically associated with chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, or chronic infection such as leprosy or tuberculosis.

AbPP amyloidosis
AbPP amyloidosis is incorrect. AbPP amyloidosis is associated with Down syndrome and Alzheimer’s disease.

β 2-microglobulin
β 2-microglobulin is incorrect, β 2-microglobulin deposition is associated with long-term haemodialysis.

stem: A 68-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes, currently receiving peritoneal dialysis, is seen in the Cardiovascular Risk-reduction Clinic. You are considering prescribing a statin. Which of the following best describes the lipid abnormalities most likely to be seen in this man?
options: A combination of hypertriglyceridaemia, raised LDL and decreased HDL levels
Mixed hyperlipidaemia with increased LDL and triglyceride levels
The predominant abnormality is low HDL cholesterol
explanation:
A combination of hypertriglyceridaemia, raised LDL and decreased HDL levels
In type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia is commonly caused by insulin resistance. Insulin resistance and the ensuing hyperinsulinemia are associated with hypertriglyceridemia, increased LDL, and low HDL cholesterol concentrations Dyslipidemia is less prominent in CKD, but CKD is also associated with elevations in LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, and low levels of HDL cholesterol.

Isolated hypertriglyceridaemia
Isolated hypertriglyceridaemia is incorrect. As this patient has type 2 diabetes and advanced kidney disease he is likely to have decreased HDL levels, hypertriglyceridemia and increased total cholesterol.

Isolated increased LDL levels
Isolated increased LDL levels is incorrect. Elevation in LDL is relatively uncommon in T2DM without associated elevation in triglycerides and a reduction in HDL.

stem: A 19-year-old patient who is recently moved to the area is admitted to the Emergency ward with multiple epileptic seizures. His epilepsy settles and he is discharged, but you note some abnormal findings on examination including an elevated BP of 149/92 mmHg, some hypopigmented patches on his face, and periungual fibromas. You send him for some investigations Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 124 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 4.9 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine dipstick Blood + Renal ultrasound Bilateral renal cysts What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis
This man has features consistent with tuberous sclerosis including the hypopigmented lesions on his face, periungual fibromas and renal cysts on ultrasound examination. Epilepsy occurs in 80-90% of cases of tuberous sclerosis, and the disease may be associated with the development of astrocytomas, such that this man will require a CT or MRI brain. Given that the epilepsy is usually a partial rather than a primary generalised form, carbamazepine or lamotrigine would be suitable agents for initial monotherapy. As well as renal cysts, renal angiomyolipomas may also occur; these are benign tumours but they may occasionally be associated with very large renal bleeds. Pulmonary, cardiac, and colonic tumours may also occur. Tuberous sclerosis is associated with a diverse range of clinical features, dependent on the number of organ systems involved, and the level of involvement. Prognosis is variable, with severely affected patients likely to die in early life, whilst others may have a relatively normal life expectancy.

MEN 2
MEN 2 is incorrect. Cutaneous features may occur in MEN2B, but these are mucosal neuromas

Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. Café au lait (pigmented) patches are seen in neurofibromatosis.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. Cutaneous features are not found in polycystic kidney disease.

Von Hippel-Lindau disease
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is incorrect. Conditions associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease include angiomatosis (usually in the retina), hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts (pancreatic serous cystadenoma), endolymphatic sac tumour, and bilateral papillary cystadenomas of the epididymis (men) or broad ligament of the uterus (women).

stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hypertrophy is prescribed a course of finasteride. He is taking no other medication. On examination, blood pressure is 98/60mmHg and pulse 65 bpm. Which of the following is most likely to be a side-effect of finasteride therapy?
explanation:
Gynaecomastia
Finasteride leads to increased conversion of testosterone to estradiol and androstenediol, and this results in breast tenderness and gynaecomastia.

Alopecia
Alopecia is incorrect. 5-α-reductase inhibitors have also been developed as a therapy for androgenic alopecia.

Increased libido
Increased libido is incorrect. Finasteride is a 5-α-reductase inhibitor that is associated with a number of adverse drug reactions including impotence, decreased libido, decreased ejaculate volume, depression and anxiety.

stem: A 19-year-old woman complains of stiff joints and a facial rash. Her blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg, she has +1 oedema, slightly swollen metacarpophalangeal joints and some ulceration of her buccal mucosa. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 86 ml/min/1.73m 2, Hb is 89 g/l and platelet count is 92 × 10 9/l. Urinalysis shows +3 blood and +3 protein. High titres of double-stranded DNA antibodies are detectable in her serum. Which one of the following would histological examination of renal tissue demonstrate?
options: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with deposits of IgG, IgM and C3
explanation:
Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with deposits of IgG, IgM and C3
This patient has lupus nephritis. The most common (and most severe) form of lupus nephritis, and one which is entirely compatible with the clinical history, is type IV: proliferative glomerulonephritis affecting > 50% of glomeruli, often with crescents present. This form of lupus nephritis frequently progresses to advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) when untreated. Therefore, patients with type IV (and also class III) should be treated with immunosuppression using prednisolone with either cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate. Additional types of lupus nephritis are class I (abnormal urine sediment with normal light microscopy), class II (mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis), class V (membranous nephropathy) and class VI (advanced sclerosed). Classes I and VI do not require immunosuppression, and the management of classes II and V is dependent on degree of proteinuria. Any patient with lupus nephritis presenting with significant proteinuria should be considered for renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) blockade.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with known chronic kidney disease presents with numbness and tingling in the lower limbs, which has been slowly becoming more problematic over a period of 6 weeks or so. She also complains of muscle cramps. In the past 2 days she has had two episodes of loss of consciousness, possibly epileptic in origin. On examination, there is loss of sensation to pinpricks below both knees and she has absent knee and ankle deep tendon reflexes with mute plantar response. Blood tests reveal a haemoglobin of 58 g/l and a serum creatinine level of 540 μmol/l. Which one of the following is the most appropriate management step?
explanation:
Renal dialysis
This patient has classical signs of uremic polyneuropathy which requires urgent intervention. Renal replacement therapy with transplantation is the best way to manage uremic polyneuropathy, but to improve symptoms at this time, dialysis must be carried out. Early dialysis may reverse sensory deficits as well as stopping further progression of symptomatology. This patient also has a significant anaemia which requires attention. This patient would ideally receive a transfusion during the time of dialysis. However, blood transfusion alone, without dialysis, can potentially be harmful. Therefore, the best next step of the options stated would be to commence dialysis. In this scenario, metabolic causes, neurotoxins or inflammatory conditions occurring in association with chronic renal disease could also contribute to such a clinical picture and should be considered/excluded (eg hypocalcaemia, diabetes, thyroid disease and myeloma). Often these investigations would be carried out alongside dialysis.

stem: A 27-year-old man has a history of hypertension and intermittent loin pain. There is a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Urine testing reveals evidence of haematuria. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
In adult polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), patients often present in young adult life with hypertension. Its prevalence rate varies from 1:400 to 1:1000 in White populations, accounting for 3–10% of patients in the West undergoing haemodialysis. The history of hypertension, painless haematuria, intermittent loin pain and family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage is highly suggestive of ADPKD. Abnormal genes responsible have been mapped to chromosomes 16 and 4. Patients may present acutely with haemorrhage or infection into a cyst. Around 8% of patients with ADPKD have asymptomatic intracranial aneurysms, but this prevalence rate is doubled in families where there is a history of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Physical examination usually reveals large, irregularly shaped kidneys. Progressive kidney disease means that by the age of 70 years 30% of sufferers require renal replacement therapy. For this reason control of hypertension is crucial, and angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are the first-line choice of treatment.

Glomerulonephritis
Glomerulonephritis is incorrect. This would present with both blood and protein in the urineChat due with to inflammation of the glomerulus. It would be uncommon to present with intermittent loin pain.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a background of type-2 diabetes, gout and bilateral knee replacements for osteoarthritis. His current medications include aspirin, metformin, gliclazide and allopurinol. He presents to hospital with a 2-month history of weight loss, polyuria, nausea, constipation and low back pain. On examination, he was pale and clinically dehydrated. His blood tests show: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 69 g/l 135–175 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 89 fl 76–98 fl Sodium (Na +) 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 13.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l 264 µmol/l (Was 65 µmol/l Creatinine 50–120 µmol/l 6 months ago) Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 3.3 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l His urine dip was negative for blood, nitirites and leucocytes. Some proteins were detected. A lumbar X-ray showed lytic lesions in multiple lumbar vertebrae. Which of the following investigations would help secure the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Bone marrow biopsy
The patient likey has multiple myeloma given the hypercalcaemia and lytic lesions on the X-ray. Myeloma is a haematological malignancy caused by neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells and characterised by: the presence of ≥10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow a serum or urine paraprotein the presence of CRAB features: Calcium raised Renal impairment Anaemia Bone lesions. This patient has all the CRAB features.

US-renal tract
US-renal tract is incorrect. US-renal tract should be requested in the setting of the acute kidney injury to ensure there are two, unobstructed kidneys present, but this would not establish the underlying diagnosis.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
An erythrocyte sedimentation rate is incorrect. An erythrocyte sedimentation rate can be performed and would be very high in the setting of myeloma. It measures how quickly red cells sediment in the first hour when placed in an upright tube. In myeloma, the presence of excess immunoglobulins predisposes red cells to form rouleaux (or a stack of cells) and this causes them to sediment faster. Although it is a reasonable test to request, it would not establish the diagnosis.

Renal biopsy
A renal biopsy is incorrect. A renal biopsy could demonstrate findings of a myeloma kidney such as cast nephropathy and light chain deposition disease, but it is far better for diagnostic and prognostic reasons to acquire a bone marrow biopsy to establish the diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

Parathyroid hormone
Parathyroid hormone is incorrect. Parathyroid hormone again is something you could request as part of your work-up for hypercalcaemia, but again would not help to secure the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her husband who is worried that she is becoming increasingly forgetful, and most recently couldn’t remember her way home after going out shopping. She has a history of hypertension, which is treated with indapamide and she has intermittent left flank pain. During the past 18 months she has suffered two episodes of mononeuritis. On examination her blood pressure (BP) is 155/88 mmHg, she has skin discoloration consistent with livedo reticularis but there are no rashes or heart murmurs. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 108 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 452 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 176 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HBsAg negative Urine blood++, protein++ Which one of the following antibodies is most likely to be associated with this clinical presentation?
explanation:
p-ANCA
The presentation including neurological decline, mononeuritis and glomerulonephritis, raises the possibility of microscopic polyangiitis, which is associated with p-ANCA. This lady needs a renal biopsy. The central nervous system features seen are likely to be as a result of recurrent episodes of cerebral ischaemia. Primary management is with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.

Anti-cardiolipin
Anti-cardiolipin is incorrect because anti-cardiolipin antibodies are found in anti-phospholipid syndrome.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane
Anti-glomerular basement membrane is incorrect because Anti-GBM antibodies are associated with Goodpasture's.

Anti-smooth muscle
Anti-smooth muscle is incorrect because Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

C-ANCA
C-ANCA is incorrect because c-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 5 secondary to IgA nephropathy. Calcium Phosphate Parathyroid hormone (PTH) Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
options: Calcium low, phosphate low, PTH low, ALP low
Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high, ALP high
Calcium high, phosphate high, PTH low, ALP normal
Calcium high, phosphate high, PTH high, ALP normal
Calcium high, phosphate low, PTH normal, ALP high
explanation:
Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high, ALP high
A patient with CKD 5 is likely to demonstrate evidence of mineral bone disease. Owing to renal impairment, there is lack of 1-α hydroxylation of vitamin D, a necessary step to produce the bioactive compound 1,25(OH) 2- cholecalciferol (1,25-dihydroxy-cholecalciferol), which plays a vital role in calcium homeostatis. It increases osteoblast activity, and increases calcium absorption in the gut and calcium retention in the kidneys. As a result of a lack of 1-α hydroxylase activity, hypocalcaemia develops.

stem: A 64-year-old man with end-stage renal disease wonders whether he is a suitable candidate for renal transplantation. He is asymptomatic and blood tests show an eGFR of 5 ml/min/1.73m 2. In which of the following conditions is renal transplantation most advisable?
explanation:
Bilateral polycystic kidney disease
Bilateral polycystic kidney disease is the only option in the question where a renal transplant is advisable. Adult polycystic kidney disease is a common cause of chronic kidney disease in the United Kingdom and a frequent indication for renal transplant, with good patient outcomes.

Generalised bronchiectasis
Generalised bronchiectasis is incorrect. It will make transplant potentially difficult because respiratory compromise may make the patient a high surgical risk and post-transplant immunosuppressants will exacerbate any underlying infection. Furthermore, bronchiectasis may limit survival and will require a high degree of rehabilitation after transplantation.

Light-chain deposition disease
Light-chain deposition disease is incorrect. This is a rare renal disease, and it has a high recurrence rate in the renal allograft, which can lead to an immediate graft loss and is a contraindication for transplant.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with Henoch–Schönlein purpura and renal involvement. What is the most likely outcome?
explanation:
Complete renal recovery
The most likely outcome here is complete recovery of renal function, and end-stage renal disease only occurs in 5% of patients.

High probability of relapse
High probability of relapse is incorrect. High probability of relapse tends to be an isolated event.

Persistent hypertension
Persistent hypertension is incorrect. The overall prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous recovery of most patients within 4 weeks.

Persistent proteinuria
Persistent proteinuria is incorrect. The overall prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous recovery of most patients within 4 weeks.

stem: A 69-year-old man presents to the GP complaining of hip and back pain. Over the past few months he has also noticed increasing symptoms of dysuria, hesitancy and dribbling when he tries to pass urine. Occasionally he has noticed that the urine may be tinged with blood. Other past history of note includes hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. On examination, his BP is 146/89 mmHg, pulse is 75/min, regular. PR examination reveals a firm, enlarged prostate with obliteration of the lateral sulcus. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 106 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 195 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alkaline Phosphatase 2980 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) 32 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Corrected Calcium (Ca 2+) 2.30 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) 3 Which of the following is the investigation most likely to deliver the underlying tissue diagnosis?
explanation:
Trans-rectal prostatic biopsy
The question is testing knowledge of the fact that some prostatic carcinomas may not be associated with an elevated PSA. Benign prostatic hyperplasia tends not to be associated with loss of the lateral sulcus on PR, and the mild anaemia, with marked elevation in serum creatinine raises the possibility of significant prostatic obstruction. Trans-rectal prostatic biopsy is therefore indicated to gain a tissue diagnosis.

Bone scan
Bone scan is incorrect. Although a bone scan may show evidence of metastases, it won’t confirm a tissue diagnosis.

Lumbar spine and hip x-ray
Lumbar spine and hip x-ray is incorrect. Another common pitfall is that prostatic metastases may mimic the appearance of Paget’s; hence progressing straight to skeletal investigations may mean the actual diagnosis is missed.

CXR
CXR is incorrect. A CXR is not diagnostic, and although may detect lung metastases, a CT is more accurate for this purpose.

stem: A 74-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with acute-onset abdominal pain for the last 24 hours. He reports constipation for the past two days and persistent vomiting for the past 24 hours. His past medical history includes Crohn’s disease with a previous history of abdominal surgery six years ago. Other significant past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolaemia and hypertension. On examination, his pulse is 104 bpm and his blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and diffusely tender with absent bowel sounds. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 140 g/l 135–175 g/l Urea 9.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 125µmol/l 50–120µmol/l Abdominal X-ray Dilated bowel loops A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen is arranged for suspected intestinal obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
explanation:
Hydration with normal saline
Intravenous (IV) administration of normal saline prior to, and for several hours after, performing contrast- enhanced CT angiography is indicated in patients who are at risk of developing contrast-induced nephropathy. Major risk factors include chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus (particularly diabetic nephropathy), non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use and dehydration. This patient's laboratory studies show elevated creatinine and borderline normal urea level, indicating impaired kidney function. Adequate prophylactic hydration is therefore vital. Laboratory monitoring is necessary following the procedure to detect worsening creatinine levels (typically highest after 3–5 days), which would be indicative of contrast-induced nephropathy.

Administer mannitol
Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that elevates blood plasma osmolality. It increases the osmotic pressure within the lumen of the proximal tubule and the loop of Henle. This causes enhanced water diuresis and, to a lesser extent, sodium and potassium excretion. Administering mannitol may cause volume depletion and promote diuresis. This will increase the risk of contrast nephropathy.

Administer N-acetyl cysteine
N-acetyl cysteine may be an option for prevention of contrast nephropathy. However, studies have shown inconsistent results of its efficacy in preventing nephropathy. Adequate hydration is more effective prevention strategy.

Perform pre-procedural haemodialysis
There is no role of haemodialysis prior to CT scan in this patient. His renal function is not severely deranged to necessitate dialysis.

Perform post-procedural haemodialysis
There is no indication to dialyse a patient routinely after CT scan and contrast administration. If patient develops contrast nephropathy, it can be managed by more conservative measures such as hydration and avoiding concomitant nephrotoxic medicines. In severe cases, emergency haemodialysis is an option.

stem: A 17-year-old man complains of malaise and the inability to take part in sports, as he gets tired easily. He has a past medical history of thyroid disease. His blood pressure is normal. His childhood development was said to be normal. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 2.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO 3 -) 34 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Chloride 91 mmol/l 95–107 mmol/l Magnesium 0.5 mmol/l 0.75 –1.00 mmol/l Glucose 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Renin 5.1 pmol/ml per hour 3–4.3 pmol/ml per hour Aldosterone 975 pmol/l 330–830 pmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Gitelman syndrome
Gitelman syndrome is characterised by hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria, hypomagnesaemia (which is pathognomic), normal blood pressure and elevated plasma renin and aldosterone You may find it useful to remember the location of the nephron defects in these conditions as being alphabetical, i.e. Bartter affects the thick ascending limb, Gitelman affects distal tubule and Liddle syndrome affects the collecting ducts. BGL is in alphabetical order, as is the order of the affected location in the nephrons.

Bartter syndrome
Bartter syndrome is incorrect. Bartter syndrome consists of metabolic alkalosis, hypokalaemia, hypercalciuria, normal blood pressure and elevated plasma renin and aldosterone; magnesium wasting is rarer in this condition. Excessive distal sodium delivery increases distal tubular sodium reabsorption and exchange with the electrically equivalent potassium or hydrogen ion. This in turn promotes hypokalaemia, while lack of chloride reabsorption promotes inadequate exchange of bicarbonate for chloride, and the combined hypokalaemia and excessive bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis. You may find it useful to remember the location of the nephron defects in these conditions as being alphabetical, i.e. Bartter affects the thick ascending limb, Gitelman affects distal tubule and Liddle syndrome affects the collecting ducts. BGL is in alphabetical order, as is the order of the affected location in the nephrons.

Chronic fatigue syndrome
Chronic fatigue syndrome is incorrect. Chronic fatigue syndrome is a condition of unknown aetiology associated with myalgia, prolonged tiredness and depression. It typically occurs after a viral infection. It is not associated with any biochemical abnormality.

Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis
Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is incorrect. Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis may be precipitated by carbohydrate intake. It is characterised by generalised weakness, including the speech and bulbar muscles, which often starts after a heavy carbohydrate meal or following a period of rest after exertion. The serum potassium concentration is usually below 3.0 mmol/l during an attack. It is generally an autosomal dominant trait caused by mutations in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel. Non-familial forms of this condition may occur in patients with thyrotoxicosis.

Liddle syndrome
Liddle syndrome is incorrect. Liddle syndrome is characterised by potassium wasting, hypokalaemia and alkalosis, but is associated with low renin and aldosterone production and high blood pressure.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is suffering from nephrotic syndrome secondary to the long-term use of penicillamine for rheumatoid arthritis. She has a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and a serum protein electrophoresis is arranged as part of a routine blood screen. Which of the following stems best fits the abnormalities that are typically seen on protein electrophoresis in patients with nephrotic syndrome?
options: Decreased α1- and increased α2-globulin fractions, decreased serum albumin
Increased α1- and α2-globulin fractions, increased serum albumin
Increased α1 and α2-globulin fractions, decreased serum albumin
explanation:
Increased α1 and α2-globulin fractions, decreased serum albumin
In the nephrotic patient, abnormal findings on serum electrophoresis include a decreased albumin level and an increase in the α 1- and α 2-globulin fractions. This increase in globulin fractions is thought to occur due to increased synthesis in patients with urinary protein loss. A monoclonal paraprotein band will also be present where myeloma is the underlying cause, and there may be associated immune paresis with reduced concentrations of one or more of the immunoglobulins IgG, IgA or IgM. Some 10% of patients with myeloma will also have renal amyloid deposition. Possibly related to immunoglobulins lost in the urine, sepsis is an important complication of nephrotic syndrome. Infection with Pneumococcus spp. is relatively common in affected individuals, and vaccination should always be offered. Early recognition of sepsis and aggressive treatment is the key to a positive outcome.

Decreased α1- and increased α2-globulin fractions, decreased serum albumin
Decreased α1- and increased α2-globulin fractions, decreased serum albumin is incorrect. The 1- and Chatαwith α 2- globulin fractions are increased.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the Renal Clinic for the evaluation of intermittent blood-tinged urine for several months. Four months ago, he had an episode of fever and sore throat that resolved without treatment after five days. During the past two years, he has also had recurrent episodes of swelling of his face and feet. Five years ago, he was diagnosed with mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. His brother died of a progressive kidney disease at the age of 23 years. The patient appears pale. His temperature is 37 °C, his pulse is 70 bpm, and his blood pressure is 145/85 mmHg. Slit lamp examination shows a conical protrusion of both lenses. Laboratory studies show a haemoglobin concentration of 110 g/l, urea nitrogen concentration of 9.6 mg/dl and creatinine concentration of 212 μmol/l. Urinalysis shows: Investigation Result Normal value Red blood count (RBC) 5–7 HPF 4 HPF RBC casts Rare Blood ++ Protein + Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Defective type IV collagen
Type IV collagen, which forms a component of basement membranes, plays an important role in the function of glomeruli and inner ear structures (particularly the organ of Corti). An X-linked defect in type IV collagen is responsible for most cases of Alport syndrome, which results in progressive sensorineural hearing loss (with high-frequency sounds affected first) and haematuria. Episodes of gross haematuria are sometimes preceded by upper respiratory tract infections. Patients with Alport syndrome may also develop an anterior lenticonus since type IV collagen is the predominant collagen fibre in the lens capsule. A family history of renal disease, as seen in this patient, is common in patients with Alport syndrome.

Immunoglobulin A (IgA) deposits
Deposition of IgA in the glomeruli is seen in IgA nephropathy and in Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP), both of which may present with nephritic syndrome. However, a purpuric rash would typically precede the onset of renal disease in patients with HSP, and other symptoms such as abdominal pain and/or joint pain would be expected. Moreover, both HSP and IgA nephropathy do not explain the sensorineural deafness and lenticonus seen here.

Phospholipase A2 receptor antibody
Antibodies against phospholipase A2 receptors on podocytes are responsible for membranous nephropathy. Membranous nephropathy typically presents between the ages of 30 and 50 years with nephrotic syndrome, unlike this 20-year-old man with nephritic syndrome.

Type II hypersensitivity reaction
Type II hypersensitivity reactions caused by antibodies against intrinsic type IV collagen antigens in the basement membrane are responsible for Goodpasture disease, which manifests with acute nephritic syndrome. However, Goodpasture disease rarely manifests during early childhood and usually progresses rapidly (unlike in this patient, who presents with a 2-year history of intermittent oedema). Also, especially in younger individuals, pulmonary symptoms (eg haemoptysis, dyspnoea) often precede the onset of nephritic syndrome.

WT1 gene mutation
A WT1 gene mutation is one of the causes of Wilms’ tumour, which can result in haematuria, hypertension and anaemia. However, Wilms’ tumour would manifest in early childhood (usually before the age of five years) and patients almost always have a palpable abdominal or flank mass on physical examination.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred to hospital due to abnormal bloods. Her bloods show: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 160 µmol/l (Was 62 µmol/l 3 months ago) 50–120 µmol/l She has been taking diclofenac for the last 2 weeks for arthralgia in her hands. A renal biopsy shows an intense interstitial infiltrate of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Which one of the following is true with respect to this side-effect of diclofenac?
options: ACE inhibitors are the first-line treatment
Steroids do not play a role in management
explanation:
The condition is mostly reversible
The clinical and histological findings are in keeping with acute interstitial nephritis due to non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drug (NSAID) use, in this case diclofenac. The renal impairment may completely resolve on removal of the offending trigger, but if this is not seen then a course of prednisolone should be trialled. If the patient presents with dialysis-dependent renal impairment or has a particularly active inflammatory infiltrate, such as this patient, steroid therapy could arguably be started at the outset.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has a 4-month history of chronic otitis media and mastoiditis; this has included two episodes of haemoptysis. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day. Urinalysis reveals haematuria, proteinuria and red cell casts. Chest X-ray reveals cavitating mass lesions and evidence of multiple nodules with diffuse alveolar changes. Urea and creatinine are both markedly raised. ESR and rheumatoid factor are likewise elevated. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with typical lung changes
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
The patient has chronic upper respiratory tract changes, which are associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis. These include sinusitis, otitis, mastoiditis, nasal crusting, epistaxis and eventually saddle-nose deformity. Lung changes may include multiple nodules and cavitating lesions with diffuse alveolar changes. Renal changes include a focal glomerulonephritis, associated with necrotising glomerular lesions. Cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA) positivity is the confirmatory immunology test for granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Bronchial carcinoma
Bronchial carcinoma is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoma is a differential diagnosis to be considered in the presence of cavitating lung lesions, but there is a clear suggestion of a multisystem disease here with aural, renal and pulmonary involvement.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) for routine health screening. On blood testing she is noted to have a corrected calcium of 3.15 mmol/l and a creatinine of 284 μmol/l. Serum protein electrophoresis is normal, Hb is 101 g/l and serum phosphate is elevated. Past history of note is chronic reflux nephropathy, hypertension and Type II diabetes. Her hypertension is poorly controlled and she currently takes amlodipine 10 mg. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
This woman has chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertension and diabetes. She has developed tertiary hyperparathyroidism, as exemplified by her hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. Metabolic bone disease is one consequence of tertiary hyperparathyroidism, with the development of mainly cortical bone destruction and cyst formation. Oral agents given to reduce phosphate absorption in patients with chronic kidney disease may serve to delay the onset of hyperparathyroidism. Treatment of choice for tertiary hyperparathyroidism is parathyroidectomy.

Milk–alkali syndrome
Milk–alkali syndrome would be a possibility in the absence of the obvious renal dysfunction. It is characterised by hypercalcaemia caused by ingesting too much calcium and alkali; common culprits include dietary supplements to prevent osteoporosis and indigestion.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes, taking antidiabetic treatment, presents with proteinuria. Apart from her diabetes she has no other past medical history of note. Her serum creatinine and HbA1c level is normal. What would be the most common renal complication in this case?
explanation:
Glomerulosclerosis
People with diabetes are prone to atherosclerosis, urinary infection and papillary necrosis, but glomerular lesions cause most of the problems. Typically, there is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and glomerulosclerosis that may be diffuse or nodular (Kimmelstiel–Wilson syndrome).

Chronic pyelonephritis
Chronic pyelonephritis is incorrect. Chronic pyelonephritis would be more likely in the setting of recurrent urinary tract infection. It frequently presents with both blood and protein in the urine.

Obstructive uropathy
Obstructive uropathy is incorrect. Obstructive uropathy could be caused by many aetiologies, such as renal tumours, calculi and sloughed papillae; diabetes would not directly cause obstructive uropathy. Ultrasound may show hydronephrosis in obstructive uropathy.

stem: A 60-year-old man presenting with periorbital and peripheral oedema is undergoing investigation for suspected nephrotic syndrome. He has a past medical history of hypertension . Dipstick of his urine shows +3 protein. What would the results of a blood test be most likely to show?
explanation:
Decreased total thyroxine levels
Thyroxine levels are depressed in nephrotic syndrome due to the enhanced urinary excretion of thyroxine- binding globulin.

Decreased fibrinogen levels
Decreased fibrinogen levels is incorrect. There is concomitant increase in fibrinogen levels with loss of clotting factors. Renal vein thrombosis occurs in 15–20% of patients with nephrotic syndrome.

Increased antithrombin III levels
Increased antithrombin III levels is incorrect. There is associated hypercoagulability due to urinary loss of antithrombin III, and proteins C and S. Therefore, there is increased predisposition to thrombosis.

stem: An 85-year-old woman complains of dysuria and increased frequency of micturition. She has no history of renal stones. Urinalysis shows no haematuria and 2–3 white cells per high power field; the urine culture is sterile; her white cell count is normal. Which one of the following treatments would be most appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
Topical oestrogen cream
The postmenopausal woman in the present case has symptoms caused by urethral syndrome, which is common in elderly women due to dryness and atrophy of the urethral tissue. The treatment is with topical oestrogen cream, which often results in a dramatic response.

Alkalinisation of the urine
Alkalinisation of the urine would not be useful in this case. Urine alkalinisation may be used in poison elimination (eg salicylate overdose). It involves giving intravenous sodium bicarbonate to produce urine with pH ≥ 7.5.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents acutely unwell to the Emergency Department. She has had gastroenteritis for a few days and has now developed a nosebleed. Past medical history of note includes furosemide and ramipril prescriptions for systolic heart failure. A full blood count and film reveals evidence of red cell haemolysis and thrombocytopenia, and serum creatinine is 290 μmol/l. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS)
Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS) is associated with Escherichia coli infection, particularly E. coli 157:H7. It has been suggested that an acute infection triggers endothelial damage in susceptible individuals. Inherited recurrent HUS has been described with both dominant and recessive patterns of inheritance.

Acute dehydration
Acute dehydration is incorrect. Dehydration leading to ‘pre-kidney disease’ in isolation would not cause haemolysis as is evident here.

Furosemide toxicity
Furosemide toxicity is incorrect. Furosemide therapy may aggravate acute kidney injury (AKI) if taken during a dehydrating illness such as gastroenteritis, but, again, would not cause haemolysis.

stem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset left flank pain and nausea for the past three hours. The pain is colicky and radiating towards his groin. He drinks multiple glasses of iced tea every day. He has had similar abdominal pain previously. His maternal uncle has similar history of abdominal pain. His temperature is 37.4 °C, his heart rate is 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 110/82 mmHg. Examination shows a non-tender abdomen with left renal angle tenderness. An X-ray of the abdomen was normal. A urinary cyanide nitroprusside test is positive. Which of the following would be expected upon further evaluation of this patient?
explanation:
Hexagon-shaped crystals on urine analysis
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with costovertebral angle tenderness is suggestive of urolithiasis. Recurrent urolithiasis in a young adult with negative X-ray findings is suspicious of cystinuria. Hexagon-shaped crystals indicate cystine stones caused by cystinuria. Cystine stones are only poorly radiopaque and often do not appear on X-ray; they are visible on computed tomography (CT), however. Regardless, the positive urine cyanide nitroprusside test confirms the diagnosis.

Increased serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) level
Increased serum PTH levels can cause hypercalciuria, which predisposes to calcium stone formation. Calcium Tutor stones are virtually always radiopaque, whereas this patient has a stone that is not visualised on X-ray. Furthermore, this young patient has none of the common risk factors for parathyroid disease, such as previous

stem: You are asked to review a 36-year-old woman who has presented to the Emergency Department with renal colic. A kidney, ureter and bladder (KUB) X-ray has revealed the presence of multiple renal stones. Her past history of note includes extensive surgical resection for Crohn’s disease. Which one of the following is the most likely chemical composition of her renal stones?
explanation:
Calcium oxalate
Calcium oxalate stones occur in around 65% of patients in the UK with renal stones, calcium phosphate in around 15% and magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones occur in around 10–15%. Oxalate stones occur in patients who ingest excess amounts of foods high in oxalate (e.g. spinach, rhubarb and tea), those on a calcium-restricted diet and those with gastrointestinal disease such as Crohn’s who have increased colonic oxalate absorption. Patients with short bowel syndrome due to surgical resection are particularly prone to the formation of oxalate stones. It is likely in the present case that the surgery for Crohn’s has precipitated the problem.

Calcium phosphate
Calcium phosphate is incorrect. Calcium phosphate stones occur most commonly with metabolic disease, but may be idiopathic. It may occur in the context of increased urinary calcium excretion and hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with the nephrotic syndrome. She has proteinuria (urinary protein–creatinine ratio 386), hypoalbuminaemia (albumin 25 g/l) and oedema. Her renal function is relatively well preserved (creatinine 148 μmol/l). Which one of the following is most likely to accompany nephrotic syndrome?
explanation:
Intravascular volume depletion
The pathophysiology of oedema formation in nephrotic syndrome is poorly understood. Hypoalbuminaemia results in decreased intravascular oncotic pressure, leading to leakage of extracellular fluid from blood to the interstitium. Primary salt and water retention may also contribute to oedema formation in some cases. Therefore, although extravascular fluid retention occurs, there is intravascular contraction due to loss of oncotic pressure. Renal vein thrombosis is particularly common (up to 40%) in patients with nephrotic syndrome

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension is not common in all forms of nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents with haematuria, proteinuria and hypertension. She has a past medical history of hepatitis C infection following intravenous drug use. Her blood tests show reduced C3 levels, normal white blood cell count and low haemoglobin. What would be the single most characteristic histological feature on renal biopsy?
options: Fusion of the foot processes of epithelial cells
Mesangial hypercellularity with crescents in > 80% of glomeruli
Thickening and splitting of the capillary basement membrane
explanation:
Thickening and splitting of the capillary basement membrane
The history of the present case is suggestive of mesangiocapillary (membranoproliferative) glomerulonephritis (MCGN [MPGN]) type I. In this condition, electron microscopy shows mainly subendothelial immune complex deposition and apparent splitting of the capillary basement membrane, giving a ‘tramline’ effect.

Fusion of the foot processes of epithelial cells
Fusion of the foot processes of epithelial cells is incorrect. Fusion of the foot processes of epithelial cells is found in minimal change disease that presents with nephrotic syndrome – peripheral oedema, hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria.

Mesangial hypercellularity with crescents in > 80% of glomeruli
Mesangial hypercellularity with crescents in > 80% of glomeruli is incorrect. Crescents are associated with severe damage to the glomerular tuft; this can occur particularly in microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Goodpasture’s disease. The presence of crescents indicates a rapidly progressing disease.

stem: A 60-year-old patient attends the renal transplant clinic. She has had her transplant for 10 years. She reports swelling of her gums that has been more noticeable in recent months. On examination, there is evidence of gingival hypertrophy. Which of the following medications is likely to have caused this?
explanation:
Ciclosporin
This is a calcineurin inhibitor and a side-effect of this class of drugs is gingival hypertrophy.

Mycophenolate mofetil
Mycophenolate mofetil is incorrect. A common side-effect is gastrointestinal disturbance, especially diarrhoea.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is incorrect. An important side-effect is myelosuppression.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. A prolonged steroid course can give rise to Cushing syndrome.

stem: A 16-year-old woman presents to the clinic for follow up after a first episode of Henoch Schönlein purpura (HSP). The purpuric rash, which was particularly marked on the buttocks and the backs of the legs, is beginning to fade. Urine is still positive to blood on dipstick, creatinine is stable at 86 micromol/l. Which of the following is most likely with respect to long-term prognosis?
options: Complete recovery with no long term sequelae
Long term corticosteroid therapy likely to be required
Long term disease modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARD) likely to be required
Need for long term ACE inhibition to control blood pressure
Recurrent episodes requiring courses of corticosteroids likely
explanation:
Complete recovery with no long term sequelae
Only one-third of patients who are diagnosed with HSP suffer from recurrent episodes. Less than 1% of patients with HSP progress to end-stage renal failure, although it is more common in adults with HSP than in children. Recommendations for renal function monitoring are given below. For those with no proteinuria, recommendations are for blood pressure checking and urinalysis at days 7 and 14 and at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months. For those with proteinuria, follow-up is recommended at days 7 and 14, monthly from 1 to 6 months and then at 12 months.

Long term corticosteroid therapy likely to be required
Long-term corticosteroid therapy likely to be required is incorrect. There is usually no requirement for immunomodulatory therapies. HSP usually resolves with no lasting impairment.

stem: A 64-year-old woman who is taking long term sulphasalazine therapy for rheumatoid arthritis is referred to the clinic by her GP as she has developed painless haematuria. Other past history of note is hypertension, for which she takes ramipril. On examination her BP is measured as 143/84 mmHg. There are obvious signs of rheumatoid affecting her hands, wrists and elbows and a rash over sun-exposed skin. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 115 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 5.0 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 190 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 13 mm/hr 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood ++, protein ++ Which of the following is the most useful investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
Sulphasalazine can cause the development of drug induced lupus. The presence of blood and proteinuria seen here is suggestive of glomerulonephritis and as such renal biopsy is the most appropriate investigation to help confirm diagnosis.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is incorrect. A cystoscopy would be indicated if she had haematuria only, which would necessitate exclusion of an underlying neoplasm.

Rectal biopsy
Rectal biopsy is incorrect. Proteinuria only would raise the possibility of amyloidosis, with rectal or renal biopsy being appropriate investigations to confirm the diagnosis.

Renal ultrasound scan
Renal ultrasound scan is incorrect. Renal ultrasound is required prior to performing renal biopsy, to look for anatomical abnormalities pre-operatively, but is not diagnostic.

Urine cytology
Urine cytology is incorrect. Urine cytology may be helpful in cases of carcinoma, but non-diagnostic.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis of both knees, for which she takes diclofenac, is admitted with progressive lethargy and nausea which has increased significantly over the course of the past few weeks. There is also a history of hypertension for which she takes ramipril and amlodipine. On examination her BP is 178/90 mmHg, pulse is 78/min and regular. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest but nil else of note. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.8 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 197 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 360 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine protein ++, blood ++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Chronic interstitial nephritis
The anaemia seen here, with progressive lethargy and nausea, points more to chronic kidney disease than an acute deterioration in renal function.

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. It does not present with haematuria; the urine dipstick is typically bland or shows minor proteinuria. It is the most common cause of intrinsic acute kidney disease. Other features on urine biochemistry would include increased urinary sodium excretion > 40 mmol/l.

Crescenteric glomerulonephritis
Crescenteric glomerulonephritis is incorrect and is associated with acute kidney disease associated with blood and protein in the urine. The history would be of acute rapid deterioration in renal function and there may be suggestive associative symptoms such as vasculitic rash, haemoptysis or ear/nose and throat symptoms, which are absent in this case.

Hypertensive renal disease
Hypertensive renal disease is incorrect. Although hypertensive renal disease is a possibility, we are provided with the history of diclofenac use, which is a pointer to chronic interstitial nephritis and the blood and proteinuria is consistent with this. Management includes discontinuation of the NSAID and control of hypertension to prevent a further deterioration in creatinine.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is incorrect and presents with nephrotic range proteinuria. The peak incidence is in the fourth to the sixth decade of life, with a male to female preponderance of 2:1. It is characterised by IgG- rich immune deposit accumulation in the outer aspects of the glomerular basement membrane due to antibodies directed against an as yet unknown antigen.

stem: A 57-year-old diabetic woman with a history of dysuria and suprapubic pain is admitted to the Emergency Department. The pain has now extended to involve the left loin region and there is associated haematuria and oliguria. Apart from diabetes she has no other past medical history of note. Blood tests show a raised glucose level and normal white blood cell count, although the CRP is elevated to 85 mg/dl. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this problem?
explanation:
Renal papillary necrosis
Urinary tract infections are relatively more common in women with diabetes. Untreated infections in people with diabetes can result in renal papillary necrosis, which results in linear breaks at papillary base, and ureteric obstruction may result if the papillae have sloughed off.

Acute tubular necrosis
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis does not present with haematuria; the urine dipstick is bland or shows minor proteinuria. It is the most common cause of intrinsic acute kidney disease. Other features on urine biochemistry would include increased urinary sodium excretion > 40 mmol/l.

stem: A week after an episode of infective diarrhoea, a 17-year-old teenager presents with fever, hypertension and haematuria. You understand that he had been doing work experience at a farm a short period before he became unwell. Blood tests reveal anaemia with an Hb of 84 g/l, and an elevated creatinine of 185 μmol/l. A possible diagnosis could be:
explanation:
Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome
