Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and varying degrees of acute kidney disease. In many cases, an infectious or immune-complex mediated cause has been proposed. Epidemics of bloody diarrhoea related to infection with a specific strain of Escherichia coli (O157:H7) have been documented. The bacteria release a verotoxin that damages endothelial cells, particularly those of the kidney. Working at a farm implies haemolytic-uraemic syndrome is the most likely cause as opposed to other inherent or acquired pathology due to medications/infections (the other options).

Acute interstitial nephritis
Acute interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Working at a farm makes HUS the most likely cause.

stem: A 26-year-old man attends the General Nephrology Clinic for follow-up as he has a history of biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy. His BP in clinic is 149/88 mmHg. His urine dipstick shows protein 2+, blood 2+ and his urine protein:creatinine ratio was 88 mg/mmol. He is not on any regular medications. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na +) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 103 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which anti-hypertensive medication would you initiate first?
explanation:
Ramipril
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are the recommended first-line agent in glomerular disease as they not only help to control blood pressure, but also help to reduce proteinuria, which confers a significant reno-protective effect and thus a positive impact on prognosis.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of depression attends with worsening peripheral oedema over the last 3 weeks. There is no history of chest pain and he has been otherwise reasonably well. He is not currently on any regular medications. He had been an inpatient about 4 weeks ago and was treated for chest infection with IV antibiotics, from which he recovered. He is afebrile and has a blood pressure of 153/78 mmHg. There is peripheral oedema to his mid-shins bilaterally. His blood tests show: Investigation On discharge from last inpatient stay Now Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 126 g/l 135–175 g/l Sodium (Na +) 145 mmol/l 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium K + (mmol/l) 4.0 mmol/l 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.9 mmol/l 9.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 78 µmol/l 151 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l eGFR > 90 ml/min/1.73m 2 44 ml/min/1.73m 2 Albumin 33 g/l 29 g/l 35–55 g/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 34 mg/l <4 mg/l 0-10 mg/l His urine dip shows protein 2+, blood 2+. Urine PCR is 150mg/mmol. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. What is the likely pathology for his peripheral oedema?
options: Reduced oncotic pressure due to nephrotic syndrome
Acute kidney injury due to interstitial nephritis
Acute tubular necrosis secondary to sepsis
explanation:
Acute kidney injury due to interstitial nephritis
The recent history of antibiotics raises the possibility of acute interstitial nephritis, especially in the absence of other clinical factors that could have precipitated an acute kidney injury such as dehydration or sepsis. Interstitial nephritis can only be diagnosed by a renal biopsy and treatment can involve immunosuppression, typically with steroids.

Reduced oncotic pressure due to nephrotic syndrome
Reduced oncotic pressure due to nephrotic syndrome is incorrect. The patient does not fulfil all the diagnostic criteria for nephrotic syndrome, which is periperheral oedema, low albumin and a urine protein:creatinine ratio of more than 300 mg/mmol.

Acute tubular necrosis secondary to sepsis
Acute tubular necrosis secondary to sepsis is incorrect. His kidney function was normal on discharge, suggesting that if he had sustained an acute kidney injury (AKI) due to sepsis, this had resolved on discharge. There is nothing at present to suggest ongoing infection.

stem: A 73-year-old widow is undergoing haemodialysis for chronic kidney disease. Which one of the following is the most common problem that can arise in this case?
explanation:
Protein–calorie malnutrition
Protein–calorie malnutrition is seen in up to 50% of patients and contributes substantially to increased morbidity and mortality. Dietary restriction of foods with high phosphate content (milk, eggs and cheese), decreased protein intake, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, may all contribute to this condition. Modern techniques of dialysis preclude chances of vitamin D or calcium deficiency, fluid and electrolyte imbalance or risk of viral hepatitis.

Arteriovenous graft infection
Arteriovenous graft infection is incorrect. Approximately 20 percent of arteriovenous fistulas which fail do so because of infection. The most common cause of graft failure is stenotic vascular lesions, however, this is still less common than the occurrence of protein-calorie malnutrition.

Hypocalcaemia
Hypocalcaemia is incorrect. Modern techniques of dialysis preclude chances of calcium deficiency, fluid and electrolyte imbalance.

stem: During the course of a routine medical examination, a 26-year-old man is found to have +3 haematuria. This is confirmed on microscopy and on a second urinalysis 9 months later. He remembers two episodes during the past year when his urine was red, and both occurred in association with an upper respiratory tract infection. The family history is negative for renal disease. His blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg and he has no oedema. Plasma creatinine is 65 μmol/l. Which one of the following would a renal biopsy most probably show?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy is the glomerular lesion most frequently found on renal biopsy. It usually presents in the manner of the case in this question or with recurrent visible haematuria, often in close temporal relationship with an upper respiratory tract infection. On light microscopy, diffuse mesangial proliferation is typical, with prominent IgA deposits evident on immunostaining.

Cast nephropathy
Cast nephropathy is incorrect. The pattern of frank haematuria after respiratory tract infection (RTI) would not indicate the presence of myeloma.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of chronic sinusitis presents to the Emergency Department with worsening shortness of breath, nausea and anorexia. Her past medical history includes asthma since childhood, which is well controlled with a low-dose steroid inhaler and PRN salbutamol. On examination her BP is 175/100 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There are scattered crackles on auscultation of the chest and you notice evidence of collapse of the nasal bridge. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 230 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 75 mm/1 st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Urine blood ++ protein ++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
The clues here are the sinusitis, crackles on auscultation of the chest and evidence of kidney disease. We are not given results of chest X-ray, which would be likely to show patchy shadowing, nor are we given pulmonary function tests, which may show increased transfer factor due to pulmonary haemorrhage.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis is normally associated with worsening of asthma symptoms. It presents with allergic rhinitis, asthma and eosinophilia with a small and medium vessel vasculitis. It affects the lungs and skin predominantly. There is equal incidence of disease among males and females, with more frequent occurrence in those aged between 30 and 50 years. The cause is unknown.

Goodpasture syndrome
Goodpasture syndrome is incorrect. It is not associated with sinusitis. This condition is also known as anti- glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease and typically presents as a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage. There would be both blood and protein in the urine. Renal biopsy would show a focal and segmental necrotising, crescentic glomerulonephritis. Bowman’s capsule may be ruptured. Immunofluorescence shows linear capillary wall staining for the anti-glomerular basement membrane (IgG) and C3 deposition in a similar pattern.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. It is not usually associated with lung pathology. It is a rare, medium-vessel, necrotising arteritis involving principally the skin, nerves, gut and kidney. It may be associated with hepatitis B infection. Typical presentations include fever, weight loss, arthralgia and myalgia. Mononeuritis multiplex and livedo reticularis may be present. If medium vessel involvement occurs in the gut, then it may also present with abdominal pain or bloody stool. Renal symptoms may include haematuria or loin pain with segmental renal infarcts.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is incorrect. There is no history to suggest post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically presents 10–21 days after streptococcal infection with the nephritic syndrome of haematuria, hypertension, oedema and oliguria. It is not associated with asthma or collapse of the nasal bridge.

stem: A 62-year-old South Asian man on peritoneal dialysis presents with a 6-hour history of vomiting, abdominal pain and pyrexia. He reports there was cloudy peritoneal dialysis fluid on his last exchange. Which organism is the most likely cause of this clinical picture?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus
The patient clinically has peritoneal dialysis (PD) peritonitis, given the history of cloudy PD effluent. PD fluid should be sent for microscopy, and culture and treatment initiated with a course of intraperitoneal (IP) antibiotics. The most common causative organism is Gram-positive cocci (45–75%) such as Staphylococcus aureus or epidermis, introduced due to poor aseptic technique when performing a PD exchange or following catheter site exit infection. IP vancomycin is usually the drug of choice to treat these infections.

Candida albicans
Candida albicans is incorrect. Fungal infections are also rare (around 3% of cases) and are usually Candida spp. The PD catheter must be removed in these patients.

stem: A 72-year-old man with acute myelogenous leukaemia on doxorubicin and cytarabine presents with severe left flank pain and oliguria. An abdominal radiograph shows no calculus, but a filling defect in the left ureter suggestive of a stone is visualised after contrast investigation. Which one of the following is the most probable cause for this problem?
explanation:
Hyperuricaemia
Chemotherapy involving rapid lysis of malignant cells can lead to the release of large amounts of nucleoprotein and increased uric acid production. This can lead to acute hyperuricaemic nephropathy (most probably the diagnosis in this case), which causes kidney disease with marked hyperuricaemia. Uric acid crystals may deposit in the collecting ducts, pelvis and ureters; ultrasound may demonstrate extrarenal obstruction due to stones.

Doxorubicin toxicity
Doxorubicin toxicity is incorrect. Features include myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, oral mucositis, oesophagitis, diarrhoea, skin reactions (ie hand foot syndrome) and life-threatening cardiotoxicity. Doxorubicin may cause red discoloration of the urine for up to 1–2 days post treatment. Although nephrotoxicity is also a known complication, the mechanism is not associated with renal stones.

stem: A 32-year-old woman complains of weakness and lethargy. Clinical examination reveals a blood pressure of 96/70 mmHg, there is no peripheral or pulmonary oedema.. Her eGFR is > 90 ml/min/1.73 m 2 and her serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/l; her serum calcium is 2.22 mmol/l and serum magnesium 0.5 mmol/l; bicarbonate is measured at 33 mmol/l. Urinary toxicology screen does not reveal any diuretic use. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the probable tubular defect?
options: Genetic defect of the Na+–Cl– cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Pharmacological inhibition of the Na+–K+–2Cl– cotransporter
explanation:
Genetic defect of the Na+–Cl– cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
This patient has Gitelman syndrome. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes are renal tubular salt-wasting disorders in which the kidneys cannot reabsorb chloride in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, or the distal convoluted tubule, depending on the mutation. Most cases of Bartter syndrome are discovered in infancy or early adolescence. Patients with Gitelman syndrome tend to have milder symptoms than those with Bartter syndrome and to present in adolescence and early adulthood. The history here is therefore most consistent with Gitelman syndrome, which is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC12A3 gene that codes for the thiazide-sensitive Na +–Cl - cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). There seems to be no firm correlation between the range and severity of clinical features in Gitelman syndrome and the underlying gene mutations: patients may be highly symptomatic (e.g. salt craving, dizziness, fatigue, muscle weakness and cramps, paraesthesiae, non-specific aches and pains), or may have minimal symptomatology. Hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia are typically present. Several different channel abnormalities have been identified in Bartter syndrome, including the Na +-K +-2Cl - channel in type 1 Bartter's.

stem: A 63-year-old patient with CKD G5 receives a home visit for her weekly erythropoietin subcutaneous injection for anaemia management. Where in the body is EPO normally produced?
explanation:
Interstitial fibroblasts
Erythropoietin is produced in adulthood predominantly by interstitial fibroblasts found within the renal cortex, in response to hypoxia. The main extrarenal site of production is in the perisinusoidal cells in the liver where production occurs in the fetal and perinatal period.

Juxtaglomerular apparatus
Juxtaglomerular apparatus is incorrect. This is responsible for renin production in response to a fall in blood pressure. The renin produced plays a critical role in autoregulation of blood pressure in the kidney via the renin- angiotensin system.

Glomerular capillary walls
Glomerular capillary walls is incorrect. The glomerular capillaries are lined by endothelial cells that contain a large number of fenestrae for filtration of blood plasma into the Bowman’s capsule.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 4-week history of oedema. Serum albumin is 22 g/l, creatinine 98 μmol/l and 24-h urinary protein output 5.3 g. She also has non-visible haematuria; apparently she had a previous episode of visible haematuria after a respiratory tract infection some years earlier. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
This patient with haematuria and nephrotic syndrome has immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy (Berger’s disease). Mesangial IgA deposition leads to proteinuria and haematuria. Only 5% present with nephrotic syndrome.

Minimal change disease
Minimal change disease is incorrect. Haematuria is very unusual with minimal change disease.

Renal carcinoma
Renal carcinoma is incorrect. Renal cell carcinoma very rarely presents with nephrotic syndrome.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She recently presented to her GP with headaches and was found to be hypertensive with a BP of 160/90 mmHg. A past history of multiple urinary tract infections as a child is noted, and an ultrasound demonstrates evidence of bilateral cortical scarring due to reflux nephropathy. Her creatinine is 215 μmol/l and urinary protein excretion is 2.5 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment for her blood pressure?
explanation:
Ramipril
In proteinuric renal disease, even if it is not due to underlying diabetes, either ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the initial therapy of choice. Ramipril is therefore the correct answer. Non-dihydropryridine calcium antagonists also have effects on proteinuria, diltiazem or verapamil may therefore be alternative first-line options in patients who cannot take an ACE inhibitor or ARB. Add-in therapy of choice to ACE inhibition would be a calcium channel antagonist. The evidence supporting dual blockade with an angiotensin II antagonist and an ARB is weak.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and these are not recommended as a lone therapy in a proteinuric state because they have been shown to worsen proteinuria and have not been shown to improve outcome in proteinuric diabetics. However, they are acceptable for blood pressure control if the patient is already on an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found to have visible haematuria, proteinuria of 1.5 g/24 h and a serum creatinine level of 153 μmol/l. He has suffered a recent upper respiratory tract infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
IgA nephropathy presents with hypertension, haematuria and proteinuria (which may be exacerbated in the presence of respiratory infections)

Diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy is incorrect. Visible haematuria is uncommon in diabetic nephropathy, and proteinuria would be much greater (> 3.5 g/24 h).

Focal glomerulosclerosis
Focal glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Proteinuria would be much greater (> 3.5 g/24 h) in focal glomerulosclerosis.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP) with malaise, anorexia, vaginal bleeding and weight loss. Screening blood samples reveals a urea of 50.1 mmol/l and a serum creatinine of 690 μmol/l. Her past history includes frequent headaches, but nil else of note. She has failed to attend her routine smear test appointments. Ultrasound reveals bilateral hydronephrosis and a suspicion of a central pelvic mass. Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely to be responsible for this woman’s hydronephrosis?
explanation:
Cervical carcinoma
There is a suspicion that this woman has been non-compliant with standard women’s health-screening measures, eg cervical screening. This, with the central pelvic mass on ultrasound examination and bilateral hydronephrosis accompanied by kidney disease, makes cervical carcinoma the most likely cause.

Retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF)
RPF rarely leads to hydronephrosis; however, this would be RPF if presenting as a ureteric mass.

Ovarian carcinoma
The central pelvic mass would be more typical of a cervical origin.

stem: A 71-year-old man has undergone conventional angiography three days earlier. There has been a steep rise in his creatinine over the past few days. On examination his blood pressure is 155/95 mmHg, and his pulse is 90/min and regular. He has livedo reticularis, and a blue discoloration over his toes with small punched-out ulcers. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Eosinophils 3.8 × 10 9/l 0–0.4 × 10 9/l Platelets 201 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 302 μmol/l (156 μmol/l pre-angiography) 50–120 µmol/l Urine microscopy Hyaline casts and eosinophils Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cholesterol embolism
This patient has undergone arterial instrumentation and coupled with a marked eosinophilia and increasing creatinine, this fits best with a diagnosis of cholesterol embolism. No treatments have been shown to be of benefit in managing the condition, and thrombolysis, anti-coagulation and further arterial instrumentation may actually worsen prognosis. Unfortunately, the majority of patients have a degree of ongoing renal impairment. In-hospital mortality after cardiac catheterisation where cholesterol embolism has occurred is as high as 16%.

Buerger's disease
Buerger’s disease is incorrect. Buerger’s disease is a condition associated with accelerated thrombosis of medium and small vessels predominantly in the lower limbs, it presents with rapidly worsening claudication in heavy smokers.

Contrast nephropathy
Contrast nephropathy is incorrect. Contrast nephropathy may be the result of a contrast load during angiographic procedure. It is defined as a greater than 25% increase in serum creatinine or an absolute increase in serum creatinine of 0.5 mg/dl after iodine contrast agent without any other clear cause for acute injury. There is no association with eosinophilia, eosinophiluria or livedo reticularis.

Renal artery embolus
Renal artery embolus is incorrect. Renal artery embolus is an infrequent and significant cause of renal impairment in patients with atherosclerosis. Patients may have a history of valvular cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation and recent acute myocardial infarction. It presents with atypical lumbar pain and raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). There is no association with eosinophilia, eosinophiluria or livedo reticularis.

Renal vein thrombosis
Renal vein thrombosis is incorrect. Renal vein thrombosis commonly presents in patients with nephrotic syndrome due to the hypercoagulable state and in renal cell cancer with involvement of the renal vein. Patients may have occasional flank or lower back pain caused by a sudden clot and sudden deterioration in renal function. The clinical history in this case is not typical of renal vein thrombosis.

stem: A 55-year-old man with biopsy-proven diabetic nephropathy undergoes haemodialysis three times a week using a radiocephalic fistula. He is due dialysis today but reports the fistula does not seem to have its usual thrill when palpated. On examination you are concerned the fistula has clotted. He does not pass any urine. Results of which blood test will guide further management acutely?
explanation:
Potassium
This patient has a clotted fistula and will therefore be unable to dialyse unless it is declotted, typically via thrombolysis treatment performed by an interventional radiologist. This procedure will have to be arranged during normal working hours at centres that provide such a service. In the meantime and acutely, the concern is whether he needs urgent dialysis. Hyperkalaemia, which can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, would be an indication to insert a temporary dialysis line into a central vein (internal jugular or femoral) and emergency dialysis performed. Most patients with hyperkalaemia can be managed with medical treatment but this patient is a dialysis patient who is anuric, and the only definitive treatment to reduce the potassium is dialysis. Other important indications for emergency dialysis includes Refractory pulmonary oedema (especially in those producing minimal urine) Refractory metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.2) Uraemic complications (e.g. encephalopathy, pericarditis)

stem: An 82-year-old man presents to his GP with increasing oedema and ascites. He is hypertensive, for which he takes amlodipine. There is shortness of breath on exercise. His alcohol history is two cans of stout per day. ECG is normal, and CXR reveals normal heart size and no signs of cardiac failure. Serum albumin is 23 g/dl; urinary albumin excretion is 7 g/24 h, with no haematuria. He has mild anaemia with a normal MCV. Total cholesterol is elevated. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by significant proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and hypercholesterolaemia. This patient has a urinary albumin excretion of 7 g/24 h and a serum albumin level of 23 g/dl, both of which are hallmark features of nephrotic syndrome. The presence of oedema and ascites further supports this diagnosis as these symptoms are commonly associated with low serum albumin levels. In elderly patients, the most common cause is membranous nephropathy, which can be idiopathic or secondary to conditions such as carcinomas or systemic lupus erythematosus.

Cardiac failure
Cardiac failure usually presents with symptoms such as shortness of breath on exertion and oedema but it typically would not cause heavy proteinuria or hypoalbuminaemia. This patient’s normal ECG and chest X-ray make cardiac failure less likely since these tests would often show signs indicative of heart inTutor problems true

stem: You are reviewing the effects of a new agent for the treatment of hypertension on renal function. Data from the main study are reported using the ‘modification of diet in renal disease’ (MDRD) equation. Which of the following has the greatest effect on glomerular filtration rate (GFR) as calculated by the MDRD equation?
explanation:
Muscle mass
The original MDRD equation for SI units is: GFR (ml/min per 1.73 m2) = 186 × (Scr/88.4)−1.154 × (Age)−0.203 × (0.742 if female) × (1.212 if African– American). Creatinine is directly related to muscle mass, hence any change in muscle mass can significantly impact on the MDRD equation.

Age
Age is incorrect. Although age does impact on the MDRD calculation, it's relative contribution is smaller.

Body weight
Body weight is incorrect. Body weight does not contribute to the calculation. MDRD is thought to be less reliable as an estimator for GFR in the population with normal renal function; as such in thisChat population other with calculators such as the CKD-Epi calculator have been developed.

stem: A 65-year-old man, who has been on haemodialysis for 12 years, presents with gradually increasing bone pain. He underwent subtotal parathyroidectomy 4 years ago. Current medications include alfacalcidol 1 μg/day and calcium carbonate 500 mg/tid. His serum calcium concentration is 2.97 mmol/l (NR 2.2 –2.6), phosphate is 2.71 mmol/l (NR 0.8–1.4) and parathyroid hormone level is 19.2 pmol/l (NR 0.9–5.4). Which one of the following is the most probable cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Hyperparathyroid bone disease
Even after total parathyroidectomy in chronic kidney disease, only 10% of patients have a total lack of parathyroid activity post-operatively. Residual parathyroid tissue may be detected using technetium-99 sestamibi scanning. Despite his previous parathyroidectomy, this patient clearly has grossly elevated PTH levels in the presence of hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. This indicates tertiary hyperparathyroidism due to hyperplasia of retained parathyroid tissue.

Adynamic bone disease
Adynamic bone disease is incorrect. Adynamic bone disease is increasing in prominence as a cause of skeletal pathology in patients with kidney disease, especially those on peritoneal dialysis. It is characterised by a low bone turnover state, with parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels usually within the normal range, absence of excess osteoid formation (distinguishing it from osteomalacia), a tendency towards hypercalcaemia and easy fracture.

stem: A 67-year-old patient is referred to the Renal Clinic for review. His GP has noted a deteriorating creatinine from 136 to 210 μmol/l, thus reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). He has had Type 2 diabetes for the past 7 years, for which he takes gliclazide 160 mg BD, aspirin 75 mg and simvastatin 20 mg. He is also prescribed amlodipine 5 mg daily for treatment of hypertension. His 24-h mean systolic BP is 136 mmHg. Investigations; Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 189 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 210 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* HbA1c 54 mmol/mol (7.1%) <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Urine albustix positive Which change would you make to the anti-hypertensive medication?
explanation:
Add Ramipril
This patient in all likelihood has diabetic nephropathy, and despite the fact that his creatinine is significantly elevated, he should still be offered a trial of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Regular monitoring of renal function post ACE inhibition is important, as the rise in creatinine may be unrelated to diabetes and in fact be due to renovascular disease.

Add Bendroflumethiazide
Add bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethiazide is a thiazide diuretic and would be useful if hypertension persists despite ACE inhibitor, similar to indapamide. Thiazides per se have decreased in usage over the past few years because of impaired glucose tolerance associated with their use.

Add Bisoprolol
Add bisoprolol is incorrect. Bisoprolol is a β-blocker and would not be the first-line anti-hypertensive in this case. However, β-blockers may be considered in younger people, particular in those who are intolerant or contraindicated to renin–angiotensin blockade or women of child-bearing potential or people with evidence of increased sympathetic drive.

Add Diltiazem
Add diltiazem is incorrect. In patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibition, evidence has shown that diltiazem may reduce proteinuria in patients with diabetic nephropathy. If hypertension persists post initiation of ACE inhibitor, a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide would be the next appropriate step.

Increase Amlodipine
Increase amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and these are not recommended as a lone therapy in the proteinuric state because they have been shown to worsen proteinuria and have not been shown to improve outcome in proteinuric diabetics. However, they are acceptable for blood pressure control if the patient is already on an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). Therefore, to increase amlodipine would not be appropriate in this case.

stem: A 18-year-old man presents with dark discolouration of urine. There is a history of upper respiratory tract infection with severe pharyngitis two weeks earlier. He was previously fit and well. On examination, he has a puffy face with periorbital oedema. His blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following is most likely to occur?
explanation:
Proteinuria
The likely diagnosis here is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, the clue being the preceding upper respiratory tract infection. The typical presentation is that of clinical nephritis, with haematuria and oedema ± hypertension. This leads to significant proteinuria, which can recur after subsequent infections. Peak occurrence is in children aged 2–12 years, although the condition may occur at any age.

Acute cardiac failure
Acute cardiac failure is incorrect. Cardiac failure is very unlikely in patients with otherwise normal cardiovascular systems.

stem: A 19-year-old woman complains of stiff joints and a facial rash. Her blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg, she has +1 oedema, slightly swollen metacarpophalangeal joints and some ulceration of her buccal mucosa. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 86 ml/min/1.73m 2, Hb is 89 g/l and platelet count is 92 × 10 9/l. Urinalysis shows +3 blood and +3 protein. High titres of double-stranded DNA antibodies (dsDNA) are detectable in her serum. Which one of the following pathogenic features has led to the renal lesion?
options: Circulating antibodies directed against the glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
Deposition of a linear dense deposit within the glomerular basement membrane
explanation:
Subendothelial deposition of immune complexes
The type of renal disease that develops in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is dependent on the site of deposition of the immune deposit, which may in turn be dependent on the site of immune complex formation. Circulating immune complexes, which tend to be large and anionic, cannot cross the glomerular basement membrane and thus become deposited between the vascular endothelium and the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) (‘subendothelial’). These complexes are efficient at fixing complement, thereby generating chemoattractants such as C3a and C5a, which have direct access to the circulation and result in the influx of immune effector cells such as neutrophils and monocytes. These changes are manifested histologically by mesangial and proliferative glomerulonephritis and clinically by the nephritic syndrome, with haematuria being prominent. Immune complexes that are formed in situ, or that are cationic, tend to deposit between the GBM and the epithelium of Bowman’s space (‘subepithelial’). These are also capable of activating complement, but the presence of the GBM between them and the circulation

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with flank pain and haematuria. His plasma creatinine concentration is 368 μmol/l and renal ultrasound reveals bilateral 14-cm kidneys with multiple cysts. There are also cysts scattered through the liver. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this condition?
options: Genetic defect in the gene encoding polycystin
Genetic defect in the von Hippel–Lindau gene
Genetic defect in the gene encoding type-IV collagen
Genetic defect in the gene encoding cystinosin
explanation:
Genetic defect in the gene encoding polycystin
This man has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Some 85% of cases of ADPKD are associated with a mutation in the PKD1 gene, which results in the absence of functioning polycystin. This novel protein has unknown functions but may operate as a cell membrane ion transporter. Most of the remaining cases of ADPKD are associated with a defect in PKD2, the transcriptional effects of which are unknown. Mutations in PKD1 tend to result in a more severe phenotype, with kidney disease typically occurring in the fifth to sixth decade of life, whereas patients with a PKD2 mutation tend to develop kidney disease more slowly.

Bilateral ureteric reflux from childhood
The presence of liver cysts in addition to bilateral renal cysts is suggestive of a systemic/genetic underlying cause.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He complains of weight loss and night sweats, generalised weakness and joint pains over the past few months. He has had increasing nausea over the past 2 weeks, shortness of breath, and a cough and a nosebleed the day before his visit to the clinic. The only past history of note includes mild asthma. General examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.2 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 181 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 75 mm/1st hour 0–10 mm in the 1 st hour Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 172 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l cANCA Positive Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
The symptoms suggestive of both nasal tract and lung pathology, coupled with raised creatinine, positive cANCA, haematuria and proteinuria, support a diagnosis of GPA. In this situation, biopsy is the optimal way to confirm the diagnosis. Given involvement of the nasal mucosa, this may represent the easiest approach to obtain a tissue sample demonstrating evidence of vasculitis and granuloma formation. Prednisolone and cyclophosphamide in combination is the initial treatment of choice.

Behçet syndrome
Behçet syndrome is incorrect. It is mucosal ulceration and uveitis that are most associated with Behçet syndrome. Behçet syndrome is a rare immune-mediated small-vessel systemic vasculitis.

Churg–Strauss syndrome
Churg–Strauss syndrome is incorrect. Churg–Strauss is associated with positive pANCA. This may present with similar constitutional symptoms, such as fever, loss of appetite and weight loss. Key features of Churg–Strauss include significant and worsening asthma, coupled with peripheral blood eosinophilia.

Microscopic polyangitis
Microscopic polyangitis is incorrect. Microscopic polyangitis is associated with positive pANCA. Microscopic polyangiitis may present with similar constitutional symptoms, such as fever, loss of appetite and weight loss. Purpura and livedo reticularis may be present.

SLE
SLE is incorrect. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is predominantly associated with positive anti-nuclear antibodies. It is more common in Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic or Asian females. It often presents in youth or young adulthood (although auto-antibodies predate the disease). About 50% of patients with SLE will develop renal impairment within 3 years of diagnosis, and about 10% will progress to end-stage renal disease by 10 years. It may present with arthralgia, weight loss and fever. cANCA is not positive.

stem: A 33-year-old man presents with fever, joint pains, nasal crusting, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. Blood results revealed an impaired renal function, raised CRP, Hb of 9g /d and ANCA positive for MPO and PR3. Renal biopsy showed a focal necrotising glomerulonephritis. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Cyclophosphamide and prednisolone
Focal necrotising glomerulonephritis is the characteristic renal lesion of granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. Typically, it presents with deteriorating renal function that progresses to kidney disease within three months, (ie as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis), although a few patients have disease that is more indolent. Proteinuria (typically 2-3 g / 24 h, but occasionally in the nephrotic range) and non-visible haematuria provide clinical evidence of glomerulonephritis, as does urine microscopy that reveals granular and red cell casts. The combination of prednisolone and cyclophosphamide is now established as the standard induction therapy for patients with generalised granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis. there is consensus on how corticosteroids should be used, but less so for cyclophosphamide. Prednisolone is given in doses of around 1 mg/kg/day initially, after which the dose is reduced rapidly, typically at weekly intervals. Controlled trials show that adding pulses of methylprednisolone is unlikely to confer additional benefit.

stem: A 28-year-old IV heroin abuser is brought by paramedics to the Emergency Department after being found collapsed on the floor by his girlfriend. When she last saw him the previous evening he seemed to have a mild head cold and was planning to score some heroin to try and make himself feel better. On examination his GCS is 13, his BP is 90/60 mmHg, with a pulse of 130/min. Apparently, the paramedics found him lying on his left side and there is extensive bruising over the left hip and lower back. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 250 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 3010 IU/l 10–40 IU/l Urine dipstick Blood 3+ Which of the following other tests is most likely to be significantly elevated?
explanation:
Creatine kinase
Creatine kinase (CK), is released as a product of muscle breakdown, and the significant elevation in AST coupled with urine dipstick blood hints at rhabdomyolysis, because of a prolonged period on the floor. If urine microscopy is performed, red cells are not found because the dipstick positivity comes from myoglobin, rather than haemoglobin.

Acid phosphatase
Acid phosphatase is incorrect. Acid phosphatase was formerly used for assessment of prostatic carcinoma. It is not affected by rhabdomyolysis.

Alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase is incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase would be raised in liver abnormalities, cardiac injury and bone disorders. It is not typically affected in rhabdomyolysis.

Lactate dehydrogenase
Lactate dehydrogenase is incorrect. Although elevation of lactate dehyrogenase (LDH), elevation will also occur, it is the latest enzyme from muscle breakdown to become elevated.

Troponin
Troponin is incorrect. Troponin is specific to cardiac muscle. Hence it is now a commonly used biomarker of cardiac injury from myocardial infarction.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a history of resected squamous cell carcinoma of the lung presents with generalised oedema and moderate proteinuria (2+ on dipstick). Urinalysis reveals proteinuria, and further workup is pending. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Membranous nephropathy
In many patients the trigger for the disease is unknown, but associations include systemic lupus erythematosus, malignancies of the bowel and bronchus, penicillamine therapy and hepatitis B infection; Plasmodium malariae infection may be a precipitant in the tropics. There is a strong association with HLA-DR3, and the condition presents predominantly in adults, with a male preponderance. Thickening of the capillary basement membrane due to immune complex deposition is the main feature of membranous nephropathy. One-third of patients develop chronic kidney disease within 10–20 years of diagnosis. Younger patients and women have the best prognosis. Spontaneous remission may occur in up to a third of patients. The value of immunotherapy is uncertain, but there is a strong consensus to treat patients with severe disease with corticosteroid therapy +/– chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide or azathioprine.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is incorrect. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is one of the most common primary glomerular diseases in adults that may present with nephrotic syndrome, in the absence/presence of renal impairment. It is progressive and accounts for 2.3% of patients needing renal

stem: A 52-year-old man of Afro-Caribbean descent presents to his General Practitioner for an annual review. His past medical history includes type II diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3, for which he takes metformin and gliclazide. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 155/95 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 bpm. His chest is clear on auscultation, with normal heart sounds. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen. Random blood glucose: 10.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the next most appropriate agent to be initiated?
explanation:
Losartan
Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker that works to preserve renal function in patients with hypertension and type II diabetes. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend the addition of an angiotensin receptor blocker over an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

Amlodipine
Although amlodipine is recommended as an antihypertensive agent for patients of Afro-Caribbean decent, patients with diabetes and hypertension should be started on an angiotensin receptor blocker for renal protection.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with visible haematuria, right loin pain, night sweats and weight loss. Physical examination reveals a mass in the right flank. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 90 g/l 130–180 g/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.7 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 89 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal cell carcinoma
This has a classic triad of visible haematuria, loin pain and unilateral palpable mass, and is associated with systemic illness such as fever, night sweats and weight loss.

stem: The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is made up of a single layer of cells that interdigitate with one another and united by apical tight junctions. It plays a major role in water and electrolyte metabolism. Which of the following is one of the most important functions of the PCT?
explanation:
Sodium reabsorption
Sodium is absorbed by the proximal tubule. The functions of the proximal tubule include regulation of the filtrate pH by exchanging hydrogen ions for bicarbonate ions into the filtrate, and the reabsorption of sodium, glucose and amino acids. Around 65 % of sodium reabsorption occurs at the PCT.

Ammonia absorption
Ammonia absorption in incorrect. The proximal tubule excretes ammonia rather than absorbing it.

Bicarbonate secretion
Bicarbonate secretion in incorrect. Bicarbonate reabsorption is mediated at the proximal tubular level.

Glucose excretion
Glucose excretion in incorrect. Glucose as well as amino acids are absorbed by the proximal tubule.

stem: A 20-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department after a road traffic collision. He has no relevant past medical history. Upon examination he has a blood pressure of 80/60 mmHg and a pulse rate of 120 bpm. Urine dipstick show +3 blood. Blood results show urea 15mmol/l and Cr 800 µmol/l. Which of the following is the single most important biochemical factor that should be kept in mind?
options: Acidosis leads to the movement of potassium from the extracellular to the intracellular fluid
Adrenaline inhibits the entry of potassium into cells, increasing the plasma potassium level
Hyperkalaemia is associated with increasing blood pH
Potassium release from muscle cells leads to gluconeogenesis
Tissue destruction or breakdown results in the release of intracellular potassium
explanation:
Tissue destruction or breakdown results in the release of intracellular potassium
This patient has rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney disease. The most important biochemical factor that may cause arrhythmia is hyperkalaemia: potassium is released from the cells during tissue destruction.

Acidosis leads to the movement of potassium from the extracellular to the intracellular fluid
compartment Acidosis leads to the movement of potassium from the extracellular to the intracellular fluid compartment is incorrect. Potassium is the main intracellular cation. Therefore, acidosis leads to the movement of potassium from the intracellular to the extracellular fluid compartment.

Adrenaline inhibits the entry of potassium into cells, increasing the plasma potassium level
Adrenaline inhibits the entry of potassium into cells, increasing the plasma potassium level is incorrect. Adrenaline stimulates the entry of potassium into cells, decreasing the plasma potassium level.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with cough, haemoptysis and glomerulonephritis. He is a long-term smoker. His c- ANCA levels are elevated. Which one of the following is the most likely cause for these features?
explanation:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Cough, haemoptysis and glomerulonephritis are features of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (option E), although Goodpasture’s disease can also present with the same clinical features. However, elevated levels of c- ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) favour the diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Almost all patients with active systemic granulomatosis with polyangiitis have positive ANCA findings, commonly directed against serine protease 3; approximately 80–95% of all ANCA found in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is c-ANCA/anti-serine proteinase 3; while most of the remaining 5–20% are p-ANCA (perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody)-positive, with antibodies directed against myeloperoxidase. The diagnostic accuracy of ANCA testing becomes greater in patients with the classic presentation, in whom c-ANCA has a 98% post-test probability of predicting the diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Goodpasture’s disease
Goodpasture’s disease is incorrect. In Goodpasture’s and microscopic polyangiitis, p-ANCA levels are elevated.

stem: A 65-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency department with progressively worsening renal function. Her GP has tracked an increase in her creatinine from 210 to 385 over the last 3 months, and she has suffered from worsening pitting oedema affecting both legs. Her blood pressure is 155/90, a pulse of 75 and regular. Her chest is clear. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no masses. Complement levels are normal. Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of her presentation?
options: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus
Glomerulonephritis associated with subacute bacterial endocarditis
explanation:
Primary membranous glomerulonephritis
The patient's worsening renal function, increasing creatinine levels, and worsening pitting oedema are indicative of nephrotic syndrome, which is often associated with primary membranous glomerulonephritis. This condition is not typically associated with low complement levels, which fits with the normal complement levels noted in this patient. The presence of significant urinary protein loss can explain the pitting oedema. Other options like shunt nephritis, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, glomerulonephritis associated with subacute bacterial endocarditis, and primary type 1 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis are typically associated with complement abnormalities, which are not present in this case.

Shunt nephritis
Shunt nephritis is associated with infections related to shunt placements and typically involves immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. This condition is often characterised by reduced levels of complement components, particularly C3, due to activation of both the classical and alternative complement Chat pathways. with The

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with haematuria. He has been suffering from an upper respiratory tract infection over the past 2 days, for which he has been taking paracetamol and ibuprofen. There is no past medical history of note. Examination reveals symptoms of the upper respiratory tract infection, a temperature of 37.6°C and a BP of 125/72 mmHg. Abdominal exam is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 102 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine Blood +++ protein + Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
IgA nephropathy
The timing of onset of haematuria, coupled with symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection, preserved renal function and relatively normal blood pressure, fits best with a diagnosis of IgA nephropathy. Symptoms tend to recur with subsequent respiratory tract infections, although long-term renal impairment is relatively uncommon. Non-visible haematuria can be noted between visible episodes. Renal function is more likely to deteriorate in patients who have hypertension and or proteinuria; in these patients both ACE inhibitors and corticosteroids are considered.

Interstitial nephritis
Interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Interstitial nephritis is rare with ibuprofen use. The typical presentation includes fever and skin rash. There may be increased eosinophils in blood and urine. The common culprits include antibiotics such as penicillin and cephalexin, proton-pump inhibitors, rifampicin, allopurinol and phenytoin. The time between exposure to the drug and development of interstitial nephritis may be anywhere from 5 days to 5 months.

Nephrolithiasis
Nephrolithiasis is incorrect. Significant obstruction due to renal stones is associated with pain. Blood and protein may be present in the urine.

Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is incorrect. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is seen much later post infection. It presents with acute glomerulonephritis and is an immune-complex-mediated glomerulonephritis occurring in childhood which is now rare in developed countries. Classically the trigger is a streptococcal sore throat some 10–21 days prior to the nephritis, although streptococcal infection elsewhere may be implicated, such as cardiac valves, cellulitis and so on. Presentation includes gross haematuria, oliguria, oedema, hypertension and pulmonary oedema. Bilateral loin pain or renal angle tenderness due to renal engorgement may be present.

Urinary sepsis
Urinary sepsis is incorrect. There are no other symptoms apart from haematuria to suggest urinary sepsis. Symptoms that would indicate sepsis would be such as fever, chills and dysuria. The biochemistry results also do not suggest sepsis as the white cell count is normal.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred with visible haematuria on two occasions. Prior to the onset of the haematuria each time he had a cold/respiratory tract infection. He also has hypertension, which is currently being monitored by the practice nurse. On the past two visits to the surgery his BP has been 155/92 mmHg, and 149/94 mmHg. On examination in the clinic his BP is 155/95 mmHg; cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination is otherwise normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.7 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 276 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urine blood +++, protein + Urinalysis tract ultrasound normal-sized kidneys, no sign of obstruction Which one of the following is the most useful investigation?
explanation:
Renal biopsy
The presentation of the case is very suspicious of IgA nephropathy with episodes of gross haematuria occurring in temporal proximity to respiratory tract infections. During the intervening period there is usually non-visible haematuria, but of course this goes undetected by the patient renal biopsy is the investigation of choice to confirm the diagnosis. Light microscopy displays extracellular matrix proliferation and mesangial proliferation, immunostaining demonstrates IgA deposits.

Cystoscopy
Cystoscopy is incorrect. A cystoscopy is likely to be normal, visible haematuria associated with a respiratory tract infection is more likely to be related to IgA nephropathy.

Abdominal CT
Abdominal CT is incorrect. Abdominal CT is most useful in evaluating possible underlying malignancy, which isn’t suggested by visible haematuria.

Urine culture
Urine culture is incorrect. Although it is important to exclude infection, UTI, this is not the primary diagnosis.

IVU
IVU is incorrect. The indications for an IVU are urinary lithiasis (stones), nephretic pain or mass, recurrent infections of the superior urinary tract – conditions this patient does not have.

stem: A 73-year-old peritoneal dialysis patient presents with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and cloudy dialysis effluent. She has been on dialysis for 2 years and also has a history of coronary artery disease. Clinically, her abdomen is rigid and distended with absent bowel sounds, blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg and pulse rate is 120/min. Culture of the dialysis fluid reveals a mixed growth of Escherichia coli, Bacteroides spp. and Enterobacter spp. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Diverticulitis/Diverticular perforation
The presence of mixed Gram-negative and/or anaerobic organisms is highly suggestive of secondary peritonitis due to a perforated large bowel or appendicitis. Diverticulitis is the most likely cause of this presentation of the options listed.

Myocardial infarction
Myocardial infarction is incorrect. Ischaemic colitis would be amongst the differential diagnoses but not myocardial infarction.

stem: A 70-year-old man with Type II diabetes is found to have an eGFR of 31 ml/min/1.73m 2. His BP is 180/100 mmHg, he has moderate left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiography and fundoscopy reveals mild hypertensive changes and background diabetic retinopathy. He has had a previous femoral popliteal bypass graft 6 years previously. Urine dipstick is negative and renal ultrasound shows a 9.2 cm left kidney and 7.0 cm right kidney, with reduced cortical thickness. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the renal impairment?
explanation:
Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis
Silent ischaemic nephropathy is common in this population, especially in the presence of atherosclerotic arterial disease elsewhere. Most patients show abnormal cardiac remodelling on echocardiography. The commonly taught wisdom that renal asymmetry is a hallmark frequently does not hold, especially with bilateral disease. CT and magnetic resonance angiography are effective as screening tests for renovascular disease.

Cholesterol emboli syndrome
Cholesterol emboli syndrome is incorrect. Cholesterol emboli are usually associated with livedo reticularis, blue toes and a history of recent vascular intervention.

stem: A 20-year-old woman returns from travelling to South America, including Brazil. She developed an itchy skin reaction and an illness with fever 4 weeks later; she now has nephrotic syndrome. Which one of the following is the most likely pathogen causing this?
explanation:
Schistosoma mansoni
Glomerulonephritis is a common occurrence in chronic Schistosoma mansoni infection in Brazil, especially in patients with hepatosplenic disease. Immunoglobulins, complement components and schistosome antigens are deposited in the mesangial area, and the condition is manifested clinically as proteinuria and/or nephrotic syndrome, sometimes with hypertension.

Hantavirus
Hantavirus is incorrect. Hantavirus (found in Europe, Asia and Africa) usually gives rise to very severe clinical syndrome of haemorrhagic fever and pulmonary-renal syndrome.

Mycobacterium leprae
Mycobacterium leprae is incorrect. Leprosy usually affects the skin and the nerves. Kidney disease may result from amyloidosis, but this is after the infection has been present for some time. This history of a 4-week illness is too acute.

stem: Of the following disorders, which one causes acute renal tubular damage?
explanation:
Myoglobinuria
Acute kidney disease follows muscle trauma or necrosis due to the appearance of myoglobin, which may cause tubular damage or blockage, intense renovascular constriction and local inflammation. It is thought that the combination of these factors leads to tubular damage. Alport syndrome is the second most common inherited cause of kidney disease (polycystic kidney disease being the most common). It is caused by mutations or deletions in any of three genes, but most cases arise from the COL4A5 gene on the X chromosome.

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is incorrect. Sensorineural deafness and kidney disease are the prominent features, not tubular damage.

Berger’s disease
Berger’s disease is incorrect. Berger’s disease (IgA nephropathy) is associated with kidney disease in up to 30% of adult cases. It is a glomerulonephritide rather than tubular disorder. Heavy proteinuria, kidney disease and hypertension indicate a poor prognosis.

stem: A 72-year-old female has been followed up in the renal clinic for several years with chronic kidney disease presumed due to diabetic nephropathy. She is now approaching CKD 5 and she has opted for haemodialysis as her mode of renal replacement therapy when she comes to needing it. What is the best form of access for her to have haemodialysis?
options: Tunnelled, cuffed, dual lumen haemodialysis catheter
explanation:
Arteriovenous fistula
These are formed by establishing a side-to-side anastomosis between an artery and a vein. Vein mapping of the patient’s vascular system using an ultrasound will help guide the optimal site. The high pressure from the artery will arterilise the vein, which will allow for it to tolerate repeated needling when connecting to a dialysis machine, as well as offer good blood flows on dialysis. These take about 6–8 weeks to fully mature. Compared to other forms of access, fistulas have the better patency rates, lower rates of access-related sepsis and confer favourable outcomes on morbidity and mortality.

Peritoneal dialysis catheter
Peritoneal dialysis catheter is incorrect. This is inserted to allow peritoneal dialysis to be performed, but this patient has opted for haemodialysis.

stem: A 40-year-old Asian man underwent kidney transplantation for end-stage renal disease. Now, 2 months after the operation, he has developed fever and features suggestive of bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonia. Blood results show neutropenia and a reduced platelet. Which one of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is the predominant cause of infection in patients within a period of 1–4 months after renal transplantation; it may be associated with interstitial pneumonia. A chest X-ray will show a bilateral interstitial or reticulonodular infiltrate that begins in the periphery of the lower lobes and spreads centrally and peripherally.

Epstein–Barr virus
Epstein–Barr virus is incorrect. It is more commonly associated with malignant lymphoproliferation post renal transplantation because there is severe T-cell immunosuppression, leading to EBV-infected B-cells expanding unchecked. The majority of these tumours (known as post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease [PTLD]) often occur within the first year of transplantation. It presents with fever, weight loss and lymphadenopathy.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with painless neck lymphadenopathy. She has had fevers and night sweats intermittently over the past few weeks, weight loss and generalised malaise. She has abandoned her Friday nights out after work due to abdominal pain after drinking alcohol. On examination, there is neck lymphadenopathy, abdominal distension and peripheral oedema. Blood results reveal a decreased serum albumin concentration, and a 24 h urine collection for protein excretion of 4.5 g over a 24 h period (<0.2 g/24 h). Light microscopy of her renal biopsy shows no significant abnormality. Which one of the following is the most likely cause underlying her renal pathology?
explanation:
Minimal-change disease
Hodgkin’s disease is a possible diagnosis with a history of painless lymphadenopathy, night sweats and pain on drinking alcohol. Minimal-change disease is associated with Hodgkin’s disease in adults and is also the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Other associations include non-steroidal anti- inflammatory agents. Diagnostic work-up includes renal biopsy, which appears normal in minimal-change disease, 24 h urine collection and urinary examination for oval fat bodies (tubular epithelial cells containing cholesterol esters). Minimal-change disease in this case is likely to improve when chemotherapy for Hodgkin’s disease is commenced; otherwise there is usually a response to prednisolone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the clinic with severe peripheral oedema. She has suffered from hypertension for the past 2 years and takes indapamide, but her blood pressure (BP) is still 152/92 mmHg. She is a non-smoker and is otherwise well. Investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 202 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 139 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l 24hr urinary protein 3.4 g Renal biopsy Suggestive ofmembranous nephropathy Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her symptoms?
explanation:
Ramipril
ACE inhibition with an agent such as ramipril, or an ARB if ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, forms the backbone of treatment with respect to both blood pressure control and reduction of proteinuria in membranous glomerulonephritis. Around 30?50% of patients may eventually progress to chronic kidney disease. Although most cases are idiopathic, it may also occur with underlying malignancy, hepatitis B infection, SLE and in response to gold or penicillamine therapy.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the anti-hypertensives of choice, and amlodipine may worsen lower limb oedema.

Cyclophosphamide
Cyclophosphamide is incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is used an immunosuppressive agent in membranous glomerulonephritis but will not improve her symptoms.

Doxazosin
Doxazosin is incorrect. Doxazosin may actually worsen fluid retention in this situation.

High-dose prednisolone
High-dose prednisolone is incorrect. Unfortunately, although membranous glomerulonephritis may improve in response to prednisolone therapy, this is much less likely than with minimal-change disease.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been receiving haemodialysis for 6 years. His PTH is elevated at 26.1 pmol/l (NR 1.2 – 5.8 pmol/l), phosphate 2.13 mmol/l and corrected calcium 2.01 mmol/l. Of the following, which one is most likely to be responsible for his biochemistry?
explanation:
Diminished activity of renal 1-α-hydroxylase
Chronic kidney disease–mineral bone disorder (CKD–MBD) is a major cause of morbidity in CKD. Diminished activity of renal 1-α-hydroxylase leads to failure of converting cholecalciferol to its active metabolite 1,25- dihydroxycholecalciferol. This leads to reduced intestinal absorption of calcium and resultant hypocalcaemia, with secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Hypoalbuminemia
Hypoalbuminemia is incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia is not a feature of CKD–MBD.

Hypophosphataemia
Hypophosphataemia is incorrect. Hyperphosphataemia is a feature of CKD–MBD.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department for the third time with recurrent urinary stones. There appear to be no predisposing factors and he is otherwise well; urine culture is unremarkable. Slightly unusually, these stones turn out to be cystine stones. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Cystinuria
Cystinuria is related to the defective renal tubular reabsorption and jejunal absorption of cystine and the other dibasic amino acids lysine, ornithine and arginine. Inheritance is recessive or incompletely recessive, and some heterozygotes may only have an increased excretion of lysine and cystine. Patients are encouraged to maintain a high fluid intake, at above 3 l per day, including drinking fluids at night. Penicillamine may be used for those patients with recurrent stones who are unable to keep their urinary cystine concentration low. Although jejunal cystine absorption is impaired, some absorption of cystine in peptide form may occur. A less aggressive, non- nephropathic form presents in young adults. In total, cystinuria is responsible for around 1–2% of all urinary calculi.

Cystinosis
Cystinosis is incorrect. This occurs due to lysosomal cystine accumulation, the nephropathic form presenting in the first year of life with failure to thrive. Cystine deposits in the retina and cornea occur, leading to progressive retinal impairment.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has been treated for 6 months for reflux disease by her GP. She also has a history of hypertension, Raynaud syndrome and telangiectasia. Autoimmune screening reveals positive extractable nuclear antibody to SCL-70. Renal function testing reveals a creatinine of 215 μmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her renal dysfunction?
explanation:
Systemic sclerosis
Oesophageal dysmotility, telangiectasia, Raynaud’s phenomenon and renal dysfunction are all features of systemic sclerosis; there is also likely to be calcinosis. Autoimmune testing involves anti-nuclear antibody testing. Rheumatoid factor is positive in 30% and anti-SCL-70 is positive in around 30% of patients; anti-SCL- 70 correlates with a higher risk of interstitial lung disease (pulmonary fibrosis). Treatment centres around symptom relief with the use of proton pump inhibitors to treat reflux disease, oxygen therapy, renal replacement therapy, and lung or kidney transplant if required. There are no proven disease-modifying drugs for this condition. Unfortunately, renal involvement in systemic sclerosis carries a poor prognosis, with rapid worsening of renal function and hypertension that is poorly responsive to therapy. Associated pulmonary fibrosis and hypertension, and cardiac fibrosis make treatment more difficult still.

Lupus
Lupus is incorrect. Anti-SCL-70 is negative in lupus. Lupus is a multisystem disease characterised by autoantibody production and impaired immune complex clearance. It is more common in Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic or Asian women (female-to-male ratio 10 : 1). Typically it presents in youth and about half of patients

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) with rapidly increasing shortness of breath and haemoptysis for the second time within three weeks. He is referred urgently to the medical on-call team. Apart from smoking 20 cigarettes per day and having mild asthma, he has no other significant past medical history. Urinalysis reveals non-visible haematuria and proteinuria. Chest X-ray reveals fluffy pulmonary infiltrates. Haemoglobin is 105 g/l, serum creatinine is 345 μmol/l, serum ANCA is negative. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Antiglomerular base membrane (GBM) disease
The male:female ratio is 6 : 1, and it accounts for 5% of all cases of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The disease is characterised by the triad of glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage and antiglomerular basement membrane (GBM) antibody. Some 80% of patients are HLA-DR2 positive. Acute management may involve treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide or plasma-exchange therapy; in patients with severe kidney disease, haemodialysis may be required.

Bronchopneumonia
Although pneumonia may be associated with acute kidney injury (AKI), this would be less likely in such a young patient with urinary sediment and atypical radiographic changes.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with polydipsia and polyuria, symptoms that started soon after a road traffic collision 6 months ago, during which she was knocked unconcious but was released from hospital after a period of observation. She has also had episodes of flashbacks of the event over the last few months also, and is susptected to have post traumatic stress disorder for which she is currently under investigation for. Her BP is 120/80 mmHg with no postural drop. The daily urine output is 6–8 litres. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Sodium (Na +) 130 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l* Plasma osmolality 268 mosmol/l Urine osmolality 45 mosmol/l 100–900 mosmol/l A water deprivation test is carried out, and stopped when urine osmolality reached 605 mosmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Diuretic phase of acute tubular necrosis
explanation:
Primary polydipsia
Primary or hysterical polydipsia is a psychiatric disturbance that leads to a fall in plasma sodium and osmolality, and a concomitant low urine osmolality in those patients who drink to significant excess. The condition is diferentiated from central diabetes insipidus by carrying out a water deprivation test, and is confirmed if the urine osmolality rises and reaches a normal value after water deprivation.

Central diabetes insipidus
Central diabetes insipidus is incorrect. This causes an increase in plasma osmolality and serum sodium, whereas both are decreased in the present case. Diabetes insipidus is characterised by polydipsia and polyuria with excessively dilute urine; a reduction in intake of fluid does not affect the concentration of urine. Central diabetes insipidus is more common than nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In central cases, there is deficiency in the production of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). This can be differentiated from primary polydipsia using a water depriavation test.

Diuretic phase of acute tubular necrosis
Diuretic phase of acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. During the resolving or diuretic phase of acute tubular necrosis, serum sodium is increased. The tubular function is restored in this resolving stage.

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is incorrect. This causes an increase in plasma osmolality and serum sodium, whereas both are decreased in the present case. Diabetes insipidus is characterised by polydipsia and polyuria with excessively dilute urine; a reduction in intake of fluid does not affect the concentration of urine. Central diabetes insipidus is more common than nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. In nephrogenic cases, the kidneys are insensitive to ADH.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is incorrect. In SIADH, there is low plasma osmolality with inappropriate urine osmolality, which is higher than plasma osmolality. SIADH is the most common cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia in hospitalised patients. The hyponatraemia and hypo-osmolality result from inappropriate, continued secretion of ADH.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends the nephrology clinic for routine monitoring of his chronic kidney disease. He has been attending 4-monthly and the last three blood tests showing his kidney function are presented below: January April August Na (mmol/l) 134 140 141 K (mmol/l) 4.2 4.3 4.1 Urea (mmol/l) 8.9 7.3 9.2 Creatinine (µmol/l) 153 164 155 eGFR (ml/min/1.73m 2) 47 45 46 His albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) is 2 mg/mmol. What stage of chronic kidney disease does he have?
explanation:
CKD G3a A1
NICE have provided classification of CKD using the glomerular filtration rate and the albumin:creatinine ratio. GFR (ml/min per 1.73 m 2)

stem: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease is referred acutely by his GP having been found to have a creatinine of 746 mol/l. He was known to have normal renal function 2 years previously. On examination he has evidence of rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability; he appears to have bilateral small pupils. He has a postural blood pressure (BP) drop from 160/72 mm/Hg when supine to 138/60 mmHg when standing; his pulse rate is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a full bladder. Which one of the following causes of obstructive kidney disease should be considered most likely given the history unless proven otherwise?
explanation:
Neurogenic bladder
Neurogenic bladder is seen in diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, cerebrovascular disease, advanced Parkinson’s disease and spinal injuries. This patient’s clinical autonomic signs are a pointer to his risk of having autonomic bladder dysfunction. If patients with Parkinson’s disease exhibit symptoms of bladder outlet obstruction due to benign prostatic enlargement, the diagnosis should be confirmed by multichannel urodynamic studies. The most common cause of post-prostatectomy incontinence in a patient with Parkinson’s disease is detrusor hyperreflexia. If transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is performed without urodynamic confirmation of obstruction, the patient may become totally incontinent after the procedure.

stem: A 39-year-old woman is diagnosed as having chronic kidney disease. When considering long-term dialysis for this patient, what is the most common complication that may occur as a result of the dialysis itself?
options: Squamous cell cancer of the skin
explanation:
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Long-term haemodialysis is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome; this is due to β-2 microglobulin deposition.

Congestive heart failure
Congestive heart failure is incorrect. High output congestive heart failure due to anaemia is rare nowadays due to erythropoietin therapy. Patients do, however, suffer significant vascular calcification and are at significant risk of ischaemic cardiovascular events, if not cardiac failure.

Gastrointestinal malignancy
Gastrointestinal malignancy is incorrect. There is no known increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancy in patients on long-term dialysis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with pain and frequency of urination. This is her third attack over the course of the year, and she has additionally had one episode of left-sided pyelonephritis. On examination she is pyrexial 38.0 oC, her BP is 110/70 mmHg and she has a pulse of 92/min. Examination reveals left loin and suprapubic tenderness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 208 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CT Abdomen suspicion of staghorn calculi MSU Proteus grown Which one of the following are the calculi most likely to be composed of?
explanation:
Magnesium ammonium phosphate
Proteus produces urease, which leads to the hydrolysis of urea to produce ammonia. This leads to precipitation of organic and inorganic salts, one of which is known as struvite, or magnesium ammonium phosphate. The other necessary environmental change to precipitate stone formation is that the urine becomes excessively alkaline.

Calcium oxalate
Calcium oxalate is incorrect. Calcium oxalate stones are most likely to be seen in patients with short bowel syndrome due to abnormalities in oxalate metabolism.

Calcium phosphate
Calcium phosphate is incorrect. Calcium phosphate stones are associated with high urinary calcium excretion and alkaline urine.

Urate
Urate is incorrect. Urate stones are associated with disordered purine metabolism and high uric acid excretion.

Cysteine
Cystine is incorrect. Cystine stones are associated with cystinuria.

stem: A 62-year-old Kashmiri immigrant presents for review with his interpreter. He is complaining of frequency and dysuria. Haematuria and pyuria are present on urine testing, but a 3-day urine culture reveals no growth. Excretion urography suggests the possibility of cavitating lesions within the left renal papillary area with calcification, and less marked changes affecting the right kidney. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
options: Staphylococcal renal sepsis with abscess formation
explanation:
Tuberculosis of the renal tract
Tuberculosis infection is increasing, particularly in the immigrant population; it should particularly be considered in immigrants from outside the developed world presenting with frequency, dysuria and haematuria. Lesions in the renal cortex result from haematogenous spread during the primary phase of infection, with later spread to the papillae where cavitating lesions are formed and mycobacteria are discharged into the urine. Infection of the ureters and bladder commonly follows later, and may result in stricture formation. Diagnosis of active infection is made via early-morning urine samples. Treatment is as for pulmonary tuberculosis: standard treatment is 2 months’ quadruple therapy followed by a further 4 months’ therapy with isoniazid and rifampicin alone. Monitoring should be via repeated ultrasound scanning, as stricture formation is not uncommon during the healing phase.

stem: Wilms’ tumour is most strongly associated with which one of the following aetiological factors?
options: Deletion on short arm of chromosome 11
explanation:
Deletion on short arm of chromosome 11
There are several syndromes associated with Wilms’ tumour, eg 'AGR' triad (involving aniridia, genitourinary problems and intellectual disability). They are all associated with deletions on the short arm of chromosome 11. Transitional cell carcinomas are associated with smoking, β nephropathy, analgesic nephropathy and schistosomiasis.

Balkan nephropathy
Balkan nephropathy is incorrect. Wilms’ tumour is a disease of childhood, which makes an environmental aetiology less likely than genetic factors.

Cadmium exposure
Cadmium exposure is incorrect. Renal cell carcinoma is associated with cadmium exposure, lead toxicity and smoking.
